p.note: : Nero left no son of his own, nor had he adopted a son who might have been chosen as his successor. Dio Cassius (ap. Xiphilinum), lxiii 29, describes him as ἔσχατος τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ Αἰνείου καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ Αὐγούστου γεγονότων and in lxii 18 mentions a "Sibylline" verse quoted by the angry populace against Nero after the great fire at Rome in his reign: ἔσχατος Αἰνεαδῶν μητροκτόνος ἡγεμονεύσει (imitated in Auson. Caes. vi, Aeneadum generis qui sextus et ultimus heres, polluit et clausit Iulia sacra Nero). Cf. also Eutrop. vii 15, in eo omnis Augusti familia consumpta est: Tac. Ann. xiv 17, (Nero) qui unus superesset e familia summum ad fastigium genita. In Tac. Hist. i 16. Galba says in his speech when adopting Piso: sub Tiberio et Gaio et Claudio unius familiae quasi hereditas fuimus: loco libertatis erit quod eligi coepimus, et finita Iuliorum Claudiorumque domo optimum quemque adoptio inveniet. The house of the Julian Caesars came to an end on the death of the emperor Gaius (Caligula), son of Germanicus. When his successor Claudius took the name "Caesar," it was no longer a family name but an imperial title, as Claudius, son of Drusus, had not been transferred into the Julian gens like his uncle Tiberius and his brother Germanicus. See Bury (Student's Roman Empire c. 15, 1), who points out that the Julian and Claudian families had been so closely connected since the marriage of Augustus and Livia that they were almost regarded as a single house.

: Livia Drusilla, daughter of Livius Drusus Claudianus, was first married to Tiberius Claudius Nero to whom she bore a son Tiberius, afterwards emperor. Octavian became enamoured of her beauty, and in 38 B.C. her husband was forced to surrender her to the triumvir, though she was with child (Drusus) at the time. Suetonius says that Augustus esteemed and loved her faithfully to the end: dilexit et probavit unice ac perseveranter (Aug. 62, 2). She outlived Augustus and died in 29 A.D.
: sc. praedium, an estate about nine miles from Rome at Veii a town in Etruria on the site of the mod. Isola Farnese. ..

: the same story is told by Pliny, N.H. xv 136: Sunt et circa divom Augustum eventa eius digna memoratu; namque Liviae Drusillae quae postea Augusta matrimoni nomen accepit, cum pacta esset illa Caesari, gallinam conspicui candoris sedenti aquila ex alto abiecit in gremium inlaesam, intrepideque miranti accessit miraculum, quoniam tenentem rostro laureum ramum onustum suis bacis; conservari alitem et subolem iussere haruspices ramumque eum seri ac rite custodiri. Quod factum est in villa Caesarum fluvio Tiberi imposita iuxta nonum lapidem Flaminia via, quae ob id vocatur ad Gallinas, mireque silva provenit; ex ea triumphans postea Caesar laurum in manu tenuit coronamque capite gessit ac deinde Caesares cuncti; traditusque mos est ramos quos tenuerunt serendi et durant silvae nominibus suis discretae, fortassis ideo mutatis triumphalibus. This story is regarded by some as the origin of the expression gallinae filius albae (Juv. xiii 141), which others explain by the statement of Columella (viii 2, 7) that white hens are delicate and unprolific.

: Fest., p. 213 Müll., pangere, figere; unde plantae pangi dicuntur, cum in terram demittantur. This verb (connected with πήγνυμι) is sometimes used with the acc. of the place and the abl. of the plant, e.g. Colum. xi 2, 18, vitiaria malleolis pangere; Prop. iii 17, 15, ipse seram vites pangamque ex ordine colles.

: Pliny (l.c.) says that it was the haruspices who ordered this to be done. Dio (xlviii 52) mentions that Livia herself took care of the hen and planted the laurel: τήν τε ὄρνιθα ἐν ἐπιμελείᾳ ἦγε (ἡ Λιουία) καὶ τὴν δάφνην ἐφύτευσε.

: = hodie quoque (hodie etiam, usque adhuc, etiam nunc); cf. Tit. 2, Claud. 19, Tib. 14, 3. This use of hodieque is post-Aug.; first in Velleius, then in Val. Max., Sen., Plin. N.H., and isolated instances in Quint. and Tac. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarbarus, I 597.

: see on Dom. 1, 1, ad Malum Punicum. At Rome one of the side-streets on the Viminal bore the name of "gallinae albae” (Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom I, 3, 374). The interesting ruins at Prima Porta which have been identified with the villa of Livia, and the excavations which have been made there, are described by Burn, Rome and the Campagna, c. xiv; see also J.R.S. xi 145.

div.p: 'illas: a correction by Burman (followed by Wolf, Baumg.-Crus., Roth, Preud'homme) of alias (which is retained by Ihm). Lipsius suggested eas. Pliny states definitely that the Caesars planted the same laurel branches which they had carried in their hands during the triumph.

p.note: : "planted"; cf. Suet. Gramm. 23, vitem manu eius institutam: Cic. Agr. ii 25, 67, iugera trecenta, ubi institui vineae possunt.

: Dio lxiii 29, καθάπερ που σαφῶς καὶ αἱ δάφναι αἱ ὑπὸ τῆς Λιουίας φυτευθεῖσαι τό τε γένος τῶν λευκῶν ὀρνίθων προδιαφθαρέντα αὐτοῦ (Νέρωνος) ἐσήμανεν: Aur. Vict. Caes. 5, 17, Hic finis Caesarum genti fuit; quem fore prodigiorum multa denuntiavere, praecipueque eorum praediis arescens lauri nemus dicatum triumphantibus; atque interitus gallinarum, quae adeo multae albaeque aptiores erant religionibus, ut iis Romae habeatur hodie locus. The withering of laurel trees is mentioned among the omens of the fall of Troy in Quint. Smyrn. xii 517, ἀπαυαίνοντο δὲ δάφναι | πὰρ νηὸν Φοίβοιο, πάρος θαλεραί περ ἐοῦσαι.

: Suetonius is very fond of this use of quidquid c. gen. either of persons or things; e.g. Oth. 10, 2, quidquid epistularum erat: Vitell. 10, 1, quidquid cohortium fuit. See Kühner-Stegmann, Lat. Gramm. I 429.

: this adv. is not ante-Aug.; Livy is the first prose writer to use it. Suetonius has it in its two senses: (a) = mox, statim, as here and in Galb. 10, 4: Vitell. 9: Tit. 5, 2; (b) identidem, saepius (Fr. souvent from subinde), as in Galb. 3, 4; 16, 1. =

: the Templum Divi Augusti on the Palatine, begun by Livia, continued by Tiberius, and completed by Caligula. Since in the course of time all the deified members of the Julio-Claudian house were worshipped there, it was known at the end of the first dynasty as the aedes Caesarum. It was destroyed by fire under Vespasian, and restored by Domitian; there was another restoration of it on a large scale by Antoninus Pius. See Jordan-Huelsen, op. cit. I 3, 80 sq.; Marquardt, Röm. Staatsverwaltung iii² 468; Platner and Ashby, Topogr. Dict. of Ancient Rome 62 sqq.

: the statue represented Augustus in triumphal garb bearing the sceptre and wearing the tunica palmata and the toga picta; an ivory sceptre crowned with an eagle was carried by the triumphator in his left hand, and a laurel branch in his right (Dion. Hal. iii 61; Val. Max. iv 4, 5; Juv. x 43; Mommsen, Röm. Staatsrecht is 425). In Aug. 94, 6 Suetonius describes a vision, which Octavius, father of Augustus, had of the future greatness of his son: sequenti nocte videre visus est filium mortali specie ampliorem, cum fulmine et sceptro exuviisque Iovis Optimi Maximi ac radiata corona, super laureatum currum bis senis equis candore eximio trahentibus.
: cf. Dom. 15, 2 (on the portents of Domitian's death): e basi statuae triumphalis titulus excussus vi procellae.

: Plutarch, Galb. 3, says that Galba was related to Livia, wife of Augustus, and owed to her his consulship. Plutarch may be referring to the fact that Livia Ocellina, stepmother of Galba (see c. 3, 3), and Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus, belonged to the same gens; Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) thinks that Plutarch confused Livia Ocellina with Livia Augusta. For contingere used of family connexions cf. Aug. 4, 1, a matre Magnum Pompeium artissimo contingebat gradu: Ner. 32, 2, ullae familiae quas ipse contingeret: Juv. viii 7, multa contingere virga | fumosos equitum cum dictatore magistros: id. xi 62, contingens sanguine caelum: Liv. xlv 7, quos sanguine ac genere contingebat. ...

: cf. Tac. H. i 49 (of Galba), vetus in familia nobilitas, magnae opes. claritas natalium: Aur. Vict. Caes. 6, 1, Galba haud secus nobilis a gente clarissima Sulpiciorum: Eutrop. vii 16, Servius Galba antiquissimae nobilitatis senator. Galba himself is represented by Tacitus (i 15) as speaking proudly of his descent from the gens Sulpicia on his father's side and the gens Lutatia on his mother's. Juvenal (viii 5) uses the family of Galba as typical of the old noble families of Rome: pictos ostendere vultus | maiorum et stantes in curribus Aemilianos | et Curios iam dimidios umerosque minorem | Corvinum et Galbam auriculis nasoque carentem.

: an archaic word found in Plaut. Curc. 393, Merc. 626. Sallust, who uses it in Iug. 85, 10, homo veteris prosapiae, is said to have borrowed it from Cato's Origines (cf. Nonius p. 94 Lindsay). Cicero uses it apologetically, Tim. 11, et eorum, ut utamur veteri verbo, prosapiam. Quintilian (i 6, 40) mentions it as a specimen of the words "ab ultimis et iam oblitteratis repetita temporibus" which are to be avoided, and later (viii 3, 26) says that the use of it denotes a lack of taste: prosapiam dicere insulsum est. The word has been variously connected with satus, supare (dissipare), the Old Eng. sib "relationship," etc. Walde, Lat. Etym. Wörterb., would connect it with the subst. sopio (see R. Ellis on Catull. 37, 10).

: there is no other mention of these statues of Galba, and in none of the extant inscriptions referring to him is he thus described. A statua triumphalis would be included in the triumphalia ornamenta which were bestowed on him for his victories in Africa and Germany (c. 8, 1), and when he became emperor, numerous statues would be erected in his honour (cf. Vitell. 9).

: Galba's mother, Mummia Achaica, was the granddaughter of Catulus. Galba's pride in this illustrious ancestor is described in Plut. Galb. 3, μέγα δὲ ἔχων εὐγενείας ἀξίωμα τὸν Σερουΐων (i.e. the Servii Sulpicii) οἶκον αὐτὸς ἐφρόνει μεῖζον ἐπὶ τῇ Κάτλου συγγενείᾳ, πρωτεύσαντος ἀνδρὸς ἀρετῇ καὶ δόξῃ τῶν καθ᾽ ἑαυτόν, εἰ καὶ τὸ δύνασθαι μᾶλλον ἑκὼν ἑτέροις παρῆκεν. Catulus, one of the leading optimates, was consul in 78 B.C., and when his colleague Lepidus tried to overthrow the Sullan constitution he defeated him in arms at the Mulvian Bridge in 77. He was one of the iudices who condemned Verres (70). He opposed the Gabinian and Manilian Laws (67, 66). He urged Cicero to include Caesar in the list of Catilinarian conspirators, and in '62 Caesar as praetor tried in vain to deprive him of the commissionership for the restoration of the Capitol (burned in 83), a post which he had held since 78, and from which he got the cognomen "Capitolinus"; his name remained inscribed on the temple till it was again burned under Vitellius (Vitell. 15, 3). Cicero speaks in the most glowing terms of Catulus, who is one of the interlocutors in the Academica (see Reid, Introd. p. 73); he calls him one of the pillars of the state (Brut. 222) and classes him with the ancient worthies of Rome (Verr. ii 3, 210). Catulus alone had the courage to rebuke equally the follies of the mob and of the senate (Sest. 122); he was not only glorious in his life, but fortunate in his death (Att. ii 24, 4). He died in 60 в.с.

: in the atrium of the noble families at Rome were placed the imagines, or waxen masks fitted to busts, kept in small cases (armaria) under which were inscriptions (tituli) of the distinctions of the various ancestors; the imagines were connected by painted lines (lineae) and the imagines and lineae together made up the stemma or genealogical, tree. Cf. Ner. 37, 1, obiectum est Cassio Longino quod in vetere gentili stemmate C. Cassii percussoris Caesaris imagines retinuisset: Plin. N. H. xxxv 6, aliter apud maiores in atriis haec erant quae spectarentur; non .. signa exterorum artificum nec aera aut marmora: expressi cera vultus singulis disponebantur armariis, ut essent imagines quae comitarentur gentilicia funera... stemmata vero lineis discurrebant ad pictas imagines: Sen. Ben. iii 28, 2, qui imagines in atrio exponunt et nomina familiae suae longo ordine ex multis stemmatum illigata flexuris in parte prima aedium collocant: Mart. iv 40, 1, atria Pisonum stabant cum stemmate toto.
: for such genealogical pretensions see on Vesp. 12.

: daughter of Helios and wife of Minos king of Crete; she was a sister of Circe and of Aeetes the father of Medea. Pasiphaë is notorious in legend as the mother of Minotaurus, and Galba must have claimed descent from her merely because she was a daughter of the Sungod. Silius Italicus (Pun. viii 468 sqq.) attributes a similar mythical pedigree to a Galba who commanded the Etruscan contingent at Cannae: Iamque per Etruscos legio completa maniplos | rectorem magno spectabat nomine Galbam. Huic genus orditur Minos, inlusaque tauro | Pasiphae.

: this form, and not the more usual Minois (Roth, Preud 'homme), has the support of M here and in Tib. 70. Priscian (vi 13, 70) notices its use in Sallust (Hist. ii frag. 5 Kritz): Daedalum ex Sicilia profectum, quo Minonis fugerat iram atque opes. Priscian says that similarly the Syracusans used ἥρων, ἥρωνος for ἥρως, ἥρωος, and he also mentions “Athos (Athon), Athonis” in Cicero, Rep. iii.
: see on c. 2 and Vesp. 1, 1.

: the inscriptions (tituli) under the imagines, giving the names, honours, and achievements of each ancestor. elogium (connected by Curtius with ἐλεγεῖον, cf. oliva ἐλαία, lopas λεπάς) is used by Cicero for an epitaph, and for a clause in a will. Suetonius has it in both these senses (Claud. 1,5: vit. Horat. 1); also for an inscription on a votive tablet (Calig. 24, 3), and for an abstract or précis of a criminal case (Calig. 27, 1).
: cf. Dom. 1, 3, n.

: the particular family of the gens Sulpicia which bore the surname of Galba; other family names of the Sulpicii under the Republic were Camerinus, Cornutus, Gallus, Longus, Paterculus, Peticus, Praetextatus, Quirinus, Rufus. "familiae” (sc. imagines et elogia) seems certainly to be the gen., though Dalmasso (p. 54) takes it as dat. The dat. with attingere only occurs a few times (Apul. Apol. 100, C.I.L. ix 5438; see Thesaurus Ling. Lat.). Suetonius uses the verb in twelve other passages, and always with the accusative.

: galbanum (χαλβάνη) was a resinous gum from a Syrian plant; it was used for the purpose of smoking away serpents (Plin. N.H. xii 126; Verg. G. iii 415; Luc. ix 916; Nicand. Ther. 51, βαρύοδμος ἐπὶ φλογὶ ζωγρηθεῖσα | χαλβάνη). 0 .. succenderit... uteretur.. visus sit: Suetonius frequently couples the impf, and perf. subj. in this way, and seems to use these two tenses quite indifferently; e.g. Vitell. 7, 2, ut domum ablocaret, utque unionem pigneraverit: Vesp. 4, 3, ut qui obligaret et descenderit: Iul. 22; 39: Tib. 52: Claud. 4: Ner. 25, etc. See Draeger, Hist. Synt. i 270 sqq.; Roth, praef. p. xxxv; Bagge, p. 94; Dalmasso, p. 84. ..

: galbeus (calbeus) or galbeum was a kind of armlet or bracelet according to the notices in Festus, p. 46 Müll., calbeos armillas dicebant, quibus triumphantes utebantur; p. 96, galbeum ornamenti genus; p. 265 (quoting from Cato's Origines), mulieres opertae auro purpuraque coronas aureas, rusceas fascias, galbeos, lineas, pelles, etc. Suetonius uses it here for a bandage (= fascia, Dom, 17, 1) put round the arm like an armlet, consisting of wool in which were wrapped healing medicines or, at times, amulets; cf. Plin. N.H. xxx 143, stellionis ("newt'') cinerem linamento (‘‘lint’”) involutum in sinistra manu venerem stimulare; xx 155, Xenocrates pulei (“pennyroyal'') ramum lana involutum in tertianis ante accessionem olefactandum dari tradit; Cels. vii 26, 5, inducendus hapsus (i.e. a lock of wool used in bandaging) lanae mollis tepido oleo repletus; id. iv '6, 9, circumdare oportet latus hapso lanae sulphuratae. ..

: this is probably the right derivation of the name Galba (a Celtic word = venter obesus), so many Roman cognomina denoted physical peculiarities. Cf. the Germ. Kalb (calf) used for a fat person. For the numerous words cognate to Kalb, e.g. Sanser. gárbhas (= uterus), Goth. kalbo, see Walde Etym. Wörterb. s.v. galba; the root meaning is "swelling." We find mention of a king of the Suessiones, a Gallic tribe, who bore the name of Galba (Caes. B.G. ii 4, 13), and Galbus is a variant for Chalbus as a name of a Spanish chieftain in Liv. xxiii 26. One of the Sulpicii may have got the nickname when serving abroad. Hofstee compares the cognomen ‘“Arvina" ("fat" "suet'") in the family of the Cornelii Cossi. ..
: Bentley would substitute for this either et obesus or ut vitulus.

: this "galba" is defined by Lewis and Short as "a small worm, the ash-borer, or the larva of the ash-spinner, Bombyx aesculi, Linn."; it does not seem to be mentioned elsewhere. An interesting parallel to this derivation of the name "Galba" would be "Cossus,'' as cossus is used frequently in Pliny for a kind of larva under the bark of trees.

div.p: § 2. familiam illustravit: Suetonius makes no reference to the ancestor who first brought distinction to the family, viz. P. Sulpicius Ser. f. P. n. Galba Maximus, who was elected consul in 211 B.C. without having filled any curule office previously, and was consul again in 204 (Liv. xxv 41, xxvi 1). Other ancestors who held office at Rome were C. Sulpicius Galba, pontifex 201 B.C. (Liv. xxx 39, xxxii 7): Ser. Sulpicius Galba, curule aedile in 188, urban praetor in 187 (Liv. xxxviii 35, etc.): C. Sulpicius Galba, urban praetor in 171 (Liv. xlii 28, 31).

p.note: : he was consul in 144 B.с., his colleague being L. Aurelius Cotta.

: this is Bentley's correction of et, the reading of all MSS. except I which omits the word. Casaubon proposed ditissimus et eloquentissimus, introducing ditissimus from Appian Hisp. 60, where this Galba is called πλουσιώτατος ῾Ρωμαίων, and this suggestion is approved by Burman. Preud'homme keeps et; Ihm marks it as corrupt.

: Cicero describes him as “eloquentissimus’(Brut. 33, 127) and “divinus homo in dicendo” (de or. i 10, 40); cf. also Brut. 21, 82, sine controversia Ser. Galba eloquentia praestitit; et nimirum is princeps ex Latinis illa oratorum propria et quasi legitima opera tractavit, ut egrederetur a proposito ornandi causa, ut delectaret animos, ut permoveret, ut augeret rem, ut miserationibus, ut communibus locis uteretur. Sed nescio quo modo huius, quem constat eloquentia praestitisse, exiliores orationes sunt et redolentes magis antiquitatem quam aut Laelii aut Scipionis, aut etiam ipsius Catonis; itaque exaruerunt, vix iam ut appareant.

: he was praetor in 151, and in 150 was allotted the province of Hispania Ulterior where war was being waged with the Celtiberians. He invaded Lusitania to relieve some Roman subjects there, and routed the Lusitanian forces, but pursuing them incautiously met with a severe reverse and lost 7000 men. On his next invasion of Lusitania the Lusitanians sent an embassy promising to resume the observance of a treaty previously made with Rome. Galba treated them with despicable treachery, pretending to sympathize with their poverty which had led to their revolt, and promising to assign them fertile lands if they assembled in three bodies, together with their women and children, at three specified places. Each of the three bodies when it assembled was ordered to surrender arms and being surrounded by a ditch, to prevent escape, was massacred by Galba's troops. Viriathus was one of the few who managed to escape. In 149 Galba was impeached for this outrage and Cato, aged 85, denounced him in a speech of great vehemence, but by bribery and by appearing as a suppliant along with his children and the orphan child of a relative he succeeded in securing an acquittal. Appian Hisp. 58-60; Cic. de or. i 53, 227; Val. Max. viii 1, 2; 7, 1; Plut. Cat. mai. 15; Nep. Cat. 3; Oros. iv 21.)

: Val. Max. (ix 6, 2) says 7000: septem milia, in quibus flos iuventutis consistebat, electa et armis exuta, partim trucidavit, partim vendidit. Quo facinore maximam cladem barbarorum magnitudine criminis (Galba) antecessit.

: after his escape from the massacre of the Lusitanians by Galba, Viriathus organised a guerilla warfare against the Romans with such success that in 145 and the following years a consul and consular army had to be sent against him. These efforts to subdue him were ineffective, and in 141 he entrapped the Roman army in a pass like the Caudine Forks and forced the proconsul Fabius Servilianus to make peace. Servilius Caepio, who commanded in Further Spain, renewed the war on some pretext in 140, and bribed three envoys of Viriathus to assassinate him. After his death (139 в.с.) the Lusitanians were driven to submit.

: Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was a cousin of Decimus Brutus (Cic. Fam. xi 7) and a friend of Cicero. A letter from him to Cicero is still extant (Fam. x 30) giving an account of the battle at Forum Gallorum 02 in which M. Antonius was defeated during the siege of Mutina in 43 B.C., Galba commanding the legio Martia on the victorious side.

: Galba, urban praetor in 54, was a candidate for the consulship in 49, but was defeated, as being an intimate friend and officer of Caesar, by the party opposed to Caesar; cf. Hirt. Bell. Gall. viii 50, propterea quod insolenter adversarii sui (i.e. of Caesar) gloriarentur L. Lentulum et C. Marcellum consules creatos, qui omnem honorem et dignitatem Caesaris spoliarent, ereptum. Ser. Galbae consulatum, cum is multo plus gratia suffragiisque valuisset, quod sibi coniunctus et familiaritate et necessitudine legationis esset. This defeat, however, could not have been the cause of the bitter estrangement between Galba and Caesar, and we must assume that at a subsequent date Caesar, when dictator, refused Galba's claim to the consulship. For repulsam see on Vesp. 2, 3.

: an instance of Galba's presumption and Caesar's forbearance is given in Val. Max. vi 2, 11, Iam Ser. Galbae temeritatis plena postulatio, qui Divum Iulium consummatis victoriis in foro ius dicentem in hunc modum interpellare sustinuit: “C. Iuli Caesar, pro Cn. Pompeio Magno, quondam genero tuo, in tertio eius consulatu (52 B.C.) pecuniam spopondi, quo nomine nunc appellor. Quid agam? dependam?” Palam atque aperte ei bonorum Pompei venditionem exprobrando ut a tribunali summoveretur meruerat. Sed illud ipsa mansuetudine mitius pectus (i.e. Caesar) aes alienum Pompei ex suo fisco solvi iussit. Cf. Cic. Fam. vi 18.

: in 57 B.C. Caesar sent Galba as legatus to subdue the Nantuates, Veragri, and Seduni; he defeated them and later resisted successfully a strong counter attack which they made on his camp at Octodurus. (Caes. B.G. iii 1-6, Dio Cass. xxxvii 48, xxix 5.)

: Galba's participation in the conspiracy against Caesar is mentioned also by Appian (Bell. Civ. ii 113). Cicero (Phil. xiii 16) threatens M. Antonius that Galba (“fortissimus et constantissimus civis’”) would use on him the same dagger (pugio) as he had used to kill Caesar.

: a law proposed in 43 B.c. by the consul Q. Pedius, interdicting from fire and water all those who had taken part in the murder of Julius Caesar: Vell. Pat. ii 69, 5, lege Pedia, quam consul Pedius, collega Caesaris tulerat, omnibus qui Caesarem patrem interfecerant, aqua ignique damnatis interdictum erat; cf. Monum. Ancyr. i 2, Qui parentem meum [interfecer]un[t, eo]s in exilium expuli iudiciis legitimis ultus eorum [fa]cin[us]. See Mommsen, Röm. Strafrecht 159, 199. Suetonius, Ner. 3, 1, says of Nero's great-grandfather: ‘“inter conscios Caesarianae necis quanquam insons damnatus lege Pedia ... solusque omnium ex iis, qui pari lege damnati erant, restitutus in patriam.'”

div.p: § 3. avus: this C. Sulpicius Galba, the historian, is mentioned as one of the authorities of the elder Pliny (N.H., index in lib. xxxvi). Peter (Hist. Rom. Frag., p. 238) cites two references to his history: Plut. Rom. 17, Ἑάλω δὲ καὶ (cum filia Tarpeia) Ταρπήϊος προδοσίας ὑπὸ ῾Ρωμύλου διωχθείς, ὡς Ιόβας φησὶ Γάλβαν Σουλπίκιον ἱστορεῖν: Oros. v 23, 6, fuisse tunc Pompeio triginta milia peditum, mille equites Galba scribit, Sertorium autem sexaginta milia peditum octo milia equitum habuisse commemorat.

p.note: : cf. Oth. 1, 1, nec praeturae gradum excessit. This use of egredi is found first in Velleius, and often in later writers, e.g. Tac. A. iii 30, vetus familia neque tamen praeturam egressa.

: an adjective used freely in post-Aug. Latin of persons, either absolutely or with the gen., abl., or in (e.g. Aug. 79, 1, in capite comendo incuriosus); its use in a passive sense of things, as here, is found in Tac. A. vi 17, acribus, ut ferme talia, initiis, incurioso fine, and earlier in a frag. of Sall. (H. iv 66, Kritz), infrequentem stationem nostram incuriosamque ab armis (= milites in statione positos, neque arma in promptu habentes).
: in what year is uncertain, but he is probably the "Ser. Sulpicius C. f. Galba" mentioned as consul suffectus in 5 B.C. (C.I.L. i², p. 69).
: see on Tit. 7, 2.

: "hunch-backed"; see on “gibba,” Dom. 23, 2. A witticism of Augustus on Galba's deformity is quoted in Macrob. Sat. ii 4, 8: Galbae, cuius informe gibbo erat corpus, agenti apud se causam et frequenter dicenti: “Corrige, in me si quid reprehendis,” respondit: “Ego te monere possum, corrigere non possum” (“corrigere" meaning "to make straight the crooked"). The schoolmaster Orbilius also jested sarcastically on the same subject; Macrob. ii 6, 4, In eundem Galbam Orbilius grammaticus acerbius inrisit. Prodierat Orbilius in reum testis. Quem Galba, ut confunderet, dissimulata professione eius interrogavit: “Quid artium facis?" Respondit: “In sole gibbos soleo fricare." In Suet. Gramm. 9, 2 (quoted on Dom. 23, 2) the repartee of Orbilius is given in a different form and is directed against A. Terentius Varro Murena, not against Galba. modicae in dicendo facultatis: Macrobius (ii 6, 3) rates his eloquence more highly: In Galbam eloquentia clarum, sed quem habitus corporis destruebat, M. Lollii vox circumferebatur: Ingenium Galbae male habitat.

div.p: § 4. Mummiam Achaicam: she may, as Borghesi says, be a daughter of the Mummius who is mentioned as legatus of M. Crassus in the Servile war against Spartacus in 71 B.с. (Plut. Crass. 10). See Dessau, Prosopographia Imperii Romani ii p. 389. The family of Mummius continued the use of the cognomen ‘‘Achaicus" won by the consul L. Mummius in 146 в.с. for the destruction of Corinth and the conquest of Greece, which was transformed into the Roman province of Achaia.

p.note: : Q. Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus (see on c. 2).

: her father may have been the Lucius Livius Ocella who was honoured with an inscription by two peoples of Hither Spain; C.I.L. vi 246, L. Livio L. f. Ocellae quaestori) Segobrigenses. L. Livio L. f. Ocellae Suessetanei (Dessau, Prosop. ii 290). The meaning of the name "Ocella" is given in Plin. N.H. xi 150, qui altero lumine orbi nascerentur Coclites vocabantur, qui parvis utrisque Ocellae; Luscini iniuriae cognomen habuerunt.
: see on c. 1.
: causal; see on Tit. 5, 1.

: consul in 22 A.D. along with D. C. Sulpicius D. Haterius consules sequuntur). Haterius (Tac. A. iii 52, The same account of his death is given in Tac. A. vi 40, C. Galba consularis et duo Blaesi voluntario exitu cecidere, Galba tristibus Caesaris litteris provinciam sortiri prohibitus. He died in 36 A.D., fourteen years after his consulship.

: i.e. the year in which he became senior ex-consul (consularis). Augustus enforced anew a rule of Pompeius that five years must elapse between the tenure of magistracy and the sortitio provinciae; but a much longer interval usually did elapse in the case of consular provinces owing to the increase in the number of ex-consuls caused by the practice of appointing consules suffecti (see on Dom. 2, 1). The consequent slowness in succession to proconsulships was relieved to some extent by the fact that some consulares were disqualified, or rejected by the emperor or by the senate, or like Agricola declined the sortitio. See Furneaux, Tac. Ann. vol. i², Introd. c. vii; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 251.
: either of Asia or Africa which were reserved for consulares, the other provinces being usually given to praetorii, though both classes of governors are properly styled proconsuls (Furneaux, l.c.).

: this is M. Valerius Corvinus Messala Messalinus, son of M. Valerius Messala Corvinus (cons. 31 B.C.) who was the literary patron of Ovid and Tibullus. The appointment of the son as one of the Quindecimviri sacris faciundis was the occasion of an extant poem of Tibullus (ii 5); cf. also Ov. Pont. i 7, ii 2. For his military achievements as governor of Dalmatia and Pannonia see Dio lv 29 sqq., Vell. Pat. ii 112.

: in the Index to Dio lv the names of the consuls for 3 B.c. are given as Λ. Κορνήλιος Λ. υἱ. Λεντοῦλος, καὶ Μ. Οὐαλέριος Μ. υἱ. Μεσσαλᾶς, ἢ Μεσσαλίνοs (L. Cornelius L. f. Lentulus, et M. Valerius M. f. Messala vel Messalinus); and in Monum. Ancyr. iii 16 the names appear as L. Lentulus and M. Messala. The praenomen “Gnaeus" in our text is probably due to a confusion by Suetonius or the copyists with Cn. Cornelius Cn. f. Lentulus, consul in 14 B.c.; another Cn. Lentulus was consul in 18 в.с.
: Dec. 24, 3 в.с. date of Galba's birth and reconciling see on c. 23. For the difficulty of determining the the conflicting statements of Suetonius

: Terracina (usually "Tarracina Carracina'") is the mod. Terracina in Latium, 62 miles from Rome, at the point where the Appia Via first touches the sea coast. Latin poets preferred to use the Volscian name Anxur as metrically more convenient than Tarrăcina. That Tarracina was the home of the Galbae is confirmed by an inscription found there, C.I.L. i 576, [Ser. Sulpic]ius Ser. f. Galba cos. pavimentum [faciendum locavi]t eisdemque probavit (see Mommsen ad loc.).
: mod. Fondi, in Latium, 12 miles from Tarracina; mentioned by Horace (S. i 5, 34) as the next stopping-place after Anxur (Tarracina) on the journey to Brundusium.

: for this use of the dat. see on Vesp. 1, 3, a Nursia Spoletium euntibus. adoptatus a noverca: she must have adopted him by her will; a similar instance of adoptio in nomen et familiam is mentioned in Cic. Att. vii 8, Dolabellam video Liviae testamento cum duobus coheredibus esse in triente, sed iuberi mutare nomen. Est πολιτικὸν σκέμμα rectumne sit nobili adulescenti mutare nomen mulieris testamento. (Dolabella did not accept the legacy at least he did not change his name; see Tyrrell and Purser ad loc.). Under Roman law no woman could adopt during her life, since she was not the head of a family and did not possess the patria potestas; in 291 A.D. Diocletian and Maximian by a special rescript allowed a woman to adopt her stepson to console her for the loss of her own children (Cod. Iust. xlviii 8 Inst. Iust. i 11, 10). See Roby, Roman Private Law i 59 n.; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 40.

: the stepmother's name was Livia Ocellina (c. 3, 4). The reading Livii (Livi Roth, Preud'homme) is only found in later MSS.; the earlier have Livia (read by Ihm), but this leaves nomen very bare. Heinsius conjectured Livium; Bentley Livianum, which may well be right (-num being lost before nomen).

: i.e. the cognomen “Ocella”; cf. Hor. S. ii 3, 25, Mercuriale cognomen: Ov. Pont. ii 5, 49, surgit Iuleo iuvenis cognomine dignus. The ed. Basil. (1533 A.D.) reads Ocellae; so too Roth. This cognomen of Galba's is not found in inscriptions or on coins.

: the praenomen ‘"Lucius” assumed by Galba on adoption was that of Lucius Livius Ocella, father of Livia Ocellina (c. 3, 4, n.). As a praenomen of Galba it appears on gladiatorial tesseraė (C.I.L. i 770, 771) where the consuls for 33 A.D. are given as L. Sulp. and L. Sull.

: Dessau (Inscr. Lat. Sel. 237 n.) points out that the title which Galba chose as emperor was "Ser. Galba imp. Caesar Augustus," as is shown by the military diplomata issued by him to the veterans of the First legion (Adiutrix); see Dessau 1988, C.I.L. x 770, 771. But in Greek inscriptions in Egypt during his reign we find his adoptive praenomen and nomen still appearing along with the nomen “Sulpicius” and the cognomen ‘“Galba," e.g. in C.I.G. iii 4957 he is styled Λούκιος Λίβιος Σεβαστός (= Augustus) Σουλπίκιος Γάλβα(ς) αὐτοκράτωρ (= imperator); so too on Alexandrian coins, Λουκ. Λιβ. Σουλπ. Γάλβα(ς) Καισ. Σεβ. αὐτ. (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii p. 285). Hofstee suggests that these inscriptions may have been cut and the coins struck before it was known that the emperor had discarded his adoptive names.

: Suetonius differs from Tacitus, Dio, and Josephus in attributing this prophecy to Augustus and not to Tiberius. Tacitus (A. vi 20) says: Non omiserim praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba tum (33 A.D.) consule; quem accitum et diversis sermonibus pertemptatum postremo Graecis verbis in hanc sententiam adlocutus est: "et tu, Galba, quandoque degustabis imperium,” seram ac brevem potentiam significans, scientia Chaldaeorum artis, cuius apiscendae otium apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit. Dio (lvii 19) relates the prediction as made by Tiberius to Galba at the time of his betrothal: οὕτω δ᾽ οὖν τὸ πεπρωμένον ἑκάστῳ τῶν πρώτων καὶ ἐξήταζε καὶ ἠπίστατο ὥστε καὶ τῷ Γάλβα τῷ μετὰ ταῦτα αὐταρχήσαντι ἀπαντήσας, γυναῖκα ἐγγεγυημένῳ, εἰπεῖν ὅτι “καὶ σύ ποτες τῆς ἡγεμονίας γεύσῃ." Josephus (Antiq. xviii 6) cites it as a remark of Tiberius to his intimates when he saw Galba come in to him: Γάλβαν οὖν ποτὲ θεασάμενος ὡς αὐτὸν εἰσιόντα, φησὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιτηδειοτάτους αὐτῷ, ὡς παραγίνοιτο ἀνὴρ τῇ ῾Ῥωμαίων ποτὲ προτιμησόμενος ἡγεμονίᾳ.
: for the imperial receptions (salutationes) see on Vesp. 4, 4.

: this may mean merely that Augustus took hold of his cheek; cf. Ap. Rhod. Arg. iii 128 (where Aphrodite is coaxing her young son Eros), γναθμοῖο κατασχομένη προσέειπε. Most commentators think that there is a reference to the peculiar method of kissing children by placing one's fingers on their lips or on their cheek and then withdrawing the fingers and placing them on one's own lips; cf. Apul. Met. vi 22, Iuppiter prehensa Cupidinis buccula manuque ad os suum relata consaviat: Suet. Aug. 94, 8, quasi Iuppiter eius (pueri) osculum delibatum digitis ad os suum rettulisset: Serv. on Aen. i 260 (oscula libavit natae), Sane multi nolunt ita intellegi, ut summum osculum filiae dederit, id est, non pressum, sed summa labella contingens; sed ita aiunt: tum hilaris Iuppiter vultus natae libavit, id est, contigit, scilicet ut nos solemus cum blandimentis quibusdam sinistram maxillam contingere liberorum et deinde ad os nostrum referre. παρατρώξῃ : = degustabis. παρατρώγειν means "to nibble at the side," "take a bite of" (Aristoph. Ran. 988, Pax 415); used metaph. in Philostrat. 595, παρατρώγειν δικῶν τε καὶ δικαστηρίων. Aristophanes also uses περιτρώγειν (e.g. Vesp. 672, σὺ δὲ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀγαπᾶς τῆς σῆς τοὺς ἀργελόφους περιτρώγων) and ἀποτρώγειν (Ran. 367, τοὺς μισθοὺς τῶν ποιητῶν . . ἀποτρώγει).

: as sed et is used after non modo, non solum, etc., so it is used fairly frequently in Silver and late Lat. with a cumulative or intensive force ("and what is more,” “aye, and") even when non modo, etc., are omitted. See the examples cited by Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 109. Suetonius is fond of this use; e.g. Aug. 31, 3, sacerdotum et numerum et dignitatem, sed et commoda auxit. He several times (as here) begins a sentence or clause with sed et when introducing a further instance or confirmation in development of what he has previously said; cf. Vitell. 14, 3: Vesp. 19, 1: 19, 2: Dom. 13, 1. Cicero uses sed etiam with an ellipse of non solum, e.g. Att. iii 15, 5, hic mihi primum meum consilium defuit, sed etiam ob fuit.

: a very similar utterance is attributed to Caracallus by Capitolinus (Maxim. Iun. c. 4): Nec defuerunt qui cavendum infantem (Maximinum) dicerent Caracallo. Tum ille dixit "longe est ut mihi iste succedat." Dio (lvii 17) conjectures that Tiberius spared Galba because Galba's fate had so ordained it, but adds that Tiberius' own explanation was that Galba would reign only in old age and long after his own death.

div.p: §2. Avo: C. Sulpicius Galba, the historian (c. 3, 3).

p.note: : procurare was a technical term for averting by prayer, sacrifice, etc., the evil effects of portents of all kinds, especially lightning and thunderbolts; cf. Val. Max. i 1, 1, sacrificio ostentorum ac fulgurum denuntiationes procurantur. The ars fulminum, derived by the Romans from the Etruscans and their libri fulgurales, was divided into exploratio, interpretatio, and exoratio (Sen. N.Q. ii 32, 2). procuratio and expiatio are often used as synonyms of exoratio. Part of the procuratio carried out by the fulgurator, or lightning-interpreter, was to encircle the place which had been struck by lightning with a stone curb (puteal) and to make sacrifices of sheep (bidentes; hence bidental = puteal).

: the portent probably occurred in the autumn; the eagle flew to the top of the oak, showing the height to which Galba would attain; the oak was already bearing acorns, which foretold that Galba would only obtain the empire in his old age (he was in his 73rd year when he became emperor).

: a proverbial expression, like our "when pigs fly"; cf. Plin. N.H. viii 173, Observatum mulas non parere. Est in annalibus nostris peperisse saepe, verum prodigii loco habitum: Cic. Div. ii 22, 49, mulae partus prolatus a te: res mirabilis, quia non saepe fit; ii 28, 61, saepius enim mulam peperisse arbitror quam sapientem fuisse: Juv. xiii 64, egregium sanctumque virum si cerno, ... fetae comparo mulae. In Hdt. iii 151 a Babylonian says jeeringly that the Persians would take Babylon “ ἐπεὰν ἡμίονοι τέκωσι” (cf. Hdt. vii 57; Arist. H.A. vi 24; ausc. mirab. 70).
: Dio lxiv 1, ἡμίονός τε ἔτεκεν, ὅπερ αὐτῷ (i.e. Galba) σύμβολον τοῦ κράτους ἔσεσθαι ἐτεθέσπιστο.

: Livy (xxvi 23, xxxvii 3) mentions “mulam peperisse" among "prodigia maioribus hostiis procurata." Walde derives obscaenus from *obs- (ob) and caenum "filth"; it was regularly used in the sense of "inauspicious," cf. Paulus (Fest. p. 201 Müll.), apud antiquos omnes fere obscaena dicta sunt, quae mali ominis habebantur: Cic. dom. 55, 140, obscaenum omen: Verg. Aen. xii 876, obscaenae volucres.

: here c. acc., as in Aug. 83, Vitell. 10, 3; Suetonius is the first to use this constr. (Cic. Cluent. 14, 41 is not an example, see Peterson's note). Suetonius also uses abhorrere a re (Ner. 43, 1: Dom. 9, 1), and employs the verb impersonally in Tib. 62, 3, Calig. 12, 3, abhorret a vero, a veritate.

div.p: § 3. sumpta virili toga: see on Vesp. 2, 2. Dio (lvi 29) says that it was on Jan. 1, 14 A.D. that Galba assumed the toga virilis (ἐς τοὺς ἐφήβους ἐνεγράφη), and that some afterwards regarded it as a remarkable coincidence that Augustus died in this year and that Galba was the first to become emperor after the family of Augustus died out with Nero. See

p.note: : Suetonius here extends to somniare the same construction (predicative pres. part.) as is commonly found with “verba videndi, audiendi, fingendi, etc." (Kühner-Stegmann, i 703). Не varies the constr. in c. 18, 2, somniavit speciem Fortunae querentis. also on Dom. 15, 3, Minervam somniavit excedere negantemque. The same dream of Galba's is narrated in Dio lxiv 1, την τε γὰρ Τύχην ἔδοξεν αὐτῷ λέγειν ὅτι χρόνον ἤδη συχνὸν αὐτῷ παραμένοι καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς αὐτὴν ἐς τὴν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ ἐσδέχοιτο, καὶ δὴ ἐὰν ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰρχθῇ, πρὸς ἕτερόν τινα μεταστήσεται,
: prob. "tired of standing"; for the infin. instead of the abl. ger. cf. Plaut. Epid. 719, ego sum defessus reperire, vos defessi quaerere: Lucr. v 1145, genus humanum defessum vi colere aevom.
: "at once,'' cf. Iul. 68, 2, ocius amoveri; in Cic. ocius has always a comparative sense "more quickly," but the meaning "at once" is common in colloquial Lat. and in poetry.

: the use of quicumque in the sense of quivis, quilibet (cf, Vitell. 14, 1; Vesp. 8, 5) is frequent in Livy (see Riemann, La Langue de Tite-Live 178 sq.) and post-Aug. writers. Cic. and Caes. nearly always use quicumque as a rel. with a verb expressed, except in the abl., e.g. quacumque ratione, quocumque modo; there are only a couple of examples in Cic. of the indefinite use in cases other than the abl. (Madvig, Cic. Fin., Excursus vi p. 834).
: in the sense of expergisci this verb is post-Aug.
: this image is mentioned again in c. 18, 2, in connexion with the omens of Galba's downfall.
: sc. simulacro; cf. Plin. N.H. viii 73, maiora cubitalibus cornua habens: xxii 86, frutex est nunquam cubitali altior.
: in Latium, about 15 miles from Rome on the Via Latina, mod. Frascati and Il Tuscolo; a favourite site for the villas of the wealthy Romans, e.g. Cicero, Julius Caesar, and Tiberius.
: see on Vesp. 24.

: this use of parte without a defining adjective is strange, and Boissevain suggested in <prima > parte (i.e. atrio), comparing Nep. praef. 6, Sen. Bem. iii 28, Val. Max. v 8, 3. Under subsequent emperors we find a golden statue of Fortuna which was kept in the imperial bedchamber and was transferred by each emperor to his successor; cf. Capitol. Anton. Pius 12, cum se gravari videret, Marco Antonino rem publicam commendavit, Fortunamque auream, quae in cubiculo principum poni solebat, transferri ad eum iussit: Capitol. Marc. Anton. Philos. 7: Spartian. Sev. 23. The goddess Fortuna figures on the coins of Galba (Cohen, Méd. Imp. i² pp. 323, 343).

: these all-night vigils (παννυχίδες) for religious purposes were unknown to the primitive worship of the Romans but were introduced along with the Greek and oriental religions of which they were so prominent a feature, and they came to be celebrated in Italy with no less licentiousness than in Greece. The nightly ceremonies which formed part of such rites as those of the Bona Dea, Bacchus, Isis, Ceres, Adonis, and Sabazius often. developed into mere orgies and were the occasion of grave scandals (Cic. Leg. ii 14 sq.). Cf. Vitell. 10, 3.

div.p: § 4. quanquam: see on Tit. 7, 2.

p.note: : settled age" "middle age," ἡ καθεστηκυία ἡλικία: cf. Cic. Sen. 20, 76, ea constans iam aetas, quae media dicitur. exoletum: cf. Claud. 22, aut exoleta revocavit, aut etiam nova instituit: Aug. 86, 2, exoletas et reconditas voces aucupari. Cicero prefers obsoletus. See also on c. 22. The custom mentioned here is not referred to by other writers.

: the ordinary morning salutation was either salve or ave (= χαῖρε); the farewell at the end of day was vale (= ὑγίαινε or ἔρρωσο). The person so addressed replied salve et tu (καὶ σὺ χαῖρε) or vale et tu (καὶ σὺ ὑγίαινε).

: cf. Ner. 52, liberales disciplinas omnes fere puer attigit: Calig. 53, 1, ex disciplinis liberalibus minimum eruditioni, eloquentiae plurimum attendit: Claud. 3, 1, disciplinis liberalibus ab aetate prima non mediocrem operam dedit: Dom. 20, liberalia studia imperii initio neglexit: Aug. 84, 1, eloquentiam studiaque liberalia ab aetate prima et cupide et laboriosissime exercuit. Under liberales disciplinae were included rhetoric, philosophy, music, poetry, jurisprudence, etc.; cf. Cic. de or. iii 32, 127, has artes, quibus liberales doctrinae atque ingenuae continerentur, geometriam, musicam, litterarum cognitionem et poetarum.

: attendere (προσέχειν), when used absolutely (without animum), takes the acc. in class. Lat., but Vitruvius and later writers use it also with the dat. This is the only construction found in Suetonius; cf. Calig. 53, 1 (quoted above), Ner. 56, attendit et extispicio.
: in the general laxity of morals which prevailed at Rome matrimony was regarded as a troublesome business, an onerous duty to be undertaken by loyal citizens in the interest of the state.

: not mentioned by name elsewhere, but she was probably the daughter of Manius Aemilius Lepidus, proconsul of Asia in 26-7 A.D. (Tac. A. iv 56), who excused himself from accepting the proconsulship of Africa in 21 A.D. on the ground that he had to arrange for the marriage of a "nubilis filia” (Tac. A. iii 35). quatenus sibi
: cf. Claud. 26, 2, confirmavit matrimonia male cederent, permansurum se in caelibatu. Widowers, as well as bachelors, were described as “caelibes.”

: condicio (uxoria) was used for a marriage-proposal and the attendant negotiations, an alliance or match, and sometimes (by metonymy) for the person to be married; cf. Iul. 27, 1, Octaviam condicionem ei detulit: Aug. 63, 2, multis ac diu, etiam ex equestri ordine, circumspectis condicionibus, Tiberium privignum suum legit: Cic. Lael. 34, dirimi (amores) tamen interdum contentione vel uxoriae condicionis vel commodi alicuius: Plin. Ep. i 10, inter altissimas condiciones, generum non honoribus principem, sed sapientia, elegit.

: daughter of Germanicus, married first (in 28 A.D.) to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus to whom she bore a son Nero, afterwards emperor; immediately after the death of Domitius in 40 A.D. she was banished by her own brother Caligula (Ner. 6), but was recalled from exile on the accession of Claudius in 41; shortly afterwards she married Crispus Passienus and was believed to have murdered him; later (in 51) she married her uncle, the emperor Claudius, such a union being legalised by a special senatus-consultum. For her death see on Oth. 3,1. Dalmasso takes Agrippinae here as dative of the agent, but it is the gen. after condicione; cf. Claud. 26, 3, nec durare valuit quin de condicionibus continuo tractaret, etiam de Paetinae, quam olim exegerat, deque Lolliae Paulinae, quae C. Caesari nupta fuerat.
: M and G have viduata, which is read by Ihm who follows Becker in inserting quae before viduata. The relative, which in n and Q comes after Domitii, is omitted in the other MSS.
: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus; see on Oth. 2, 1.

: at Rome from ancient times there was a conventus matronarum, apparently a guild of religious origin, of which little is known. Assemblies of matrons are mentioned in Liv. v 25, xxvii 37. Seneca (De Matrimon. ed. Haase iii p. 428) describes how a husband has to listen to his wife's nightlong reproaches: per noctes totas garrulae conquestiones “illa ornatior procedit in publicum, haec honoratur ab omnibus, ego in conventu feminarum misella despicior." The guild had its curia or meeting-place on the Quirinal and perhaps another in Trajan's Forum. It met for certain festivals, also when a bride through her marriage entered the class of consulares feminae. Elagabalus built a senate-house (senaculum) for it on the Quirinal, and this feminine senate decided a number of points of etiquette: “quae quo vestitu incederet, quae cui cederet, etc." (Lamprid. Heliogab. 4). Aurelian seems to have restored its old religious character by assigning the highest position in it to those who had been priestesses (Vopisc. Aurel. 49). See Friedlaender, Sittengeschichte i¹º 282: Daremberg-Saglio, Dict. Antiq. iii 1660. observant.

div.p: § 2. observavit: for observare “to show respect to” (θεραπεύειν) cf. Tib. 70, 1, quem senem adulescens observaverat: Cic. Att. ii 19, Caecilium colimus et observamus diligenter: Verg. G. iv 210, regem The reverence of Galba for Livia Augusta is shown by his coins with her image and the legend Augusta or Diva Augusta (Eckhel, Doctrina numorum veterum, vi pp. 292-3).

p.note: : i.e. Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus; see on c. 1, 1. By the will of Augustus she was adopted into the Julian family and received the title of Augusta: Tac. A. i 8, Livia in familiam Iuliam nomenque Augustum adsumebatur. After this adoption Tacitus always speaks of her as "Augusta” or “Iulia Augusta"; Suetonius has "Iulia Augusta" in Calig. 16, 3, and "Augusta" in Claud. 3, 2, but inaccurately styles her "Livia Augusta'' here and in Oth. 1, 1; Calig. 10, 1; 15, 2; 23, 2.
: according to Plutarch (Galb. 3) he owed to her his consulship (see on c. 2, 1), but this is doubtful, since Livia died in 29 A.D. and Galba was not consul till 33 (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii p. 285).

: this is the only instance in Suetonius of namque occupying the second place, as in Varro ap. Gell. iii 10, is namque numerus, and frequently in Livy and Quintilian; in Cic. and Caes. it always begins the sentence (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 109).
: sc. centena milia, 50,000,000 sesterces, about £425,000. Casaubon regarded this sum as incredibly large, and would read quinquagies, i.e. 5,000,000.

: here used as a subst. denoting a first charge on an estate, what is taken from it before the general distribution of the assets, the adj. being often used in this sense in legal writers, e.g. praecipua dos (Ulp. Dig. xxxiii 4, 2); cf. Sidon. Apoll. Ep. vi 12, illud autem deberi tibi quodam, ut iurisconsulti dicunt, praecipui titulo. In Plin. Ep. v 7 we find praecipere 'to take preferentially and praeceptio “a preferential legacy."
: "legatees"; a word apparently first used here but common in the later legal writers. = 500,000 sesterces and
: i.e. merely marked in figures or symbols and not written fully in words; the difference between HS D HSD = 50,000,000 sesterces is very slight.
: sc. sestertia; 500,000 sesterces.

: this use of revocare in the sense of reducing is remarkable, and no other example is cited; Suetonius elsewhere uses the normal redigere ad or recidere ad. For the aoristic use of the present participle (= cum revocasset) see Appendix I. § 10. b.

: Tiberius suppressed the will of his mother Livia and paid none of the legacies; cf. Dio lix 1, οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνης διαθηκῶν ἀπήλλαξεν. Suetonius (Calig. 16, 3) says that Caligula paid these legacies and those under Tiberius' own will (though it had been set aside) faithfully and without dispute: legata ex testamento Tiberi quanquam. abolito, sed et Iuliae Augustae, quod Tiberius suppresserat, cum fide ac sine calumnia repraesentata persolvit.

: Augustus issued an ordinance determining the conditions and sequence of the magistracies in the cursus honorum. The young Roman, before holding the first of these magistracies, the quaestorship, had to qualify himself by a term in one of the departments of the vigintivirate (decemviri stlitibus iudicandis, quattuorviri viarum curandarum, triumviri capitales, triumviri monetales) and by some brief military experience, generally as tribunus militum; the earliest age for the quaestorship was 25; a year must elapse between this and the next magistracy, the tribuneship of the plebs (or the curule aedileship), and between either of these offices and the praetorship, and a period of two years between the praetorship (minimum age 30 years) and the consulship (minimum age 32). The restriction of attaining a certain age for an office or waiting for a certain period between offices could be removed by the candidate being father of three children (ius trium liberorum) or by special grace of the emperor. See Mommsen, Staatsr. I³ 572 sqq.

: under the Republic the aediles (first appointed in 366 в.с.) were gradually given control of all the games except the Ludi Apollinares and Piscatorii which were in the charge of the praetors. In 22 B.C. Augustus transferred the cura ludorum to the praetors, assigning to them the management of all games and spectacles (Dio liv 2, τοῖς μὲν· στρατηγοῖς τὰς πανηγύρεις πάσας προσέταξεν). We find references to the praetors administering the Ludi Megalenses (Juv. xi 193), Florales (Dio lxxviii 3), the Augustalia (Tac. A. i 15), gladiatorial shows (Dio lv 31), etc.. See Mommsen, op. cit. ii³ 237. comcommissione: the regular word for the opening of the games. mittere (like συμβάλλειν, συνιέναι) meant to bring men together (in a hostile sense), to set them to fight; it was used primarily of pitting or matching gladiators in the arena, and then more widely of starting a contest or games of any kind; cf. Ner. 23, 1, commisit musicum agona: Claud. 21, 1, ludos dedicationis Pompeiani theatri e tribunali posito in orchestra commisit.

: the Floralia or Ludi Florales were a festival first celebrated in 238 B.c., when in consequence of a dearth a temple was dedicated to Flora ad Circum Maximum; it was made an annual festival (Apr. 28-May 3) under the charge of the aediles in 173 B.c., and consisted mainly of theatrical performances, especially by mimi, accompanied by drinking and licentious merrymaking; cf. Cic. Verr. v 14, 36: Val. Max. ii 10, 8: Sen. Ep. 97: Mart. i 35. The games concluded with the coursing of hares and roes in the Circus Maximus (Ov. Fast. v 371). See Warde Fowler, Roman Festivals 92 sqq.

: an elephant on tight ropes was a feature of the spectacles of Nero; cf. Ner. 11, 2, notissimus eques Romanus elephanto supersidens per catadromum decucurrit (a performance more clearly described by Dio, lxi 17, who says that an elephant which had been brought up to the top of the theatre ran down stretched ropes with a rider on its back: ἐλέφας ἀνήχθη ἐς τὴν ἀνωτάτω τοῦ θεάτρου ἁψίδα καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐπὶ σχοινίων κατέδραμεν ἀναβάτην φέρων). Pliny (N.H. viii 3) marvels at such elephants: mirum maxime et adversis quidem funibus subire, sed regredi magis utique pronis; Seneca also mentions them (Ερ. 85, 41): elephantem minimus Aethiops iubet subsidere in genua et ambulare per funem. Numerous references to the rope-walker (funambulus, schoenobates, σχοινοβάτης) are collected by Mayor on Juv. xiv 272.

: as a legatus Augusti pro praetore, probably in 31 or 32 A.D. (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 285). Augustus divided Gallia into four provinces: Narbonensis, Aquitania, Lugdunensis, and Belgica. In 22 B.c. he assigned Narbonensis to the senate, while the others remained under imperial legati. Aquitania was in Southern Gaul, between the Loire and the Pyrenees.
: for the ablative of duration of time see App. I § 3. D. b.
: for the distinction between consules ordinarii and consules suffecti and the period for which the office was held see note on Dom. 2, 1. Galba was consul in 33 A.D.

: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus; see on c. 5, 1: Oth. 2, 1. The praenomen “Lucius" instead of "Gnaeus" is a slip on the part of Suetonius or the copyists. "Lucius" was the praenomen of his father (cons. 16 в.с.). Torrentius corrected L. to Cn.; Ihm suggests as an alternative the deletion of L.
: see Oth. 1, 2; as consul suffectus he succeeded Galba in the consulship on the Kalends of July, 33 A.D.

div.p: § 2. Gaio Caesare: i.e. Caligula, who reigned from 37 to 41. Galba's appointment was made in 39. ८

p.note: : a conjectural restoration by Roth, which is adopted by Preud'homme; in the MSS. there is a lacuna between in locum Caesare and lici (al, licio, licis, liciis, lice). Ihm reads <..... Gaetulici, suggesting legatus Germaniae superioris in locum Gaetu>lici. Madvig, who regarded Roth's method of filling the gap as inadequate, proposed <in administratione exercitus Germanici in locum Gaetulici. Earlier readings are Gartulico (Stephanus, Turnebus) and Gaetulici vice (Heinsius).

: Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus, who inherited the cognomen "Gaetulicus" received by his father Cossus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus for victories over the Gaetuli in Africa in 6 A.D. He was consul in 26 A.D., and afterwards commanded the legions in Upper Germany for ten years, the mildness of his discipline making him immensely popular: mirum amorem adsecutus erat, effusae clementiae, modicus severitate (Tac. A. vi. 30). His daughter was betrothed to Sejanus, and it was generally believed that Tiberius would have had him condemned along with the other connexions of Sejanus at the latter's downfall, had he not feared a revolt of the legions in Germany (Tac. l.c.). Caligula put him to death in 39 A.D., charging him with conspiracy and currying favour with the army (Dio lix 22, Suet. Claud. 9). As an epigrammatist he is mentioned in Mart. i praef.; Plin. Εp. v 3, 5. From the fact that in Suet. Calig. 8 he is cited as an authority on the birthplace of Caligula he is supposed to have written history (see Peter, Hist. Rom. Frag. p. 291).

: the tessera militaris (σύμβολον) had two uses: (1) to make known to the soldiers the password; (2) to circulate any orders of the general as to intended movements, etc.; for this latter use cf. Liv. ix 32 quod postquam consuli nuntiatum est, extemplo tesseram dari iubet, ut prandeat miles firmatisque cibo viribus arma capiat: Liv. vii 35, xxvii 46: Sil. Ital. vii 347, discurrit tessera castris | intentique docent quae sint properanda, monentque | quisque suos: xv 475.

: a reading introduced by Salmasius, the MSS. varying between manus paenulas, manus paenulis, and manu paenulas. The paenula was a sleeveless cloak of frieze or leather drawn on over the head and worn by all classes in bad weather or when travelling; its use by soldiers is mentioned in Ner. 49: Sen. Ben. v 24, 1. In its ordinary form it prevented any free movement of the arms (cf. paenulatus = paenula irretitus, Cic. Mil. 10) and in a couple of the very few representations on monuments of soldiers wearing the paenula (and not the sagum) there are openings for one or both arms. See Baumeister, Denkmäler p. 1836: Marquardt, Privatl.2 564 sqq.: Smith, Dict. Ant. ii³ 308. Disce ...

: a trochaic tetrameter catalectic or trochaic septenarius (IC/II/IC/IC/II/II/IC/C), which was a favourite metre for the soldier's ditties; cf. the very free lines on Caesar's immorality which were shouted by his soldiers in the licence of his Gallic triumph, Iul. 51: “Urbani, servate uxores; moechum calvum adducimus. | Aurum in Gallia effutuisti, hic sumpsisti mutuum"; ib. 49, "Gallias Caesar subegit, Nicomedes Caesarem: | ecce Caesar nunc triumphat qui subegit Gallias, | Nicomedes non triumphat qui subegit Caesarem.”

div.p: § 3. interdixit peti: the infin. for the usual ne c. subj.; the dat. and infin. are found in Sen. Vit. Beat. 18, 3, cum sibi interdixerit habere, interdixit et poscere. (Ter. Phorm. 708 is wrongly cited by L. and S. as an example of interdicere with infin.).

p.note: : among the abuses in the army at this period was the improper granting of furlough, the soldiers being able to purchase from the centurions exemption from duties (vacatio munerum) and leave of absence (see Tac. H. i 46, A. i 17); weak commanders allowed the legions to be depleted by grants of furlough and this at times led to disaster, e.g. the defeat of Paetus by the Parthians in 62 A.D. (legiones promiscis militum commeatibus infirmaverat, Tac. A. xv 9).

: Galba was victorious over the Chatti (see on Dom. 6, 1) in 41 A.D.; Dio lx 8, τούτῳ τῷ ἔτει ὁ Γάλβας ὁ Σουλπίκιος Χάττους ἐκράτησε. His distinguished command of the army in Germany is mentioned in Plut. Galb. 3, λέγεται δὲ καὶ στρατεύματος ἐν Γερμανίᾳ καλῶς ἄρξαι : Tac. H. i 49, dum vigebat aetas, militari laude apud Germanias floruit.

: for Caligula's expedition to Germany in 39 A.D. see on Vesp. 2, 3. On that campaign the emperor posed as a stern disciplinarian; cf. Calig. 44, 1, postquam castra attigit, ut se acrem et severum ducem ostenderet, legatos, qui auxilia serius ex diversis locis adduxerant, cum ignominia dimisit. At in exercitu recensendo, plerisque centurionum maturis iam, et nonnullis ante paucissimos, quam consummaturi essent, dies, primos pilos ademit, causatus senium cuiusque et imbecillitatem: ceterorum increpita cupiditate, commoda emeritae militiae ad sex milium summam recidit. ..

: Calig. 43, legionibus et auxiliis undique excitis, dilectibus ubique acerbissime actis, contracto et omnis generis commeatu, quanto numquam antea, iter ingressus est. Dio (lix 22) gives the number as 200,000 or 250,000.

: decursus and decursio were terms applied sometimes to a defile of soldiers under arms on ceremonial occasions (funerals, etc.), sometimes, as here, to manoeuvres designed to accustom the soldiers to carry out rapidly long marches in full armour and to keep their ranks. Vegetius (de arte mil. i 9) says that recruits were trained to cover in five summer hours (almost 6t of our hours) at an ordinary marching pace (militari gradu) a distance of 20 milia passuum, and in the same time at an accelerated pace (pleno gradu, qui citatior est) 24 milia passuum. Scipio Africanus made his troops execute on every fourth day a decursio of 4 milia passuum (Liv. xxvi 51); cf. also Liv. xxiii 35, xxiv 48, xl 6, 47, xlii 52; Tac. A. ii 55). Vegetius calls such manoeuvres campicursio, See Daremberg-Saglio, which is the same as campestris decursio here. ii p. 41.

: Galba controlled the manoeuvres, marching in front and bearing the heavy scutum with which he directed the various movements; cf. Ner. 7, 2, where Nero at the beginning of his public career personally headed the praetorians at a special command display of manoeuvres: indicta decursione praetorianis scutum sua manu praetulit.
: even after the fatiguing decursio he had energy enough leït to run for such a long distance by the emperor's chariot.

: Caligula also made senators in their togas run by his chariot; Calig. 27, nihilo reverentior leniorve erga senatum: quosdam summis honoribus functos ad essedum sibi currere togatos per aliquot passuum milia .. passus est. In 297 A.D. Diocletian treated in the same humiliating way his son-in-law Galerius, in anger at his defeat by the Persians; Amm. Marc. xiv 11: Eutrop. ix 15, Galerius pulsus (a Persis) et ad Diocletianum profectus, cum ei in itinere occurrisset, tanta insolentia a Diocletiano fertur exceptus, ut per aliquot passuum milia purpuratus tradatur ad vehiculum cucurrisse. It is mentioned as an indignity inflicted by Eastern kings in Plut. Lucull. 21.
: 20 Roman miles, the Roman mile being 1618 yds., or about 1 of an English mile; the passus was 4 ft. 101 in.

: on Jan. 24, 41 A.D. the emperor Gaius (Caligula) was assassinated by Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus, tribunes of the praetorian guards, in the vaulted corridor through which he was passing from the Palace to see the Ludi Palatini (Calig. 58).
: sc. capiendi imperii. Becker proposed ad occasionem <captandam >.

: = comites (Vesp. 4, 4, n.), the companions of the emperor on a journey or campaign. Horace (Ep. i 3, 6, 8, 14) uses cohors for the suite of Tiberius who was sent by Augustus to the East in 20 B.c., also (Sat. i 7, 23) for the staff of a commander or provincial governor (cf. cohors praetoria, Cic. Verr. ii 1, 14). The poet Lucan was admitted to Nero's cohors amicorum (Suet. vit. Lucani). Domitius, father of Nero, was expelled by Caligula from his cohors amicorum for an outrage committed by him when a comes of Caligula on a journey to the East (Ner. 5). At one of his pageants Caligula was attended by his cohors amicorum driving in Gallic chariots (Calig. 19). The amici of the emperor were those admitted to his receptions (salutationes, see on Vesp. 4, 4); from them were chosen his judicial and administrative advisers (consilium) as well as his comites. See also on Tit. 7, 2.
: dignatio (ἀξίωσις, ἀξίωμα) is used by Suetonius either passively (as here, Dom. 2, 1 Vesp. 4, 3) or actively (Calig. 24, 3, reliquas sorores nec cupiditate tanta, nec dignatione dilexit).
: see on Oth. 5, 2.
: see on Vesp. 4, 1. The words of Suetonius imply that Galba took part in the expedition, though there is no other evidence of it.

: his successful administration of Africa is mentioned in Plut. Galb. 3, λέγεται καὶ Λιβύης ἀνθύπατος (proconsul) γενόμενος σὺν ὀλίγοις ἐπαινεθῆναι: cf. Tac. H. i 49, pro consule Africam moderate, iam senior citeriorem Hispaniam pari iustitia continuit. Vespasian and Vitellius also were proconsuls of Africa (Vesp. 4, 3; Vitell. 5).

: 45 and 46 A.D.; the normal tenure of the governorship of senatorial provinces was for one year. Julius Caesar had fixed the period in consular provinces as two years, in praetorian provinces as one (Cic. Phil. i 8, 19). Augustus restored the period of one year (Suet. Aug. 47, Dio liii 13, Tac. A. iii 58), but a special appointment like that of Galba might be renewed for the following year (see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 250 n., 254 sq.). Dio (lx 25) mentions that Claudius allowed some of the proconsuls to govern for two years: ἐπὶ δύο ἔτη τινὰς ἐῶν αὐτῶν ἄρχειν, αἱρετούς τε ἔστιν οὓς πέμπων (αἱρετοí means extra sortem electi, opp. to κληρωτοί). For the tenure of governorships in imperial provinces see on c. 9, 1.

: the provinces of Africa and Asia were usually assigned by lot to the senior consulares; see on c. 3, 4. Galba was specially appointed to Africa by Claudius, just as the younger Pliny was specially chosen by Trajan for the administration of Bithynia in 111 A.D. Tiberius on an earlier occasion had nominated a proconsul for Africa on the outbreak of war with Tacfarinas in 21 A.D.; Tac. A. iii 35, Tiberius.. Manium Lepidum et Iunium Blaesum nominavit, ex quis pro consule Africae legeretur; Blaesus was appointed by the senate and continued in office for a second year (ib. 58).

: ordinare = turbatum ordinem restituere; cf. Iul. 40, 1, ad ordinandum rei publicae statum: Aug. 13, 3, cum Antonius Orientem ordinandum recepisset: Flor. ii 16: Plin. Ep. viii 24. See also on Vesp. 23, 2.
: such conflicts as that described by Tacitus (H. iv 50) between Oea (Tripoli) and Leptis in 70 A.D. See Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp. (trans. Dickson) ii 316.

: the Mussulamii, who earlier had carried on warfare for eight years (17-24), were again defeated in the reign of Claudius; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 4, caesa Mussulamiorum manus. Other tribes which constantly menaced the peace of the Roman province of Africa were the Garamantes and Gaetuli (genus insuperabile bello, Verg. A. iv 40). Augustus stationed a legion in Africa, and it was the only senatorial province with an army. Caligula changed this by putting Numidia and the Roman legion under an imperial legatus and confining the proconsul's power to the civil administration of Africa Vetus. If Claudius adhered to this arrangement, Galba when sent as proconsul to Africa must have been specially empowered to take command of the army.

div.p: § 2. artissima annona: for arta annona (arta “tight" in the sense of "scarce'") cf. Tib. 8, cura annonae, quae artior inciderat: Claud. 18, 2, artiore annona ob assiduas sterilitates: Liv. xxvi 20; so arti commeatus, Liv. ii 34: Tac. H. iv 26.

p.note: : the modius ( of a medimnus) was nearly our “peck” (1 of a bushel); the denarius was worth about 9d. Similar avariciousness on the part of starving soldiers is described in Luc. iv 93 sqq. (where Caesar's army surrounded by floods near Ilerda in Spain was suffering from famine): iamque comes semper magnorum prima malorum | saeva fames aderat: nulloque obsessus ab hoste | miles eget; toto censu non prodigus emit | exiguam Cererem. Pro lucri pallida tabes! | non deest prolato ieiunus venditor auro. A famous example of the same thing was the sale of a mouse for 200 denarii during the siege of Casilinum (near Capua) by Hannibal in 215 в.с.; Plin. N.H. viii 222, venisse murem ducentis denariis, Casilinum obsidente Hannibale, eumque qui vendiderat fame interiisse, emptorem vixisse annales tradunt (cf. Val. Max. vii 6, 3; Frontin. Strateg. iv 5, 20; Strab. v 248).
: cf. the iambic senarius quoted by Cicero (Tusc. iii 12): Refugere oculi, corpus macie extabuit.
: see on Vesp. 5, 5.
: see on c. 9, 2, conventum agens.
: this seems to be the earliest instance of the use of proprietas in the sense of ownership" (dominium). In Cic. it means "id quod proprium alicuius rei est," a peculiar property or special quality.

: adaquare (ποτίζειν) is a post-Aug. verb, used of watering plants in Plin. N.H. xvii 63, etc. A deponent adaquari "to fetch water" is given by the MSS. in Caes. B.C. i 66, but the reading is very doubtful, as in six other passages in that work (and in Sall., Liv., etc.) the simple aquari is the form used of soldiers getting water.
: see on Vesp. 4, 2.

: Vitellius was honoured in the same way, Vitell. 5, non solum honoribus verum et sacerdotiis amplissimis auctus; Vespasian received a duplex sacerdotium in addition to the ornamenta triumphalia for his services in Britain (Vesp. 4, 2).

: the care of the Sibylline books was originally entrusted to duumviri under the kings; in 367 B.C. the number of priests was increased to 10, five patrician and five plebeian, later to 15 (quindecimviri sacris faciundis) probably by Sulla; in addition to consulting the Sibylline books as directed by the senate, they also had charge of the games of Apollo (Liv. x 8) and the Secular games (Hor. C.S. 70, Tac. A. xi 11), and as priests of Apollo each of them kept in his house a bronze tripod dedicated to the god (Val. Fl. Arg. i 6). sodales Titios: the origin of this ancient confraternity is obscure. Tacitus (H. ii 95) says that Romulus founded it in honour of the Sabine king Titus Tatius: Augustales, quod sacerdotium, ut Romulus Tatio regi, ita Caesar Tiberius Iuliae genti sacravit. In A. i 54 Tac. gives another version: idem annus (14 A.D.) novas caerimonias accepit addito sodalium Augustalium sacerdotio, ut quondam Titus Tatius retinendis Sabinorum sacris sodales Titios instituit. The view that Tatius founded this priesthood at Rome to preserve his native Sabine rites is supported by Varr. L.L. v 85, sodales Titii dicti ab Titiis avibus, quas in auguriis certis observare solent, the priests preserving the ancient Sabine auguries, as distinct from those of other Italian peoples, when the Sabines as the Tities or Titienses were united with the other two tribes, the Ramnes and Luceres, under Romulus. Augustus revived this priesthood and invested it with great dignity; in the Monum. Ancyr. (i 7) he mentions that he was ἑταῖρος Τίτιος. Nero Caesar (son of Germanicus) and the emperor Claudius were among the sodales Titii. See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 446 sq.; Daremberg-Saglio, v 347.

: often used by Suetonius merely in the sense of et or etiam, and in enumerations he has it alternating with et, e.g. Iul. 43, 1, lecticarum usum item conchyliatae vestis et margaritarum ademit: Aug. 4, 1, superstitibus liberis Octavia maiore et Octavia minore item Augusto.

: a sacerdotium instituted by Tiberius for the worship of Augustus and the Gens Iulia; see Tac. A. i 54, H. ii 95 (quoted above). Originally there were 21 members “e primoribus civitatis" and Tiberius, Drusus, Claudius, and Germanicus were added ‘“supra numerum” as honorary members; afterwards the number rose to 28. When the cultus of Claudius (after his deification) was added, they are called at times sodales Augustales Claudiales. For similar priesthoods in honour of other emperors see note on “collegium Flavialium,” Dom. 4, 4.

: the great priestly bodies, such as the Augures and Pontifices, at first filled vacancies in their number by cooptatio, but by the Lex Domitia (103 в.с.) the comitia sacerdotum (17 out of the 35 tribes, chosen by lot) were given the election from a list of nominees supplied by the colleges; the candidates elected were then coopted by the colleges, this cooptatio, though now a mere formality, being necessary to complete the election. From the time of Tiberius these elections, like those of magistrates, were transferred to the senate. In 29 B.C. Augustus was given the right of choosing as many priests as he pleased even beyond the statutory number. As a member of the various colleges the emperor had the right of nominatio, and also exercised the right of commendatio which was tantamount to appointment, the candidate recommended by the emperor being elected by the senate and then coopted by the priestly bodies, e.g. Pliny was recommended by Trajan for the augurship (Plin. Εp. iv 8).

: Vespasian passed a like period of retirement, through fear of Agrippina, between his consulship (51 A.D.) and proconsulship (63 A.D.); Vesp. 4, 2, medium tempus ad proconsulatum usque in otio secessuque egit. =
: ne gestationis quidem causâ; for the passive use of gestandum see on Dom. 11, 1, and for the gestatio see on Vesp. 21.

p.mentioned: umquam iter ingressus, quam ut efferret
p.note: : it is perhaps possible with Hofstee to defend the ellipse of aliter here by the ellipse of aliud in Claud. 10, commilitones fluctuantes nec quicquam adhuc quam frementes. Torrentius inserted aliter before iter, where it would easily have fallen out; Casaubon would read aliter ingressus (omitting iter), and Lipsius suggested aliter egressus (sc. domo).
: sc. centena milia, 1,000,000 sesterces, about £8,500.
: for this use of in cf. Tib. 49, 2, quod partem rei familiaris in pecunia haberent. In case of sudden flight Galba had provided himself with 10,000 aurei (aureus = 100 sestertii, see on c. 20, 2).

: see on c. 4, 1. Hispania Tarraconensis: under Augustus Spain was formed into three provinces, Hispania Ulterior being divided into the two provinces of Baetica and Lusitania, and Hispania Citerior receiving the name of Tarraconensis from Tarraco (mod. Tarragona), which was made the capital instead of New Carthage. Baetica was a senatorial province, Lusitania and Tarraconensis imperial provinces.

: Plutarch (Galb. 3) says that Nero anticipated no danger to himself in appointing Galba to Spain: ἐπέμφθη δὲ ὑπὸ Νέρωνος Ιβηρίας ἄρχων, οὔπω δεδιδαγμένου φοβεῖσθαι τοὺς ἐν ἀξιώμασι μεγάλους τῶν πολιτῶν. ἐκείνῳ δὲ καὶ φύσει δοκοῦντι πράῳ γεγονέναι προσετίθει πίστιν εὐλαβείας τὸ γῆρας. Galba was 65 years old when he received this appointment in 60 A.D.

div.p: § 2. rerum mutationem: cf. Dom. 16, 1, n.

p.note: : Nero died in his 32nd year, and Galba succeeded him in his 73rd. Dio (lxiv 1) mentions the same prodigy and gives the same interpretation: παῖς λιβανωτὸν αὐτῷ θύοντι προσφέρων πολιὰς ἐξαίφνης ἔφυσεν, καὶ οἱ μάντεις τὴν τοῦ νεωτέρου ἀρχὴν πρὸς τὸ γῆρας αὐτοῦ μεταστήσεσθαι ἔφησαν.
: Bentley suspected the genuineness of these words; see on Vesp. 11, Dom. 17, 1.
: a mountainous district about midway on the N. coast of Spain, forming part of the province of Tarraconensis.
: Torrentius conjectured lucum; so, too, Bentley. .

: the duodecim lictores cum fascibus were among the regia insignia marking the imperium of the old Roman kings; cf. Cic. Rep. ii 17, 31, Liv. i 8, Dion. Hal. ii 29, iii 61, 62. In later days these 12 lictors, bearing rods and axes, were granted to the consuls and proconsuls, Augustus limiting the privilege to those proconsuls who as ex-consuls governed the provinces of Asia and Africa (Mommsen, Staatsr. i 382, ii³ 5). For the lictors who attended on the emperors themselves see on Dom. 14, 3.

: 60-68 A.D. The tenure of office by a legatus in an imperial province depended on the emperor's pleasure (Dio liii 13, Tac. A. i 80); Tiberius kept Sabinus as governor of Moesia for 24 yrs. and Silius as governor of Upper Germany for 7 yrs. (Tac. A. vi 39, iv 18); Otho was legatus in Lusitania for 10 yrs. (Suet. Oth. 3, 2). See Mommsen Staatsr. ii 259, Greenidge, Roman Public Life 434.

: Tacitus (H. i 49) praises Galba's administration: pro consule Africam moderate, iam senior citeriorem Hispaniam pari iustitia continuit. Plutarch (Galb. 4) says that Nero's unscrupulous “receivers” (ἐπίτροποι, procuratores) harassed the provincials in the most cruel manner; Galba could not assist them against the persecutors, but his concern for their misfortunes, a concern as great as if he had been a sufferer himself, afforded them some consolation even while they were condemned and sold as slaves. Lampooning verses were written against Nero and sung everywhere; and as Galba did not try to suppress them and did not share the resentment of the receivers of the revenue, this endeared him still more to the natives.
: cf. the remark of Paetus Thrasea on Roman provincial administration, Tac. A. xv 21, initia magistratuum nostrorum meliora ferme, finis inclinat.

: a post-Aug. word for mensarius, argentarius, a money-changer or money-broker; cf. Petron. Satyr. 56, Mart. xii 57, 18; the nummularius also conducted auctions and did banking business, e.g. receiving deposits; cf. Ulp. Dig. xvi 3, 7, quotiens foro cedunt ("become bankrupt'") nummularii, solet primo loco ratio haberi depositariorum, hoc est eorum qui depositas pecunias habuerunt, non quas faenore apud nummularios vel cum nummulariis vel per ipsos exercebant.
: cf. Iul. 74, 2, quamvis omnia ex fide rettulissent; this use of ex fide in the sense of cum fide is found in writers from Tacitus onwards.

: “handling'" "dealing with" = tractanti; cf. Cic. Div. in Caecil. 10, pecuniam publicam tu tractabas. Torrentius explains versanti as contrectanti et exploranti, thus limiting it to the actual handling and testing of the coins exchanged, such as is referred to in Aug. 4, 2; Apul. Met. x 9, ne forte aliquis istorum quos offers aureorum nequam vel adulter repperiatur nummulario praesente comprobentur. Casaubon would omit pecunias or read in pecuniis.

: cf. Dom. 10, 5. Claudius on one occasion had this punishment inflicted in court; Claud. 15, 2, proclamante quodam praecidendas falsario (“a forger," cf. Tit. 3, 2) manus, carnificem statim acciri cum machaera mensaque lanonia flagitavit.

: substituere heredem (alicui) was a lega! phrase for a testator naming a person as secundus heres in the event of the primus heres refusing to accept the inheritance or dying before reaching puberty; similarly a tertius heres could be named to succeed the secundus in a like event: cf. Dig. xxviii 6, 1, Heredes aut instituti dicuntur aut substituti: instituti primo gradu, substituti secundo vel tertio. Heredis substitutio duplex est aut simplex, veluti: “Lucius Titius heres esto: si mihi Lucius Titius heres non erit, tunc Seius heres mihi esto: si heres non erit, sive erit et intra pubertatem decesserit, tunc Gaius Seius heres mihi esto." Cf. Tib. 76, heredes aequis partibus reliquit Gaium et Tiberium, substituitque invicem (i.e. should either die, the other was to succeed): Quint. vii 6, 9, substitutus heres erat, si postumus ante tutelae annos decessisset. To appoint the tutor of the primus heres as secundus heres showed an implicit confidence on the part of the testator; Cicero enjoyed such confidence, as he tells us in Fam. xiii '61: T. Pinnio familiarissime me usum esse scire te arbitror: quod quidem ille testamento declaravit, qui me cum tutorem tum etiam secundum heredem instituit.

: Cic. Verr. i 9, cum cives Romanos morte, cruciatu, cruce adfecerit; so adficere exilio, verberibus, etc. More usual expressions for crucifying are cruci figere (and compounds); cf. Dom. 10, 1, n. imploranti leges: the laws invoked by Cicero in his passionate denunciation of Verres for scourging and crucifying Gavius, a Roman citizen, at Messana, Verr. v 63, O nomen dulce libertatis! O ius eximium nostrae civitatis! O lex Porcia legesque Semproniae! The lex Porcia (с. 197 в.с.) exacted penalties for scourging or killing a Roman citizen (Liv. x 9); the lex Sempronia of Gaius Sempronius Gracchus (123 в.с.) confirmed and widened the right of appeal (provocatio) for the condemned man to the people (Cic. Rab. 12). Under the provisions of the lex Iulia de vi (46 B.с.) Galba's victim was entitled to appeal to the emperor against the sentence of the legatus; Paul. Sent. v 26, 1, lege Iulia de vi publica damnatur qui aliqua potestate praeditus civem Romanum antea ad populum, nunc ad imperatorem appellantem necarit necarive iusserit torserit verberaverit condemnaverit inve publica vincula duci iusserit. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 269.

: cf. Cic. Verr. v 62, nulla vox alia illius miseri inter dolorem crepitumque plagarum audiebatur nisi haec: “civis Romanus sum." Asinius Pollio (Cic. Fam. x 32), describing how his quaestor Balbus burned Fadius alive, says: et illi misero quiritanti ('crying out'"): “civis Romanus natus sum,” responderet “Abi nunc, populi fidem implora." St. Paul used the plea of Roman citizenship to escape scourging (Acts 22, 25). •

: Galba's response to the privilege claimed by a Roman citizen was as contemptuous as that of Verres who ordered the cross of Gavius to be set up facing the Straits of Messina, "ut ille quoniam se civem Romanum esse diceret, ex cruce Italiam cernere ac domum suam prospicere posset." multo praeter ceteras altiorem: for the pleonasm cf. Vitell. 13, 1, famosissima super ceteras: Dom. 12, 2, praeter ceteros acerbissime. Bentley needlessly conjectured prae ceteris here.
