: cf. Tac. H. i 49 (of Galba), sed claritas natalium et metus temporum obtentui, ut quod segnitia erat sapientia vocaretur: Tac. Agr. 6 (of Agricola), mox inter quaesturam ac tribunatum plebis atque ipsum etiam tribunatus annum quiete et otio transiit, gnarus sub Nerone temporum, quibus inertia pro sapientia fuit: Tac. Ann. xiv 47 (of Memmius Regulus in Nero's reign), vixit . quiete defensus: Plin. Ep. viii 14, at nos iuvenes fuimus quidem in castris, sed cum suspecta virtus, inertia in pretio.

: sc. invidiae; cf. Cic. Phil. xi 9, 21, ut aut suspicioni crimen aut invidiae materiam dedisse videamur: Liv. iii 46, non praebiturum se illi eo die materiam (seditionis): Suet. Aug. 16, 2, praebitam materiam exprobrandi: Claud. 4, 2, praebenda materia deridendi et illum et nos non est hominibus.

: referring to the famous maxim of Cato the censor cited by Cicero, Planc. 27, 66, M. Catonis illud, quod in principio scripsit Originum suarum, semper magnificum et praeclarum putavi, clarorum virorum atque magnorum non minus otii quam negotii rationem exstare oportere; cf. Colum. ii 22, tam otii quam negotii rationem reddere oportere maiores nostri censuerunt: Justin (Hist. Philip. praef.), ut otii mei, cuius et Cato reddendam putat, apud te ratio constaret.

div.p: § 2. Carthagine nova: mod. Cartagena in Hispania Tarraconensis at the S.E. extremity; founded by Hasdrubal in 242 B.c.; captured by Scipio in 210; a Roman colony under the Empire with the title of Colonia Victrix Iulia Nova Carthago.

p.note: : for judicial purposes the province was divided into districts called conventus iuridici, the courts being held in the chief town of each district; "agere conventum" was the phrase for "to hold the assizes" and the circuit judge was said “circumire conventus" (e.g. Iul. 7, 1, cum iure dicundo conventus circumiret). Pliny (N. H. iii 18) enumerates the 7 conventus of Tarraconensis as those of Carthago Nova, Tarraco, Caesaraugusta, Clunia, Lucus Augusti, Bracara Augusta, Asturica Augusta; these contained 472 towns and villages.

: C. Julius Vindex, a descendant of a royal Celtic family and governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, revolted against Nero in 68 A.D. As Lugdunum would take no part, Vienna on the Rhone was made the centre of the rebellion. Some of the Gallic tribes, such as the Arverni, Aedui, and Sequani, joined Vindex; but others, such as the Lingones, Treviri, and generally all that "pars Galliarum quae Rhenum accolit” (Tac. H. i 51) refused their aid. The revolt was crushed by the army from Germany which remained loyal in spite of the solicitations of Vindex; see on c. 11, 1.
: see on c. 6, 1; its legatus would have no army under his control. Tacitus (H. i 76) mentions Julius Cordus as governor of Aquitania at the beginning of 69 A.D.

: Plutarch (Galb. 4) says that before the rebellion broke out Galba had intimations of it in letters from Vindex; but he neither countenanced it nor disclosed it to Nero as the governors of other provinces did. After Vindex commenced hostilities he wrote to Galba inviting him to accept the imperial dignity and to give a head to the strong Gallic body which needed one (παρασχεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἰσχυρῷ σώματι ζητοῦντι κεφαλήν); already there were 100,000 Gauls in arms, and further forces could be raised. Dio (lxiii 23) gives a speech of Vindex to the Gauls in which, after denouncing the villanies of Nero, he calls upon them to rid the world of such a monster.

: "liberator"; cf. Iul. 80, 1, populo detrectante dominationem atque assertores flagitante: Ov. Rem. Am. 73, publicus assertor dominis suppressa levabo | pectora; also used for "a champion of," e.g. Tib. 2, 4, assertores unicos dignitatis ac potentiae patriciorum. See further on "asserere,” Oth. 9,3, Vesp. 3; "assertio," Dom. 8,1. On some of the coins of Galba are found the words salus gen. humani (Eckhel, vi 297; Cohen, i² 334).

: according to Plutarch (Galb. 4), he held a council of his friends, and while some advised him to await developments, he was influenced in his decision by the argument of T. Vinius, his lieutenant, who pointed out that having once entertained the idea of revolt they were already committed to it (cf. Tac. H. ii 77, nam qui deliberant, desciverunt).
: recipere instead of the usual accipere is found also in Vell. Pat. i 48, 5, condiciones pacis
: Tac. A. ii 81, non receptae condiciones.

: cf. Ner. 43, 1, Initio statim tumultus (the revolt of Vindex and Galba) multa et immania, verum non abhorrentia a natura sua creditur destinasse; successores percussoresque summittere exercitus et provincias regentibus, quasi conspiratis idemque et unnım sentientibus. с, 9, 2-с. 10, 1.] ..

: Plutarch's description of the strained relations between Galba and the procurators has been already referred to (see above, note on "varie rexit'"). In the senatorial provinces there were procurators to look after the interests of the fiscus and the emperor's private affairs, but it was in the imperial provinces (like Tarraconensis) that they held a most important position independent of the governor, and often at variance with him. In Britain the legatus Suetonius Paulinus was thwarted by the procurator Classicianus, and the quarrel between them was so bitter that Nero sent Polyclitus to compose it (Tac. A. xiv 38); the feeling of the Britons under their oppressors is described in Tac. Agr. 15, binos reges imponi, e quibus legatus in sanguinem, procurator in bona saeviret. Agricola avoided such feuds when he was in Britain: ib. 9, procul a contentione adversus procuratores.
: = honesto genere ortae (Vesp. 1, 3); so honeste natus (Aug. 43, 3).

: a Celtiberian town, at this time the seat of a conventus iuridicus in Tarraconensis (see above on “conventum agens''). After the death of Vindex, Galba remained inactive at Clunia till news arrived that he had been made emperor at Rome (see c. 11, 1); he continued to be a patron of the town (C.I.L. ii 2339) and on coins of his reign Clunia bears the additional name of Sulpicia (Eckhel, i 46, vi 294; Cohen, i² 324, 86).
: cf. Tac. H. iv 61, (Germani) plerasque feminarum fatidicas arbitrantur; Cic. N.D. i 18, anus fatidica; Verg. Aen. viii 340, vates fatidica.

: oracula, sortes, and prophecies in general took the form of verse; e.g. Liv. i 45, cecinere vates . fore ., idque carmen pervenerat ad antistitem: Prop. iv 1, 51, Pergameae sero rata carmina vatis (i.e. Cassandra). Cf. θεσπιῳδός, Carmenta, Camena.

: Galba, though merely a Roman governor in Spain, took these prophecies as referring to himself; they were more literally fulfilled when Spaniards by birth or descent, like Trajan, Hadrian, and Theodosius, became emperors. Similarly the prophecies that men from Judaea would rule the world were supposed to be fulfilled when Vespasian, the Roman commander in Judaea, made himself emperor (see Vesp. 4, 5).

: Plut. Galb. 5, ἐκ τούτου προγράμματι ("by edict'') μὲν ἐδήλωσεν ὁ Γάλβας ἡμέραν ἐν ᾗἢ τὰς κατὰ μέρος ἐλευθερώσεις ἀποδώσει τοῖς δεομένοις. Galba chose the day on which in the normal course the court would have requests for manumission to make public his intention of "emancipating" the empire from the despotism of Nero. The usual process of manumission was per vindictam, i.e. by the touch of the wand of the lictor who acted as assertor libertatis, accompanied by the words "Hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritium liberum esse aio" and by the master turning the slave round and releasing his hold on him. This proceeding required the presence of a consul, praetor, or provincial governor. Pliny (Ep. vii 16) offers to get a friend of his, who is going to Baetica as proconsul, to stop at Ticinum to perform the ceremony of manumission (vindicta liberare). For other modes of manumission see on Vesp. 3, Latinae condicionis.

: vacare c. dat., used of a judge, meant that he was free to hear certain cases on a certain day; cf. Plin. Ep. vii 33, cum explorasset consules postulationibus vacaturos (“would be free to hear claims for restitution'"); so sedere c. dat. "to sit to hear certain cases," e.g. Ulp. Dig. xxxviii 17, 2, 43, ubi primum potuit, id est, praetoris copiam habuit huic rei sedentis.

: i.e. Baliaris Maior. The Balearic islands (Baliaris Maior and Minor, mod. Majorca and Minorca) are off the E. of Spain; under the Empire they formed part of Hispania Tarraconensis and belonged to the conventus of Carthago Nova (c. 9, 2); they served as one of the places of exile for those banished by the Roman emperors (cf. Tac. A. iv 42, xiii 43, and see note on Tit. 8, 5). consalutatus imperator: Plutarch (Galb. 5) says that he was thus saluted the moment he appeared on the tribunal: Οὐκ ἔφθη γοῦν φανερὸς ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος γενόμενος καὶ πάντες αὐτὸν ὁμοφώνως αὐτοκράτορα (imperatorem) προσεῖπον. Ὁ δὲ ταύτην μὲν εὐθὺς οὐ προσεδέξατο τὴν προσηγορίαν, κατηγορήσας δὲ τοῦ Νέρωνος καὶ τῶν ἀνῃρημένων (occisorum) ἀνδρῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοὺς ἐπιφανεστάτους ὀλοφυράμενος ὡμολόγησεν ἐπιδώσειν τῇ πατρίδι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ πρόνοιαν, οὔτε Καῖσαρ οὔτ᾽ αὐτοκράτωρ, στρατηγὸς δὲ συγκλήτου καὶ δήμου ῾Ρωμαίων (senatus populique R.) ὀνομαζόμενος. Dio calculates the duration of Galba's reign from the day (April 2, 68) on which he was thus acclaimed emperor in Spain (see on c. 23 infr.); similarly Vespasian's reign was reckoned from the day on which he was saluted as emperor by his soldiers (see Vesp. 6, 3). On imperator as a title of the princeps see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 781. Dio (lii 41) says of Augustus: καὶ τὴν τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἐπίκλησιν ἐπέθετο. λέγω δὲ οὐ τὴν ἐπὶ ταῖς νίκαις κατὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον διδομένην τισίν (see on Tit. 5, 2)... ἀλλὰ τὴν ἑτέραν τὴν τὸ κράτος διασημαίνουσαν, ὥσπερ τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ τῷ Καίσαρι.. ἐψήφιστο. ..

: thus renouncing his allegiance to Nero who had appointed him as legatus Augusti pro praetore in the imperial province of Tarraconensis. A similar recognition of the supreme authority of "the senate and the Roman people" was professed by Verginius Rufus who crushed the revolt of Vindex (c. 9, 2, Dio lxiii 25) and by Clodius Macer in Africa (see c. 11 infr.). Mommsen (Hermes xiii 90 sqq.) argues that a return to a senatorial or republican government was seriously contemplated at this period. The exultation of the senate in its brief freedom after Nero's death finds expression on the coins it issued inscribed with Libertas P.R., Libertas restituta or renascens, Roma renascens, Mars or Hercules Adsertor, etc. (Eckhel vi 293 sqq.). See Schiller, Geschichte der röm. Kaiserzeit i 366.

div.p: § 2. iustitio indicto: a iustitium (= iuris quasi interstitio quaedam et cessatio, Gell. xx 1) was a suspension of legal and other business at Rome on occasions of national danger; it was proclaimed (indicere, Calig. 24, 2, Liv. ix 7; edicere, Liv. iii 27) by a dictator, consul, or praetor; under the Empire we find a iustitium ordered on account of religious festivals, a famine, a funus publicum, and (most frequently) the death of a member of the imperial house. .. ..

p.note: : legiones may be a mistake or a corruption (as Heraeus, on Tac. H. i 6, suggests) for legionem, as there is no evidence that Galba enrolled from his province more than the one legion, viz. vii Galbiana, which is mentioned by Tacitus (e.g. H. iii 25, Iulius Mansuetus ex Hispania inter septimanos a Galba conscriptus). The theory of Grotefend that Legio prima Adiutrix (see on c. 12, 2) was enrolled by Galba and not by Nero is rightly rejected by Mommsen (C.I.L. iii p. 907); see also Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa xii 1380 sqq., Parker Roman Legions 99 sq.

: in the Roman army “auxilia” were auxiliaries from the provinces (also, at times, from allied states and princes, and even from independent nations), corresponding in number approximately with the legionaries; cf. Tib. 16, bellum . per quindecim legiones paremque auxiliorum copiam gessit: Tac. A. iv 5.

: under Augustus and Tiberius there were three legions quartered in Spain: iv Macedonica, vi Victrix, x Gemina; Galba as legatus of Hispania Tarraconensis had one legion, vi Victrix (Tac. H. i 16, v 16), by which he was proclaimed emperor.
: auxiliary cavalry, divided into alae miliariae of 960 men each (24 turmae of 40 each) and alae quingenariae of 480 (16 turmae of 30).

: these are cohortes auxiliariae, sociae, and might be infantry (cohortes peditatae) or include a certain proportion of cavalry (cohortes equitatae); the cohors miliaria equitata had 240 cavalry and 760 infantry, the cohors quingenaria equitata had 120 cavalry and 360-380 infantry. Sometimes these cohortes were equipped with their native weapons, and are described as sagittarii, funditores, contarii, cataphracti, etc. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 468 sqq.

: i.e. a copy of the Roman senate whose legatus and champion he now professed to be. For the uses of instar in Suet. see on Vesp. 5, 2. The MSS. vary between velut (read by Preud'homme) and vel (read by Ihm); velut is supported by the equally pleonastic use of quasi in Cic. Tusc. i 17, 40, terra ad universi caeli complexum quasi puncti instar obtinet.

: Suetonius uses quotiens more often than any other particle in introducing iterative clauses; it occurs 30 times in the Lives, 29 times with the subjunctive (imperf. or pluperf.) and once (Aug. 88) with pres. indicative. In class. Lat. quotiens takes the indic.; post-Aug. writers frequently use the subjunct. (Draeger, ii² 584). Suetonius also uses quotiensque (not quotienscunque): Aug. 37, quotiensque opus
: Calig. 7, quotiensque introiret. (Düpow, De Suet. consuetudine sermonis 19 sq.)

div.p: $ 3. manente anulorum aureorum usu: i.e. without sacrificing their rank as equites; an eques who became a centurion in a legion lost his rank as eques (see Mommsen Staatsr. iii³ 504 n. where our passage is cited). The gold ring had come to be a badge of the equestrian order (cf. Iul. 33; 39, 2; Galb. 14, 2; Vitell. 12). Originally it was given at public expense (de publico) to those senators who were sent as ambassadors (legati): then it came to be worn by the nobiles, by the equites equo publico, and later by all the knights. The gift of the anulus aureus, e.g. by Sulla to the actor Roscius, conferred equestrian status. Under the early Empire it was freely bestowed; so many wealthy freedmen obtained it that in 23 A.D. a decree of the senate was passed: “ne cui ius anulorum esset nisi cui ingenuo ipsi, patri avoque paterno sestertia cccc census fuisset" (Plin. N.H. xxxiii 8; cf. Daremberg-Saglio, i 296 sqq.). Six months' service as tribunus legionis carried with it the rank of eques and the ius anuli aurei (Juv. vii 88, with Mayor's note).

p.note: : Galba gave to this special bodyguard the title of "evocati” or volunteer veterans (see on Vesp. 1, 2) because the evocati in the Roman army formed at times the personal guard (cohors praetoria, Cic. Fam. x 30) of the general, as in the case of the evocati of Octavian before the battle of Mutina (Appian Bell. Civ. iii 40); sometimes this personal guard was composed of Roman equites (Polyb. vi 31, 2). excubias agerent: they were to act as excubitores, a name specially given to the cohort of praetorians which guarded the emperor in his palace and accompanied him to entertainments at other houses (cf. Oth. 4,2; 6, 1; Ner. 8; 21, 1; Tac. 4. xii 69, H. i 29; 38); their officer (tribunus excubitor) received the password (tessera) from the emperor (Calig. 56, 2; Claud. 42, 1; Ner. 9; Tac. A. i 7, xiii 3).

: Otho, in Lusitania, was the first of the provincial governors to declare for Galba (Oth. 4, 1; Plut. Galb. 20); then all the others, except Clodius Macer in Africa and Verginius Rufus in Germany, sided with him (Plut. c. 6). A coin of Galba's bears the words concordia provinciarum (Eckhel, vi p. 293).

: for a similar change of construction cf. Iul. 88, placuit Idus Martias Parricidium nominari, ac ne umquam eo die senatus ageretur. Such changes are common in poetry and are found at times in Cicero, e.g. Deiot. 10, quibus ille studiis se imbuerat, non saltandi, sed bene ut armis, optime ut equis uteretur.
: in all the MSS. except IQ the reading is in singulis which is adopted by Ihm but not by Preud'homme, Roth, or the early editors. communem causam = causam rei publicae.

div.p: § 4. oppidi: its name is unknown; Galba made it the headquarters for the assembly of men and munitions for the campaign, and fortified it in case of attack.

p.note: : cf. Tac. H. i 65, where Vienna (in Gallia Narbonensis) is spoken of as "sedes Gallici belli."

: the wonderful skill of ancient lapidaries (gemmarii scalptores) enabled them to depict a great variety of designs on signet rings; Pompey's ring, like the ring mentioned here, represented. three trophies (Dio xlii 18); the seal of Galba's family was a dog looking from the prow of a ship (Dio li 3); Pliny (N.H. xxxvii 8, 10) tells us that the gem on Sulla's ring showed the surrender of Jugurtha, and that Augustus had as a signet first the figure of a Sphinx, later a portrait of Alexander the Great, and finally a faithful likeness of himself which subsequent emperors also used. Cf. Aug. 50.
: Dio (lxiv 1) says that there were more than one of these miraculous ships: καὶ πλοῖα ὅπλων μεστὰ πρὸς Ἰβηρίαν ἀνθρώπων ἄγοντος αὐτά, προσωρμίσθη. αὐτόματα, μηδενὸς

: in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the left bank of the Hiberus (Ebro) and near its mouth; mod. Tortosa. Livy (xxiii 28) calls it "Hibera urbs"; Strabo (iii 160, 195) mentions it as a Roman colony. Some of the coins of Dertosa show the figure of a ship, it being an important trading port. See Pauly-Wissowa, v 246 sq. ..

: for this use of “cum inversum” (= tum, a relative form of proposition being substituted for a demonstrative) see Draeger, ii² 569; it is used principally by the historians to introduce something unexpected and surprising; Cicero also is fond of it, e.g. Verr. 2, 29, non dubitabat Minucius quin iste quaesiturus non esset, cum repente iubetur dicere: Sest. 37, 79, venit obnuntiavit consuli, cum subito manus illa Clodiana exclamat.

div.p: § 5. alarum: see c. 10, 2.

p.note: : for paene with perf. ind. in the .. apodosis of an unreal condition in past time, cf. Iul. 52, 1, paene Aegyptum penetravit, nisi exercitus sequi recusasset: Plaut. Pers. 594, paene in foveam decidi, ni hic adesses: Cic. Att. xv 26, 4, paene fecit, nisi tua malitia adfuisset: Liv. ii 10, 2, pons sublicius iter paene hostibus dedit, ni unus vir fuisset, Horatius Cocles. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 171, 174.
: the pres. ptc. is here used in a perf. or aorist sense; see on c. 5, 2.

: Vindex (c. 9, 2) was defeated at Vesontio (Besançon) in Gallia Belgica by Verginius Rufus, the legatus of Upper Germany (Тас. Н. і, 51, iv 57); it is doubtful whether he was slain ("caeso cum omnibus copiis Vindice," Tac.) or committed suicide (Plut. Galb. 6, and Dio lxiii 24). The victorious legions offered the empire to Rufus but he declined it and in his epitaph which he wrote he prides himself on his refusal: "Hic situs est Rufus pulso qui Vindice quondam | imperium asseruit non sibi sed patriae" (Plin. Ep. vi 10). Juvenal (viii 221) says that of all the crimes of which Nero was guilty his poetic and musical efforts called most for the vengeance of Verginius, Vindex, and Galba: Quid enim Verginius armis | debuit ulcisci magis aut cum Vindice Galba quod Nero tam saeva crudaque tyrannide fecit?

: Plutarch (Galb. 6) describes the panic of Galba and his subsequent inactivity at Clunia: τότε δὴ περίφοβος γενόμενος ὁ Γάλβας ἔγραψε τῷ Οὐεργινίῳ παρακαλῶν κοινοπραγεῖν καὶ διαφυλάσσειν ἅμα τὴν ἡγεμονίαν καὶ τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τοῖς ῾Ρωμαίοις· αὖθις δὲ μετὰ τῶν φίλων εἰς Κλουνίαν, Ἰβηρικὴν πόλιν, ἀναχωρήσας ἐν τῷ μετανοεῖν περὶ τῶν γεγονότων καὶ ποθεῖν τὴν συνήθη καὶ σύντροφον απραγμοσύνην μᾶλλον ἢ πράττειν τι τῶν ἀναγκαίων διέτριβεν.

: in Cic. renuntiare in the sense of cancelling an agreement or breaking off relations usually takes the acc. of the thing cancelled and the dat. of the person notified, e.g. Verr. 2, 2, 89, incensus hospitium ei renuntiat (so amicitiam alicui renuntiare, Suet. Calig. 2, 3, Liv., Tac., etc.): Verr. 2, 1, 141, renuntiat Habonius illam decisionem tutoribus told the guardians the offer was withdrawn"; in post-Aug. Lat. the dat. is used of the thing abandoned as though it were a person receiving notice (see Summers on Sen. Ep. 108, 15, inde ostreis boletisque in omnem vitam renuntiatum est), so we find such phrases as renuntiare civilibus officiis (Plin. Ep. ii 1, Quint. x 7), foro (Suet. Rhet. 6), inertiae (Plin. Pan. 59, 2), Naturae (Sen. Prov. 6, 8).

: according to Plutarch (Galb. 7) it was Icelus, a freedman of Galba, who first brought the news of Nero's death and Galba's appointment (see c. 22 infr.); two days later Titus Vinius and others brought full details.
: for Nero's death see on Dom. 11, 2, more maiorum puniendi.

: cf. c. 16, 1; Oth. 8, 1; Vitell. 15, 1; Tac. A. i 7, consules primi in verba Tiberii Caesaris iuravere, apudque eos Seius Strabo et C. Turranius, ille praetoriarum cohortium praefectus, hic annonae; mox senatus milesque et populus. So also in nomen principis iurare'” (Claud. 10, 4, etc.). This oath taken by the whole people and provinces was a recognition of Caesar's sole proconsulare imperium (Furneaux on Tac. l.c.), and was an extension of the old military oath (sacramentum) by which the soldier was said “iurare in verba consulum, etc." The oath of fealty to the emperor was taken afresh every New Year's day (cf. c. 16. 2) and on the anniversary of the day on which it had first been taken (Plin. Ep. x 52; Tac. A. i 8, H. i 55). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 792 sq.

: cf. Dio ap. Zonar. xi 14, Γάλβας δ', ἐπεὶ ὁ Νέρων διέφθαρτο καὶ ἡ βουλὴ τὴν ἀρχήν οἱ ἐψηφίσατο καὶ ὁ ῾Ῥοῦφος αὐτῷ προσεχώρησεν, ἀνεθάρσησεν, οὐ μέντοι καὶ τὸ Καίσαρος ἀνέλαβεν ὄνομα πρὶν τοὺς τῆς βουλῆς πρεσβευτὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν. ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ τὸ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος (imperatoris) πρότερον εἰς οὐδὲν γράμμα ἐνεγεγράφει. “Caesar” is now adopted as a mere title for the Roman emperor since "progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit” (Galb. 1). See further on Dom. 1, 3. iter ingressus est: Galba left Hispania Tarraconensis in June 68 A.D. and did not reach Rome till September (Tac. H. i 6, tardum iter Galbae).

: wearing the paludamentum or general's cloak, usually of purple or scarlet (cf. Vitell. 11, 1, n.). Under the Empire, when the military imperium was concentrated in the emperor, the paludamentum became one of the insignia of his power. Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 432. ..

: the dagger of military officers was worn either on a bandolier round the neck or on a girdle by the side (Mommsen, i³ p. 434, n. 1); the pugio (less frequently called gladius, ξίφος) was an emblem of the proconsular power of the princeps, the assumption of empire being described as the taking of the dagger in the hand, and the surrender of the empire as the giving back of the dagger; cf. Vitell. 8, 1; 15, 4; Tac. H. iii 68 (of Vitellius' abdication) adsistenti consuli exsolutum a latere pugionem velut ius necis vitaeque civium reddebat: Sen. Clem. i 11, 3 (of Nero), nulli umquam citius gladius commissus est. The right of wearing the pugio as a symbol of military command was granted by the emperor, especially to the praefectus praetorio who is often described as the bearer and custodian of the imperial dagger, e.g. Aurel. Vict. Caes. 13, 9 (of Trajan appointing Suburanus as praefectus praetorio), cum insigne potestatis, uti mos erat, pugionem daret; cf. Plin. Pan. 67, Plut. Galb. 8, Philostr. Apoll. iv 42, viii 16, Lamprid. Comm. 6, tunc primum tres praefecti praetorio fuere, inter quos libertinus, qui a pugione appellatus est. Dio (Xiph.), lxiv 3, says that the wearing of a "large sword" by Galba (a feeble old man of 73) on his march from Spain excited great ridicule : ὅτι δὲ ξίφος μέγα διὰ πάσης τῆς ὁδοῦ ἐξηρτᾶτο, καὶ γέρων καὶ ἀσθενὴς τὰ νεῦρα ὤν, καὶ πάνυ πολὺν γέλωτα ὠφλίσκανε. ..

: Suetonius in his fondness for participial constructions sometimes uses prius .. quam and ante.. quam in neg. sentences (1) with the ptc., e.g. Vesp. 6, 1, nec.. ante temptavit quam sollicitatus: Vesp. 15: Iul. 58, 2: Aug. 53, 3: Calig. 27, 4: (so in Cic. Phil. i 25, Tusc. i 13, Fin. i 49, N.D. i 68, Liv. vii 35, etc.); (2) with the ptc. in the abl. abs., as here: Vitell. 8, 2, nec ante rediit quam flagrante triclinio: Tib. 22 and 37, 3: (earlier in Livy, e.g. xxiv 18, non ante quam bello confecto: Plin. N.H. viii 144).
: this use of reciperare in the sense of repetere "to resume" does not seem to occur earlier.

: son of Nymphidia, a freedwoman, and Martianus, a gladiator (Plut. Galb. 9); though he himself alleged that he was a son of Caligula (Tac. A. xv 72). He was made praefectus praetorio by Nero in 65 after the conspiracy of Piso. When Nero's affairs were in a desperate state, Nymphidius persuaded the praetorian guards to declare Galba emperor, hoping to exercise the real authority himself; but finding that Galba preferred his own officers Vinius and Laco (who was appointed praefectus praetorio in his stead), he tried to induce the praetorians to proclaim him as emperor; they refused, and when he tried to force an entrance to their camp he was slain by them (Tac. H. i 5, 25, 37).

: consul in 67, legatus of Lower Germany in 68; according to Plutarch (Galb. 13) and Suetonius he entertained treasonable designs against Galba who had him put to death, but from the account in Tac. H. i 7 it appears that his guilt was doubtful: Forte congruerat ut Clodii Macri et Fontei Capitonis caedes nuntiarentur. Macrum in Africa haud dubie turbantem Trebonius Garutianus procurator iussu Galbae, Capitonem in Germania, cum similia coeptaret, Cornelius Aquinus et Fabius Valens legati legionum interfecerant, antequam iuberentur. Fuere qui crederent Capitonem ut avaritia et libidine foedum ac maculosum, ita cogitatione rerum novarum abstinuisse; sed a legatis bellum suadentibus postquam impellere nequiverint, crimen ac dolum ultro compositum; et Galbam mobilitate ingenii, an ne altius scrutaretur, quoquo modo acta, quia mutari non poterant, comprobasse. Tacitus also mentions (i 58) that when Vitellius became emperor, Capito's soldiers, who held his memory dear, demanded the death of his accuser. Dio (lxiv 2) says that Nymphidius and Capito were so wantonly arrogant that on one occasion when an accused person appealed from Capito to Caesar, Capito at once leaped into a higher chair and invited him to plead his cause before Caesar, and having heard his appeal put him to death.

: appointed legatus of Africa by Nero and guilty of much extortion and bloodshed as governor. On Nero's death he revolted and laid claim to the throne, being instigated by Crispinilla (magistra libidinum Neronis, Tac. H. i 73) who crossed to Africa and advised him to starve Rome by cutting off the African corn supply. He aimed at restoring the Republic, and on coins which he had struck he put his own image and the inscription s(enatus) c(onsulto) pro praetore Africae, instead of leg. Aug. pr. pr. prov. Africae (Eckhel vi p. 289, Cohen i² p. 316). He also enrolled a new legion in Africa which he called “Legio I Liberatrix Macriana." When Galba had secured the empire, he caused Macer to be put to death by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus (Tac. H. i 7, 37, 73; ii 97; Plut. Galb. 6, 15). The legio Macriana was disbanded by Galba but was again pressed into service by Vitellius and finally disappeared on his death (Parker, Rom. Legions 106).

: vices masquerading under the guise of severitas and parsimonia, according to Otho in his speech denouncing Galba to the soldiers, Tac. H. i 37: quae usquam provincia, quae castra sunt nisi cruenta et maculata aut, ut ipse (Galba) praedicat, emendata et correcta? nam quae alii scelera hic remedia vocat, dum falsis nominibus severitatem pro saevitia, parsimoniam pro avaritia, supplicia et contumelias vestras disciplinam appellat. The "saevitia Galbae” is mentioned also in Тас. Н. і 87; cf. Oros. vii 8, 1, cumque omnes avaritia saevitia segnitiaque offenderet.

: we have no details of the particular Spanish civitates which were treated vindictively by Galba, but he punished those cities and communities in Gaul (such as Lugdunum, the Treveri and the Lingones) which had remained loyal to Nero during the revolt of Vindex (c. 9, 2), and he rewarded those which had supported that abortive rising (such as Vienna, the Sequani, Aedui, and Arverni); cf. Tac. H. i 65, Galba reditus (“revenues'') Lugdunensium occasione irae in fiscum verterat; multus contra in Viennenses honor: i 53, Treveri ac Lingones quasque alias civitates atrocibus edictis aut damno finium Galba perculerat. The plurals Hispaniae and Galliae denote the various provinces mentioned in the notes on c. 8, 1 (‘‘Hispania Tarraconensis'') and c. 6, 1 (“Aquitania’”).
: for the use of the reflexive see on Vesp. 15, 1, qui se salutaverat.

: cf. Liv. viii 14, in Veliternos, quod totiens rebellassent, graviter saevitum; et muri deiecti, etc. The subst. destructio occurs first in Quintilian (x, 5, 12) as a rhetorical term, sententiarum destructio (= ἀνασκευή, refutatio; opp. to confirmatio, κατασκευή.)

: a vague title which has been variously interpreted. Ernesti and Bremi explain it of the provincial governors put to death by Galba, such as Clodius Macer in Africa and Fonteius Capito in Germany (c. 11), but Suetonius is speaking of executions connected with Spain and Gaul. Stahr takes it as higher officials, and La Harpe as Gallic and Spanish chieftains. Baumg.-Crus. is probably right in understanding by it "militiae praefecti (so Hofstee “duces militares"), as the word is used for military officers in c. 16, 1: Oth. 1, 2: Tac. H. i 36, etc. Tacitus (H. i 37) mentions Obultronius Sabinus and Cornelius Marcellus as slain by Galba in Spain, and Betuus Chilo as slain in Gaul, but does not state what positions they held there; again (H. i 6) he says: tardum Galbae iter et cruentum interfectis Cingonio Varrone consule designato et Petronio Turpiliano consulari: ille ut Nymphidii (see Galb. 11, n.) socius, hic ut dux Neronis, where Ritter takes "dux Neronis" to mean that Turpilianus was selected by Nero to command against Vindex and Galba. procuratores: for these and their hostility to Galba see on c. 9, 2.

: the citizens of Tarraco, the capital of Hispania Tarraconensis (c. 8, 1). confiasset: ''melted down" to coin into money; cf. Aug. 52, argenteas statuas conflavit exque iis (i.e. with the money coined from them) aureas cortinas ("tripods'') Apollini Palatino dedicavit. Suetonius also uses conftare in the fig. sense, Ner. 36, 1, coniuratio Beneventi conflata.

div.p: §2. classiarios: the classiarii or classici were the marines (ἐπιβάται), either libertini or peregrini, thousands of whom had been brought by Nero to Rome to support his waning power. Much controversy has arisen with regard to the formation of the first legion of classiarii and whether the classiarii mentioned here as so severely dealt with by Galba were those already formed into that legion; the accounts given by Tacitus, Suetonius, Plutarch, and Dio being difficult to reconcile. Heraeus and Spooner on Tac. H. i 6 hold that Nero had formed the best of the classiarii into a legion "prima Adiutrix classicorum” (cf. Tac. i 31, 36: ii 43, 67: iii 44: Dio, lv 24, says that Galba created this legion); the rest wished to be regularised in the same way as legionaries; Galba did not interfere with Nero's legio classica, but dealt drastically with the other classiarii who came out to claim similar privileges; his slaughter of them alienated the legio classica, which consequently supported Otho against him, Tac. i 31, legioni classicae diffidebatur infestae ob caedem commilitonum, quos primo statim introitu trucidaverat Galba: i 36, universa classicorum legio sacramentum eius (i.e. Otho) accepit; Otho on his accession released the classiarii who had escaped the slaughter, and had been imprisoned by Galba; he gave them the organisation of a legion and held out hopes of a more honourable service (i.e. in the legions) to other classiarii for the future, thus securing the loyalty of the fleet (Tac. i 87). If Tacitus were our only authority, these are certainly the most natural conclusions to draw from his statements. On the other hand, Suetonius here seems to agree with Plutarch (Galb. 15) who says that those who met Galba with their demands were the ἐρέται (remiges or classiarii) whom Nero had formed into a legion and declared to be legionary soldiers (οὺς εἰς ἓν τάγμα ὁ Νέρων συλλοχίσας ἀπέφηνε στρατιώτας), and most modern writers accept this as correct, assuming that the legion had not been fully organised at the time of Nero's death and had not yet received its aquila and signa. (See Dessau, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1, 307; Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa xii 1382; Parker, Rom. Legions 100.) Dio, lxiv 3, erroneously states that it was the bodyguard (δορυφόροι, praetoriani) of Nero who met Galba and claimed to be kept on in the same service.

p.mentioned: cum redire ad pristinum statum cogeret
p.note: : Suetonius is alone in stating that Galba had already ordered them to resume their former position and that they had refused. Plutarch says that when they made their demand Galba was for postponing the matter, and that they, taking this postponement as a refusal, followed him with shouts and some of them even drew their swords; whereupon he ordered the cavalry to charge. Dio agrees with Plutarch.

: Marius made the aquila the standard of the legion; the 30 signa were the ensigns of the legionary maniples (the maniple consisting of two centuries). In form, a signum was a silver-plated pole with a cross-bar near the top; below the bar were silver discs (phalerae) along the pole, and from the bar hung ribands, often with silver ornaments at their ends. The aquila was generally made of silver, sometimes of gold (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 438).

: so Plut., ἐκέλευσε τοὺς ἱππεῖς ἐμβαλεῖν αὐτοῖς. Dio says that Galba attacked them with his army: ἐφῆκέ (inmisit) σφισι τὸ στράτευμα. This happened at the Pons Mulvius, on the Tiber two miles above Rome (Tac. H. i 87). Dio asserts that 7000 were slain, and Tacitus (i 6) talks of many thousands: introitus in urbem trucidatis tot milibus inermium militum infaustus omine atque ipsis etiam qui occiderant formidolosus. Plutarch says that some were knocked down immediately and others were cut down as they fled, and that it was a bad omen for Galba that his entry into Rome should be through streams of blood and over heaps of corpses. Any previous contempt for his age and weakness was now changed into a universal horror and apprehension (πᾶσι φρικώδης καὶ φοβερὸς ἐγένετο.)

: cf. Tac. i 37, where Otho says: Horror animum subit, quotiens recordor feralem introitum et hanc solam Galbae victoriam, cum in oculis urbis decumari deditos iuberet, quos deprecantes in fidem acceperat. Polybius (vi 38) describes decimatio (δεκάτευσις), which was the penalty when whole companies had failed in their duty. The tribune assembles the legion, calls the defaulters to the front and after severely censuring them selects about a tenth of them by lot. Those selected are punished without mercy either by the fustuarium or by military execution; the rest are put on rations of barley instead of wheat and quartered outside the protection of the vallum. Appius Claudius thus dealt with his mutinous army in 471 в.с. (Liv. ii 59); decimatio was also used by Crassus (Plut. Crass. 10), Caesar (Dio xli 35), Octavian (Suet. Aug. 24, 2; Dio xlix 38), etc.

: Augustus at first had a bodyguard of Calagurritani from Hispania Tarraconensis until he had defeated M. Antonius, and then of Germans (prob. Batavi, cf. Dio lv 24) until the clades Variana in 10 A.D. when Varus lost his legions in the Saltus Teutoburgiensis and was himself slain (Aug. 49). The German bodyguard was restored by Tiberius (Tac. A. i 24); Caligula also had Germans (Batavi) as "corporis custodes," and they slew several of his assassins (Calig. 43; 58, 3). From numerous inscriptions (C.I.L. vi 4337-4345, 4716, 8802-8812) we see that the bodyguards of Tiberius, Claudius, and Nero were drawn from various German tribes subject to Rome, the Batavi, Frisii, Ubii, Suebi, etc. They were legally slaves and not organised as soldiers into centuriae or turmae but as a collegium divided into decuriae (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii 471; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 808). The dismissal of the Germans by Galba seems to have been final, as they are not mentioned later. Julius Caesar had a bodyguard of Spaniards which he had dispensed with before his assassination (Iul. 86); M. Antonius was guarded by Ityraeans (Cic. Phil. ii 112). = multis experimentis fidelissimam : quae saepe se fidelissimam probaverat; cf. Sall. Iug. 46, sed Metello iam antea experimentis cognitum erat genus Numidarum infidum.

: commodum was the regular word for the "bounty" of money or land granted to time-expired soldiers (veterani, emeriti) on their discharge (missio); Aug. 24, 2; 49, 2: Calig. 44, 1: Ner. 32, 1: Vitell. 15, 1, n.: Cic. Phil. v 53, etc.

: probably a son of P. Dolabella (cons. 10 A.D.); his wife Petronia had been earlier wedded to Vitellius before he became emperor (Vitell. 6, Tac. H. ii 64); he was a relative of Galba (Tac. H. і 88), and when Galba at the beginning of 69 was thinking of adopting a successor, some of his friends recommended Dolabella (Plut. Galb. 23); Otho banished him to Aquinum (Tac. l.c., Plut. Oth. 5); on Otho's death (Apr. 69) he returned to Rome, but was put to death by Vitellius on a charge of tampering with the troops (Tac. H. ii '63).

: the horti Dolabellae, according to Gilbert (Topogr. Rom iii 377), extended from the Mons Pincius to the Campus Agrippae in which was the castra of the cohors Germanorum. The Mons Pincius was known as the Collis hortorum; on it, or close to it, were the horti Sallustii, Variani, Lucullani, etc.

: tendere properly meant to stretch tents (tentoria)," and then was used in the general sense "to be quartered or stationed," whether the troops were under canvas or in buildings; cf. c. 19, 1; Tac. H. i 31, 55, 59: ii 66, etc. ..

div.p: §3. verene an falso: see note on Oth. 1, 1, incertum an ingenua.

p.note: : a “servus ordinarius” was a servant who was duly appointed to a definite permanent position (officium ordinarium) and exercised authority over those under him; the verb “ordinare” being used of appointing to an "officium ordinarium,” e.g. Vesp. 23, dispensatorem ordinavit. Cf. Sen. Ben. iii 28, Quo tandem ab istis gerulis raperis? ad ostium alicuius ostiarii, ad hortos alicuius ne ordinarium quidem habentis officium: id. Ep. 110, 1, unicuique nostrum paedagogum dari deum non quidem ordinarium, sed hunc inferioris notae, ex eorum numero quos Ovidius ait "de plebe deos": Ep. 53, 9, exercet philosophia regnum suum; dat tempus, non accipit; non est res subsiciva; ordinaria est, domina est; adest et iubet (see Summers ad loc.): Ulp. Dig. xiv 4, 5, si vicarius servi mei negotietur, ordinario sciente.
: see on Vesp. 22.

: "abstract of accounts” (= “breviariae rationes," Scaev. Dig. xxxiii 8, 26); see on Vesp. 21. In some of the MSS., including M, rationem is read, and Bücheler would delete the word or write breviariam rationem.

: restored by Stephanus; M has par obsidem and the other MSS. give parabsidem, parapsidem, per obsidem. παροψίς (ὄψον) was used by the Gr. comic writers either for a dainty side-dish or entrée or for the actual dish on which the dainty was served, though this latter use was condemned by the Atticists (Phryn. παροψὶς τὸ ὄψον, οὐχὶ δὲ τὸ ἀγγεῖον. Rutherford New Phrynichus p. 265). In Latin writers it is always used for the actual dish; see Mayor on Juv. iii 142, quam multa magmaque paropside cenat?

: this famous flute-player is mentioned by Martial (iv 5, 8; x 3, 8). Philostratus (vit. Apoll. v 21) describes an interview at Rhodes between Canus and Apollonius of Tyana on the subject of flute-playing, and Plutarch (an seni res p. ger. sit, c. 5 p. 786c) quotes a dictum of his that his audience never knew how much more pleasure he was getting from his playing than they, otherwise they would demand payment from him instead of paying to hear him.

: the choraules (χοραύλης) accompanied a chorus, generally on double pipes. Martial (v 56) mentions the profession of a choraules as a lucrative one, but (ix 77) would exclude such choral performances from dinners, as drowning conversation: Quod optimum sit quaeritis convivium? In quo choraules non erit.

: Plutarch (Galb. 16) says that Galba gave Canus some gold pieces, and emphasized the fact that he was giving them out of his own purse and not out of state funds: βουλόμενος δὲ τῆς περὶ τὰς δωρεὰς ἀμετρίας καὶ πολυτελείας τοῦ Νέρωνος ἀποδεικνύναι μεγάλην μεταβολὴν ἀστοχεῖν ἐδόκει τοῦ πρέποντος ("to miss the mark of propriety"). Κάνου γὰρ αὐλήσαντος αὐτῷ παρὰ δεῖπνον (ἀκρόαμα δὲ ἦν ὁ Κάνος εὐδοκιμούμενον) ἐπαινέσας καὶ ἀποδεξάμενος ἐκέλευσεν αὑτῷ κομισθῆναι τὸ γλωσσόκομον (“purse"), καὶ λαβὼν χρυσοῦς τινας ἐπέδωκε τῷ Κάνῳ, φήσας ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων, οὐκ ἐκ τῶν δημοσίων χαρίζεσθαι. Dio (lxiv 2) says that Galba was so penurious that on occasions he would not even give denarii when making presents, but only sestertii: χρήματα ἀπλήστως, ἅτε καὶ πολλῶν δεόμενος, ἤθροιζε, καὶ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐλάχιστα ἀνήλισκεν, ὥστε μηδὲ δραχμὰς ἔστιν οἷς, ἀλλ᾽ ὀβολοὺς χαρίζεσθαι. Contrast the lavish sums which Vespasian gave to musicians (Vesp. 19, 1).

: = propriis, ἰδίοις, denoting what was his own private property; cf. Iul. 76, 3, peculiares servi (opp. to publici): Aug. 5, quasi proprio suo ac peculiari deo. This adj. (from peculium "a slave's savings'') is used in another sense in Vitell. 4.

: loculi (always plur.) was used of any kind of a casket or case with compartments for holding keys, jewels, etc.; in the sense of money-box or purse it occurs in Hor. S. i 3, 17 ii 3, 146, Ер. ің 1, 175; Juv. i 89 (see Mayor), x 46, xi 33; Mart. v 39, 7; etc.

: this elliptical use of perinde with the implied comparison omitted is frequent in Silver Latin; the meaning may often be expressed in full by non perinde ac facile crederes, "not so much as you might expect" and so "not very much"; e.g. Tib. 52, 1, itaque ne mortuo quidem perinde adfectus est "not moved by his death in the way you would expect'": Tac. A. ii 88, Romanis haud perinde celebris "not so famous as he should have been": id. Agr. 10, mare perhibent ne ventis quidem perinde attolli: id. H. ii 84, Vespasiano haud perinde obstinante. See also on "non adeo,” Oth. 5, 2. .

: the spectacles or shows were divided into the Circus, the Amphitheatre, the Theatre, and the Stadium; theatrical performances being, as Friedlaender says, the most frequent, the least costly and troublesome, and the least appreciated.

: the Atellani were the actors in the Atellanae (fabulae), a burlesque popular comedy (transplanted from Atella in Campania to Rome), which at first was an improvisation, but in Sulla's time had become literary. It was generally a one-act piece with four stock characters: Pappus (the dotard or pantaloon), Dossennus (the wise man, the dottore, the cunning sharper), Bucco (the glutton), and Maccus (the booby). The Atellanae were full of broad humour and indecent allusions. See Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 112 sq., where a list of the subjects of the Atellanae is given.

: this word was used in two senses: (a) a canticum proper was a lyrical monody accompanied by a flute and sung with appropriate gesture; (b) in a wider sense cantica included all the parts of a play which were *written in trochaic septenarii and declaimed with musical accompaniment as a kind of recitative. Livius Andronicus (c. 284-204) introduced the custom of having the words of the lyrical canticum sung by a young slave standing beside the flute-player, thus leaving the actor free to perform the accompanying gestures. Such cantica formed part of the Atellanae and Mimi as well as of the ordinary tragedies and comedies. The words and airs of some of the cantica became so familiar to the public that they were often sung separately like our operatic airs; cf. Suet. Iul. 84, where cantica are sung at the funeral of Caesar and move the people by the allusions which they find in them to the fate of the dictator. In Vitell. 11, 2, "cantica Neroniana” composed or sung by Nero are mentioned; in Tac. A. xiii 15 we read of Britannicus singing a canticum from the Andromache of Ennius which fitly described his own treatment by Nero. The licence of actors in conveying political allusions by lines in the Atellanae and the keen appreciation of such "hits" by the audience are often referred to by Suetonius; see the passages cited on Vesp. 19, 2. ...

div.p: "Venit Onesimus a villa": the reading is uncertain: venit onesimus is found only in a late MS., the others give venitione (or veditione) simus (or simul). The name "Onesimus" had been conjectured by Augustinus and is accepted by Oudendorp, Roth, and the recent editors. Lachmann suggested "Dorsennus" (adopted by Ribbeck Com. Rom. frag. p. 274), Dorsennus or Dossennus being a standing character in the Atellan plays (see note above, and Wilkins on Hor. Ep. ii 1, 173). Other conjectures are venit io Simus (Turnebus) and venit ohe Simus (Iac. Gronovius), Simus "snub-nosed" being a rustic in comedy (cf. Pollux iv 19, τῷ ἀγροίκῳ ἡ ῥὶς σιμή) and Galba being described as "adunco naso" in c. 21 infr. It seems however from the context that the allusion must rather be to the niggardly grasping nature of Galba, and Hofstee finds a special appropriateness in the name Onesimus: “nomen Onesimi a verbo quod est ὀνινάναι, aptissimum est ad designandum hominem avarum.” This canticum was probably a lament of the familia on the unwelcome arrival of the old master from the country. Galba had been long absent from Rome, having lived for many years in secessu before the governorship in Spain was offered to him in 60; see c. 8, 1.

p.note: : they went through all the gestures appropriate to the singing of the canticum; for the use of agere cf. Liv. vii 2, 9, (Livius Andronicus) suorum carminum actor dicitur, cum vocem obtudisset, puerum ad canendum cum statuisset, canticum egisse aliquanto magis vigente motu, quia nihil vocis usus impediebat. .. ...

: the truth of the maxim ἀρχὴ δείξει ἄνδρα was illustrated in the case of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 49, maior privato visus dum privatus fuit, et omnium consensu capax imperii nisi imperasset: Auson. Caes. vii, Spe frustrate ("deceptive in thy promise'") senex, privatus sceptra mereri visus et (es, Peiper) imperio proditus inferior, fama tibi melior iuveni; sed iustior ordo est | complacuisse dehinc, displicuisse prius. ...

: of this use of adeo “ad augendas singulas voces, quibus postponitur sicut ye" there are numerous instances (including this) collected in the Thes. Ling. Lat. i col. 614 sq., e.g. Claud. 37, 1, nulla adeo suspicio tam levis exstitit: Ner. 35, 4, nullum adeo genus est: Iul. 14, 2, obtinuissetque adeo: Plaut. Amph. 1133, multo adeo melius (where see Palmer's note): Verg. G. i 94, multum adeo iuvat: Cic. de or. ii 15, magis adeo id facilitate quam alia ulla culpa mea contigit.

: used by Suetonius 15 times with the subjunctive (never with the indicative). The few apparent instances of this constr. in Cicero are to be explained either by the potential force of the subjunctive or by assimilation of moods (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 442). A few examples are found in Varr., Nep., the poets (e.g. Verg. Aen. vi 394, Ov. Met. xiv 465), Liv., Colum., Sen., etc. The subjunctive is more frequent than the indicative in Tacitus (Draeger, Synt. Tac. 201) and in the younger Pliny (Merrill on Plin. Ep. i 12, 3).

: cf. Claud. 15, 1, proprio negotio documentum daturus, quam aequus iudex in alieno negotio futurus sit.; for the personal genitive following documentum cf. Vell. Pat. ii 42, documentum tanti mox evasuri viri.

: Tac. H. i 7, ceterum utraque caedes (i.e. the killing of Clodius Macer and Fonteius Capito, see c. 11 supr.) sinistre accepta, et inviso semel principi seu bene seu male facta parem invidiam adferebant. Dio (lxiv 2) says that Galba, however guiltless himself, was held responsible for the outrages committed by his freedmen, because he either permitted them or was culpably ignorant of them.

div.p: § 2. regebatur trium arbitrio: the same statement is made in Tac. H. i 13, potentia principatus divisa in Titum Vinium consulem, Cornelium Laconem praetorii praefectum; nec minor gratia Icelo Galbae liberto. Corneille (Othon i 1) makes Otho say of them: Je les voyais tous trois se hâter sous un maître, Qui, chargé d'un long âge, a peu de temps à l'être; Et tous trois à l'envi s'empresser ardemment A qui dévorerait ce règne d'un moment. paedagagos: (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 6, trium amicorum consilio, id est Vinii, Cornelii, et Iceli cuncta disponens, adeo ut intra Palatinas aedes pariter habitarent, et vulgo paedagogi dicerentur. So Tigellinus, the infamous minister of Nero, was denounced by the people as “τὸν διδάσκαλον· καὶ παιδαγωγὸν τῆς τυραννίδος” (Plut. Galb. 17). The παιδαγωγός (whence our "pedagogue" and "page'') was the slave-tutor who looked after the manners and morals of children and conducted them to and from school; his qualifications and his duties in a Roman house are described by Wilkins, Roman Education, p. 40 sq. The word came to be used in an extended sense for a leader or guide, e.g. Sen. Ep. 110 unicuique nostrum paedagogum dari deum inferioris notae.

p.note: : his career is sketched in Tac. H. i 48. His father was of a praetorian family and his maternal (paternal, Dio xlvii 7) grandfather was proscribed by the triumvirs in 43 в.с. He was born in 12 A.D. and served as military tribune under Calvisius Sabinus, legatus of Pannonia in Caligula's reign, but was disgraced and imprisoned for an intrigue with his general's wife. Liberated under Claudius, he passed through the cursus honorum and after his praetorship was appointed legatus legionis. Though suspected of having stolen a gold cup from the table of Claudius, he was made proconsul of Gallia Narbonensis and administered the province strictly. Later he served in Spain as legatus of Galba, and when Galba was made emperor, held the consulship with him in 69 A.D.; he was the next victim of Otho's soldiers after they had slain Galba. Tacitus (l.c.) says that he was "audax, callidus, promptus, et, prout animum intendisset, pravus aut industrius eadem vi," but in i 6 (quoted below) he tersely stigmatizes him as "deterrimus mortalium."

: sc. legionis; cf. Plut. Galb. 4, Τίτος Οὐίνιος ὁ τοῦ στρατιωτικοῦ τάγματος ἡγεμών (where see Hardy). Galba as governor of Hispania Tarraconensis had one legion, vi Victrix (c. 10, 2). Vinius persuaded Galba to aid the designs of Vindex; see on c. 9, 2.

: Plut. Galb. 12, ἦν δὲ Οὐίνιος ἀργυρίου ἐσχάτως καὶ παρ᾿ ὁντινοῦν (praeter omnes) ἥττων. Plutarch also tells how the notorious Tigellinus bought his life by vast presents to Vinius, a striking proof that there was nothing he would not do for money (μέγα δίδαγμα τοῦ μηδὲν ἄπρακτον εἶναι παρὰ Οὐινίῳ μηδὲ ἀνέλπιστον τοῖς διδοῦσιν, Galb. 17). For cupiditas see on Vesp. 1, 1.

: nothing is known as to his previous history; Tacitus (H. i 6) describes his character: invalidum senem (i.e. Galba) Titus Vinius et Cornelius Laco, alter deterrimus mortalium, alter ignavissimus, odio flagitiorum oneratum contemptu inertiae destruebant (i.e. the flagitia of Vinius and the inertia of Laco). The three "paedagogi” quarrelled over the nomination of a colleague and successor to Galba, Vinius supporting the adoption of Otho, Laco and Icelus that of Piso (ib. 13); Laco refused to be sent by Galba to appease the discontent of the Germanic legions under Vitellius (ib. 19); he concealed from Galba the murmurings of his soldiers (ib. 26, multa erumpentis seditionis indicia per conscios suppressa: quaedam apud Galbae aures praefectus Laco elusit, ignarus militarium animorum consiliique quamvis egregii, quod non ipse afferret, inimicus et adversus peritos pervicax); he persuaded Galba to adopt his fatal advice that he should present himself to the angry soldiers who had declared for Otho (ib. 33); on Otho's accession he was sentenced to be deported, but Otho secretly commissioned his guard to assassinate him (ib. 46); Plutarch (Galb. 27) says, however, that he was slain at the same time as Galba. "conassessore: "assessores” (πάρεδροι), also called in later writers siliarii,””‘“iuris studiosi,” were men versed in the law who sat as legal advisers to various civil and military functionaries when administering justice, assisting by their technical knowledge consuls, praetors, governors of provinces, iudices, the praefectus praetorio, the praefectus urbi, etc. The emperors appointed salaried assessores (consiliarii) to act with the legati provinciarum (Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 318, ii³ 245). Paulus, who wrote a work De Officio Adsessoris, specifies the matters with which they dealt: Dig. i 22, 1, Omne iudicium adsessoris, quo iuris studiosi partibus suis funguntur, in his fere causis constat: in cognitionibus, postulationibus, libellis, edictis, decretis, epistulis. The famous jurisconsult Ulpian, like Laco, held the position of assessor before becoming praefectus praetorio under Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 31).
: see on Tit. 4, 2 and 6, 1.

: this freedman of Galba was imprisoned at Rome by Nero when he learnt of Galba's revolt in Spain, but he was released on Nero's death, and allowed Nero's body to be cremated: Ner. 49, 4, permisit hoc Icelus, Galbae libertus, non multo ante vinculis exsolutus in quae primo tumultu coniectus fuerat. He conveyed to Galba the news of Nero's death and of Galba's acclamation as emperor (Galb. 11 and 22), and Galba rewarded him with the rank and insignia of an eques. He supported Laco against Vinius (Tac. H. i 13) and opposed the adoption of Otho by Galba. On Galba's death Otho had him executed as a “libertus,” ignoring the ingenuitas conferred by his rank as "eques”: Tac. i 46, in Marcianum Icelum ut in libertum palam animadversum.

: the sign of equestrian dignity; see on c. 10, 3. Plutarch says he became the most influential of the freedmen: Galb. 7, τῷ δ᾽ ἀπελευθέρῳ (liberto) δακτυλίους τε χρυσοῦς ἔδωκε καὶ Μαρκιανὸς ὁ Ἴκελος ἤδη καλούμενος εἶχε τὴν πρώτην ἐ ντοῖς ἀπελευθέροις δύναμιν : cf. Tac. H. i 13, пес minor gratia Icelo Galbae liberto, quem anulis donatum equestri nomine Marcianum vocitabant. Other instances of the bestowal of equestrian rank on unworthy freedmen were by Nero on Pallas (Plin. Ep. viii 6), by Vitellius on Asiaticus (Suet. Vitell. 12), and by Vespasian on Hormus (Tac. Η. iv 39).
: his new name would be Servius Sulpicius Marcianus, as he would assume the gentile nomen (Sulpicius) and praenomen (Servius) of his patronus Galba. See Hardy on Plut. Galb. 7.

: the “summa equestris," i.e. the highest office attainable by equites, was the praefectura praetorii (see on Tit. 4, 2). Under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, an eques, according to the office he held, was designated as (1) vir eminentissimus (ἐξοχώτατος), a prefect of the praetorian guard; (2) vir perfectissimus (διασημότατος), any other prefect, from the praefectus classis to the praefectus annonae, or a head of the secretariate or of the finance department; (3) vir egregius (κράτιστος), a holder of any of the lesser offices open to equites. Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 565.

: see on Vesp. 6, 2, omni rapinarum genere grassati. Tacitus (H. i 37) uses the same word in Otho's speech denouncing the rapacious outrages of Galba's ministers: Septem a Neronis fine menses sunt et iam plus rapuit Icelus quam Polycliti et Vatinii et Aegiali (extortionate freedmen of Nero) quoad perierunt. Minore avaritia ac licentia grassatus esset T. Vinius, si ipse imperasset: nunc et subiectos nos habuit tanquam suos et viles ut alienos.

: cf. the words of Nymphidius Sabinus in Plut. Galb. 13, ἔφη Γάλβαν μὲν αὐτὸν εἶναι πρεσβύτην ἐπιεικῆ καὶ μέτριον, ἐλάχιστα δὲ τοῖς αὑτοῦ χρώμενον λογισμοῖς ὑπὸ Οὐινίου καὶ Λάκωνος οὐκ εὖ διοικεῖσθαι. abutor was used with the acc. in early Lat., hence the gerundive; Cicero has utendus, fruendus, perfruendus, fungendus (Kühner-Stegmann, i 733).

: he had shown the same inconsistency in his administration of Hispania Tarraconensis; see c. 9, 1. parcior: Tacitus (H. i 49) describes Galba as "pecuniae alienae non appetens, suae parcus, publicaė avarus.”

: the emperors before him had succeeded to the empire as a kind of inheritance: cf. Galba's own words in the speech attributed to him in Tac. H. i 16, Sub Tiberio et Gaio et Claudio unius familiae quasi hereditas fuimus: loco libertatus erit, quod eligi coepimus.

: 73 years of age. For the adverbial accusative cf. Cic. Phil. viii 5, cum illud esset aetatis; similarly id (hoc, istuc) aetatis, id temporis, hoc noctis, illud horae (Ner. 26, 2, numquam publico se illud horae commisit); in Tac. A. xii 18 we find nemo id auctoritatis aderat. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 306. 8, 3.

div.p: § 3. ex utroque ordine: senatorio et equestri; cf. Vesp. 9, 2: Dom.

p.note: : = indictâ (incognita) causâ, re inoratâ, a post-Aug. use found in Tac., Plin. Ep., etc.; cf. Vitell. 14, 4: Claud. 38, 2. In class. Lat. inauditus means 'unheard of,” “strange," in which sense it is used in Calig. 19, 1; 40: Ner. 42, 1.

: Galba granted the franchise to the Gallic communities of the Sequani, Aedui, and Arverni, who had supported Vindex (Tac. H. i 8, 51); it is doubtful whether it was bestowed on these people at large or only on a certain number of their leading men (see Heraeus and Spooner on Tac. l.c. and Hardy on Plut. Galb. 18). The ius civitatis was very charily conferred by Augustus (Aug. 40, 3, civitates R. parcissime dedit); so too by Tiberius and Caligula; Claudius was very lavish (Dio lx 17, τὴν πολιτείαν πάνυ ἀνέδην, τοῖς μὲν κατ' ἄνδρα, τοῖς δὲ καὶ ἀθρόοις, ἐδίδου), and Nero also gave it indiscriminately (cf. Ner. 12, 1, where he bestows “diplomata civitatis R.'' on Greek dancers).

: under the Lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus (18 B.c.) and an amplification of it, the Lex Papia Poppaea (9 A.D.), Augustus rewarded those with three or more children and penalised the unmarried and those who were married but childless. The unmarried were taxed and could not inherit by will, and the childless could only take half a hereditas or legatum, the remainder going to the Treasury as a caducum. A fictitious ius liberorum, however, was granted by the senate in several cases and later by the emperors from Claudius on (Dio lv 2, Suet. Claud. 19). Martial obtained it from Domitian (Epigr. ii 91, 92) and Statius (Silv. iv 8, 20) mentions another grant by him; Pliny the Younger was granted it by Trajan (Plin. Ep. x 2) and also obtained it for some of his friends including Suetonius (Ep. x 94, 95). A preference in election to offices and choice of provinces was given to persons having children (Tac. A. ii 51 xv 19 Plin. Ep. vii 16). See Roby, Roman Private Law i 381; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 888.

: "one or two," "a few"; cf. Vesp. 4, 6, uno atque altero proelio: Iul. 20, 5, uno atque altero frustra nominatis: Tib. 63, 2: Claud. 12, 3. Suetonius has only unus et (or atque) alter; Tacitus uses unus et alter, unus alterque, unus aut alter, unus alterve to denote "indefinitum numerum eumque non magnum” (Gerber and Greef, Lex. Tас.).

: three decuriae of iudices were formed by the Lex Aurelia (70 B.C.) which enacted that the iudices should be chosen from the three classes of senatores, equites, and tribuni aerarii. Julius Caesar by a Lex Iulia iudiciaria (46 B.c.) did away with the decuria of the tribuni aerarii, but a third decuria was restored by M. Antonius (44 в.с.), the property qualification being removed and service as a centurion or in the cavalry or in the legio Alauda substituted. Augustus added to the three existing decuriae (which, according to Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 535, he composed entirely of equites) a fourth of ducenarii, i.e. those whose census reached 200,000 sesterces (half that of an eques), this fourth decuria adjudicating in cases involving smaller amounts ("de levioribus summis,” Aug. 32, 3). Caligula added a fifth decuria to lighten the labours of the jurymen ("ut levior labor iudicantibus foret," Calig. 16, 2).

: Claud. 23, 1, Rerum actum divisum antea in hibernos aestivosque menses coniunxit (“actus rerum" denotes the legal term-time during which the courts sat). Augustus, to expedite legal business, added to the law-term thirty extra days which had previously been given over to ludi honorarii, and as the jurymen tried to shirk their onerous duties, he reluctantly granted each decuria, in its turn, exemption for one year, and gave all four decuriae vacation in November and December (Aug. 32). By the time of Claudius this had come to be altered, and there were legal vacations in spring and autumn; Claudius apparently arranged that the iudices should serve continuously from spring to the beginning of winter (see Smilda on Claud. 23, 1). For "beneficium” see note on Tit. 8, 1.

: the positions held by senators under the Principate included the offices of state at Rome, provincial governorships, the command of the legions, the prefectship of the city, and commissionerships (curationes) of the water-supply, roads, public works, etc. See Greenidge, Rom. Publ. Life p. 401. On the other hand, the knights (equites) held a number of administrative and financial positions from which senators were excluded: the government of Egypt was reserved to them, and the smaller provinces to the north of Italy were under equestrian governors; the commanders of the fleet were equites, as were many of the prefects appointed by Augustus, e.g. the praefectus annonae, pr. praetorii, pr. vigilum; most important of all were the financial offices entrusted to them: the imperial tax-officers (procuratores Augusti) in the provinces were chosen from the equites alone. Presumably the officia which Galba wished to circumscribe were more especially the provincial governorships and fiscal procuratorships.

: Galba may have hoped by this novel. method of appointment to secure provincial governors and commanders of legions, who, being free from any desire of self-aggrandisement, would not endanger the emperor's position; also fiscal procurators who would not oppress by merciless exactions the wretched provincials as those in Galba's own province had done (see on c. 9, 1). Vespasian promoted the most rapacious procurators, that they might be the richer when he condemned them later (Vesp. 16, 2). Galba's mode of appointing to public offices was adopted by Alexander Severus: praefectum praetorii fecit, qui ne fieret etiam fugerat, dicens invitos non ambientes in re publica conlocandos (Lamprid. Alex. 19).

: liberalitates = dona (abstract for concrete, see on "custodias" Dom. 14, 4) as in Claud. 29, 1, revocatas liberalitates eius; so in sing., Tib. 46, una modo liberalitate milites prosecutus. Tacitus is the first to use liberalitas in this way. The enormous sum of 2200 million sesterces (nearly £20,000,000) is said to have been lavished by Nero (Tac. H. i 20); cf. Ner. 30, 2, Quare nec largiendi nec absumendi modum tenuit. In Tiridatem, quod vix credibile videatur, octingena nummum milia diurna erogavit abeuntique super sestertium milies contulit. Menecraten citharoedum et Spiculum murmillonem triumphalium virorum patrimoniis aedibusque donavit.

: the efforts made by Galba to recover Nero's bounties from the recipients are described also in Tac. H. i 20: Appellari ("to be sued") singulos iussit, decuma parte liberalitatis apud quemque corum relicta. At illis vix decumae super portiones erant, isdem erga aliena sumptibus, quibus sua prodegerant, cum rapacissimo cuique ac perditissimo non agri aut faenus (“capital'') sed sola instrumentà vitiorum manerent. Exactioni triginta (Suet. says 50) equites R. praepositi, novum officii genus et ambitu ac numero onerosum. Ubique hasta et sector ("sales and brokers'") et inquieta urbs actionibus ("trials"; auctionibus, Ritter and Orelli). Dio (lxiii 14) mentions that the sum of a million sesterces given by Nero to the Ἑλλανοδίκαι (judges at the Olympic games) was recovered by Galba, and also 400,000 sesterces given to the Pythian prophetess for favourable oracles. In 24 A.D. Tiberius wrested from the estate of C. Silius the bounty granted him by Augustus (Tac. A. iv 20, liberalitas Augusti avulsa).

: stage-players, actors (histriones); cf. Cic. Off. i 31, 114; Planc. 30; Verr. iii 184. Nero himself is spoken of contemptuously as “ille scaenicus" in Tac. A. xv 59; in his mania for the stage he even thought of appearing as a professional actor (inter scaenicos) when one of the praetors offered him a million sesterces to perform at one of his shows (Ner. 21, 2).

: athletes"; Aид. 45, 4, xysticorum certationes: Tertull. Spect. 30, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasio sed in igne iaculati; ib. 20, atrocitas harenae, vanitas xysti: Ulp. Dig. iii 2, 4, omnes opinantur ignoet utile videtur ut neque thymelici neque xystici neque agitatores miniosi habeantur. The xystus was a covered colonnade where athletes exercised in winter (Vitruv. v 11); it is the Gr. ξυστός (from ξύειν το scrape, make smooth) and may originally have denoted the part of the gymnasium where the athletes scraped off the oil and dust with the strigilis, though some think that the name came from the smooth polished floor. xystus was also used for an open colonnade, a garden-walk or terrace adorned with flowers and shrubs, as in Aug. 72, 3, xystis et nemoribus excoluit praetoria ("country mansions'') sua, and in Pliny's description of his villas (Ep. ii 17, v 6). Nero's passion for Greek athletics is mentioned in Ner. 12, 3: Instituit et quinquennale certamen primus omnium Romae, more Graeco triplex, musicum, gymnicum, equestre, quod appellavit Neronia; dedicatisque thermis atque gymnasio senatui quoque et equiti oleum praebuit; Tac. A. xiv 47, etc.
: this is omitted by Tacitus (H. i 20) but mentioned in Plut. Galb. 16, τοὺς πριαμένους παρ' αὐτῶν ἢ λαβόντας ὁτιοῦν ἀνεζήτει καὶ παρ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐξέπραττε.
: quando is used here in a temporal and not in a causal sense; see on Vesp. 16, 3.

div.p: §2. comites: see on Vesp. 4, 4.

p.note: : Tac. H. i 7, venalia cuncta, praepotentes liberti, servorum (used contemptuously for libertorum) manus subitis avidae et tanquam apud senem festinantes; eademque (i.e. the same as in Nero's court) novae auiae mala, aeque gravia, non aeque excusata. The freedmen are Icelus and Halotus (Spooner on Tac. l.c. adds Tigellinus, but he was not a freedman). Plutarch (Galb. 16) blames Vinius for bringing Galba into disrepute by the attempt to recover the bounties of Nero and for his own shameless trafficking: φθόνον δὲ καὶ μῖσος εἶχεν Οὐίνιος, ὡς τοῖς μὲν ἄλλοις ἅπασιν ἀνελεύθερον παρέχων τὸν ἡγεμόνα καὶ μικρολόγον, αὐτὸς δὲ χρώμενος ἀσώτως καὶ λαμβάνων πάντα καὶ πιπράσκων. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ησίοδος ἀρχομένου τε πίθου καὶ λήγοντος κορέσασθαι φησὶ δεῖν, ὁ δὲ Οὐίνιος ὁρῶν ἀσθενῆ καὶ γέροντα τὸν Γάλβαν ἐνεπίμπλατο τῆς τύχης, ὡς ἅμα μὲν ἀρχομένης, ἅμα δὲ φθινούσης.

: the regular word for knocking a thing down at an auction; e.g. Aug. 24, 1, equitem Romanum bonaque subiecit hastae ("auction''), quem tamen liberto suo addixit: Calig. 38, 4, nec licendi ('bidding'") finem factum quoad tredecim gladiatores sestertio nonagies addicerentur.
: see on Vesp. 16, 1, omissa sub Galba vectigalia. Cf. Plut. Galb. 18, ἐδόκουν γὰρ οὐ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος, ἀλλ᾽ ὠνούμενοι παρὰ Οὐινίου τυγχάνειν ἀνέσεώς τε δασμῶν καὶ πολιτείας.
: the pl. is not found earlier, but Cicero has immunitates.

: in the circus and in the theatre the people clamoured for the death of Tigellinus; cf. Plut. Galb. 17, οὐδένος γὰρ οὕτω θεάματος ἐρασθεὶς ὁ ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος ὡς τοῦ Τιγελλῖνον ἰδεῖν ἀπαγόμενον, οὐδὲ παυσάμενος ἐν πᾶσι θεάτροις καὶ σταδίοις αἰτούμενος ἐκεῖνον : Tac. Η. i 72, non alium pertinacius ad poenam flagitaverunt Eo infensior populus, addita ad vetus Tigellini odium recenti Titi Vinii invidia, concurrere ex tota urbe in Palatium ac fora, et ubi plurima vulgi licentia, in circum ac theatra effusi seditiosis vocibus strepere. See also Dio lxiv 3, cited below. ...

: a eunuch who held the position of "food taster” (“praegustator," Claud. 44) at the court of Claudius. He was one of the agents used by Agrippina to administer to Claudius the poison prepared by Locusta (Тас. 4. xii 66), and he continued his infamous career under Nero.

: “Tigillinus'" (not "Tigellinus'') is the form attested by our MSS. here, by those of Martial (iii 20, 16), and by the Schol. on Juv. i 155; the Medicean MS. of Tacitus also gives "Tigillinus" except in Ann. xiv 48, xv 37. On the other hand, "Tigellinus" is found in the text of Juvenal (l.c.) and in most of the MSS. of Plutarch, Dio, and Josephus; see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 250. There is also doubt with regard to the first part of his name, whether it was "Sophonius" or "C. Ofonius"; the best MSS, in Tac. H. i 72 (see Heraeus) and inscriptions give "Ofonius." He was a son of a native of Agrigentum, and early became notorious for his beauty and immorality. He was banished by Caligula for intriguing with the emperor's sisters. Favoured by Agrippina he was made praetorian prefect by Nero in 63 and encouraged Nero in his licentious career (intimis libidinibus adsumptus, Tac. A. xiv 51). He and the empress Poppaea formed Nero's privy council (intimum consiliorum, A. xv '61); to them was largely due the number of executions after Piso's conspiracy in 65. He deserted Nero at his downfall and helped to win the soldiers for Galba. On Otho's accession he was forced to commit suicide (Tac. H. i 72, infamem vitam foedavit etiam exitu sero et inhonesto). See Mayor's note on Juv. i 155, Pone Tigellinum: taeda lucebis in illa | qua stant ardentes qui fixo gutture fumant.
: see on Dom. 11, 1.

: Dio (lxiv 3) says that Galba, true to his principle that an emperor should not act under compulsion, refused to yield to the popular clamour, though, had it not been for this clamour, he would probably have executed Tigellinus and his fellows, as he executed Narcissus, Locusta the poisoner, and others. According to Tacitus (H. i 72) it was the influence of Vinius which protected Tigellinus: Apud Galbam Titi Vinii potentia defensus (Tigellinus) praetexentis servatam ab eo filiam. Haud dubie servaverat non clementia, quippe tot interfectis, sed effugium in futurum, quia pessimus quisque diffidentia praesentium mutationem pavens adversus publicum odium privatam gratiam praeparat. Plutarch (Galb. 17) adds that Tigellinus had secured the protection of Vinius by large sums of money.
: the particular procuratorship is nowhere specified; he may be the same Halotus as is mentioned in C.I.L. vi 8833, Halotus Aug(usti) l(ibertus) proc(urator).
: cf. Calig. 39, 2, avaritiae singulos increpans: Apul. Apol. 77, levitatis et inconstantiae increpitus. For the wide use of the Genitive of the Charge in non-class. Latin see Kühner-Stegmann, i 463.

: Plutarch (l.c.) says that the edict alleged that Tigellinus was' dying of a wasting disease, and it asked the people not to stain the rule of Galba by needless bloodshed: ὁ ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος ἐπεπλήχθη (increpitus est) διαγράμματι (edicto) τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος Τιγελλῖνον μὲν οὐ πολὺν ἔτι βιώσεσθαι φάσκοντος χρόνον ὑπὸ φθινάδος νόσου δαπανώμενον, ἐκείνους δὲ παραιτουμένου μὴ διαγριαίνειν μηδὲ τυραννικὴν ποιεῖν τὴν ἡγεμονίαν.
: propere, a variant in the later MSS., was approved by Burman and read by Oudendorp.

: in all the other passages (Iul. 19, 2; Tib. 13, 2: 34, 2; Calig. 27, 4; Ner. 2, 1:38, 1) where Suetonius uses offensus it means "offended," and so the reading offensis here is preferable to the variant offensus (XN) "offensive," which is adopted by Roth.
: see on Dom. 19.

: "was in a blaze of unpopularity"; cf. Aug. 27, 3, multiplici flagravit invidia: Tib. 44, 1, maiore adhuc et turpiore infamia flagravit. The phrases flagrare invidia, infamia, etc. are common in Cicero. Wickham on Hor. S. i 4, 125, cum flagret rumore malo, explains flagrare as meaning "to be in the full glow of," i.e. to be the conspicuous victim of.
: see on c. 11.

: Plutarch (Galb. 2) says it was 7500 drachmae (= 30,000 sesterces) to each of the praetorians, and 1250 drachmae (= 5000 sesterces) to each of the other soldiers. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) calculates the total sum thus promised as 900 million sesterces, and suggests that Nymphidius, when making the promise, probably knew that Galba would refuse to pay the sum and hoped to gain by the consequent dissatisfaction of the troops. For the practice of granting such donativa to the soldiers, and the amounts given by other emperors see on Dom. 2, 3.
: Nymphidius Sabinus (see on c. 11) and the other officers who repeated his promises to their men.
: = promisissent; cf. Dom. 4, 5: Calig. 46: Iul. 19, 1: 26, 2. So in Cicero, e.g. Att. i 16, 13, P. Clodium pronuntiare solitum esse et non dare. ..

: Tacitus (H. i 5) says that these were noble words from the point of view of the commonwealth but dangerous for Galba himself: accessit Galbae vox pro re publica honesta, ipsi anceps, legi a se militem, non emi. Dio (lxiv 3) mentions the incident as an example of Galba's strength of will in refusing to submit to dictation: εἰ καὶ τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τῇ τε νόσῳ ἐκεκμήκει, ἀλλὰ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἤκμαζεν, οὐδ᾽ ἠξίου τὸν αὐτοκράτορα ἀναγκαζόμενόν τι ποιεῖν· ἀμέλει καὶ τοῖς δορυφόροις (praetorianis) αὐτοῦσι χρήματα οὐκ ἔδωκε, καὶ ἔφη γε ὅτι “καταλέγειν στρατιώτας ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀγοράζειν εἴωθα.” Plutarch characterizes this utterance of Galba as “ φωνὴ ἡγεμόνι μεγάλῳ πρέπουσα” (Galb. 18).
: eâ causâ; see on Vesp. 4, 3.
: Plut. (l.c.), πυθομένοις τοῦτο δεινὸν εἰσῆλθε μίσος καὶ ἄγριον πρὸς αὐτόν. Tacitus (H. i 25) says that the soldiers were turned against Galba "ira et desperatione dilati toties donativi.”

: indignitas is used here in its subjective sense of "indignation"; cf. Cic. Att. x 8, 3, tacita esse poterit indignitas nostra?: Liv. vii 7, 2, plenus irae et indignitatis. The objective sense of "indignity" is much more frequent, and Baumg.-Cr. explains indignitas in our passage by contumelia. In Calig. 23, 2, indignitates means "indignities," but in the only other place where Suetonius uses the word, Claud. 36, Messalinae amorem flagrantissimum non tam indignitate contumeliarum quam periculi metu abiecit, it seems to mean "indignation" (cf. Liv. viii 28, 6, ingens vis hominum cum aetatis miseratione tum indignitate iniuriae accensa concurrit); Rolfe and Pike, however, explain indignitate contumeliarum as "her unseemly and insulting conduct."

: Tacitus (H. i 20) gives the names of some of the officers cashiered by Galba when he heard of the revolt of the legions in Germany: exauctorati per eas dies tribuni, e praetorio Antonius Taurus et Antonius Naso, ex urbanis cohortibus Aemilius Pacensis, e vigilibus Iulius Fronto.

: those who owed their promotion to Nymphidius incurred the suspicion of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 25, stimulant primores militum per beneficia Nymphidii ut suspectos. For the attempts of Nymphidius to seduce the praetorians from their allegiance to Galba see note on c. 11. His favourites, after their humiliation by Galba, flocked to support Otho; Plut. Galb. 23, πλεῖστοι δὲ τῶν περὶ Τιγελλῖνον καὶ Νυμφίδιον ἐν τιμῇ γεγονότων ἀπερριμμένοι καὶ ταπεινὰ πράττοντες ἐφθείροντο (“rushed headlong") πρὸς αὐτὸν (i.e. Otho) καὶ συνηγανάκτουν καὶ παρώξυνον.

div.p: § 2. superioris Germaniae exercitus: the army of Upper Germany consisted of the following legions: iv Macedonica, xxi Rapax, xxii Primigenia (ii Augusta, which originally belonged to it, had been sent to Britain by Claudius, Tac. A. xiv 37). Tacitus (H. i 8) describes the dangerous temper of the armies in Germany at this time: Germanici exercitus, quod periculosissimum in tantis viribus (7 legions in all), solliciti et irati, superbia recentis victoriae (over Vindex) et metu tanquam alias partes (i.e. the side of Verginius Rufus) fovissent. Tarde a Nerone desciverant; nec statim pro Galba Verginius: an imperare noluisset dubium: delatum ei a milite imperium conveniebat. Fonteium Capitonem occisum (note on c. 11) etiam qui queri non poterant, tamen indignabantur. Dux deerat, abducto Verginio per simulationem amicitiae; quem non remitti atque etiam reum esse tanquam suum crimen ("an accusation against themselves'') accipiebant. Galba replaced Verginius by Hordeonius Flaccus, a feeble old man incapable of maintaining discipline, and sent Aulus Vitellius to command in Lower Germany (Vitell. 7, 1). Cf. also Dio lxiv 4, and Plut. Galb. 18 where an example is given of the mutinous spirit of the army under Hordeonius Flaccus: one day when games were being held and the officers according to custom made vows for the happiness of the emperor, the soldiers turbulently added the words "If he deserves it." For the boundaries, etc., of the two Germanies (superior and inferior) see on Vitell. 7, 1.

p.note: : see on c. 9, 2, and c. 11. Plut. (l.c.), οἱ ὑπὸ Φλάκκῳ, μεγάλων μὲν ἀξιοῦντες αὑτοὺς διὰ τὴν μάχην, ἣν ἐμαχέσαντο πρὸς Οὐΐνδικα, μηδένος δὲ τυγχάνοντες, ἀπαρηγόρητοι τοῖς ἄρχουσιν ἦσαν. Kal. Ian. adigi

: Tac. H. i 12, Paucis post kalendas Ianuarias diebus Pompeii Propinqui procuratoris e Belgica litterae adferuntur, superioris Germaniae legiones rupta sacramenti reverentia imperatorem alium flagitare et senatui ac populo Romano arbitrium eligendi permittere, quo seditio mollius acciperetur. Tacitus (c. 55) says further that the army of Lower Germany did take the oath to Galba, though not without a turbulent display on the part of some, whereas in Upper Germany the two legions (iv and xxii) which were quartered at Moguntiacum (Mainz) broke in pieces the images of Galba; cf. Plut. Galb. 22, τὰς μὲν εἰκόνας τοῦ Γάλβα προσελθόντες ἀνέτρεψαν καὶ κατέσπασαν, αὐτοὶ δ᾽ ὀμόσαντες ὑπὲρ συγκλήτου (senatus) καὶ δήμου ῾Ῥωμαίων διελύθησαν.
: for the oath of fealty to the emperor and its renewal at certain times see on c. 11.

: cf. c. 10, 1. Tacitus (i 55) observes that such a form of words was so long disused that it had become meaningless: ac ne reverentiam imperii exuere viderentur, senatus populique Romani oblitterata iam nomina sacramento advocabant: c. 56, in senatus ac populi Romani verba iurasse, id sacramentum inane visum.

: the various occasions on which the praetorians played the part of "king-makers" are collected by Cagnat (Daremberg-Saglio, iv 632 sqq.). Caligula's death was due to them, and on the next day they saluted Claudius as emperor; Nero was recognised by them, and the senate conformed to their decision; they support Galba, and then desert him for Otho; they overthrow Domitian and choose Nerva; Marcus Aurelius and Verus on their adoption hasten to secure the support of the praetorians by a largess of 20,000 sesterces to each; they plot the death of Commodus; they elevate Pertinax to the throne, and in 87 days put him to death; they auction the Roman empire to Didius Julianus, who promised to each of them 6,250 denarii. Septimius Severus (193-211 A.D.) dealt sternly with them and reorganised them, but they soon recovered their dominant influence in state affairs. They put to death Maximus and Balbinus, and hailed Gordian III as emperor (238 A.D.); to them Maxentius, the predecessor of Constantine, applied to be saluted as Augustus. They were finally disbanded by Constantine in 312 A.D.

: the jealousy felt by the troops in Germany at the elevation of Galba by those in Spain is illustrated by the words of one of the mutineers in Upper Germany urging the selection of Vitellius, the commander in the Lower province: “φέρε, τοῦτον ἑλόμενοι δείξωμεν ἀνθρώποις πᾶσιν ὡς Ἰβήρων καὶ Λυσιτανῶν ἀμείνους ἐσμὲν αὐτοκράτορα αἱρεῖσθαι.” (Plut. Galb. 22).
