Galba's proclamation as emperor by the 6th legion in Spain disclosed what Tacitus calls a "constitutional secret," that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome (H. i 4, evolgato imperii arcano, posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri).
: Tacitus (H. i 12) says that the Germanic legions left the ““arbitrium eligendi" to the senate and Roman people; but the senate, of course, could merely ratify the choice made by the praetorians.
: by a despatch from Pompeius Propinquus, procurator of Gallia Belgica; see Tac. H. i 12 quoted on c. 16, 2.

: despectus in Caesar (and Lucretius) is used in the sense of a "view downwards"; it is once used for an "object of contempt' in Rhet. Her. 1v 39, 51, filii parvi ludibrio et despectui paternis inimicis erunt oppositi; in post-Aug. prose it is used both for "contempt" and "object of contempt" (in this latter sense only in dat., as here and Tac. H. iv 57, non adeo turbatam rem Romanam ut Treveris etiam despectui sit). Cf. contemptui, despicatui, esse, habere, ducere. Cicero has despicientia despising," "contempt."

: Plut. Galb. 19, ὁ δὲ (Γάλβας) φοβηθείς, ὡς μὴ μόνον διὰ τὸ γῆρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὴν ἀπαιδίαν καταφρονούμενος, ἐβουλεύετο παῖδα θέσθαι (“adopt ") τῶν ἐπιφανῶν τινα νεανίσκον καὶ διάδοχον ἀποδεῖξαι τῆς ἀρχῆς: Tac. H. ii 1 materia sermonibus senium et orbitas principis et intemperantia civitatis, donec unus eligatur, multos destinandi.

: the full name was Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi Licinianus. He was son of M. Licinius Crassus Frugi (cons. 27 A.D.) and Scribonia, a granddaughter of Sex. Pompeius. Of his three brothers one was put to death by Claudius, one by Nero, and the third, Licinius Crassus Scribonianus, refused the empire when it was offered to him by Antonius Primus (Tac. H. iv 39). Born in 38, he was for long exiled by Nero (Tac. i 48) and so held no magistracies at Rome. He only survived his adoption by Galba for four days, as he was dragged from the temple of Vesta and murdered by Otho's soldiers at the time when Galba was slain. egregium iuvenem: Plutarch (Galb. 23) describes him as “veavíaς ἐν τῇ πρὸς πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν εὐφυΐᾳ τὸ κόσμιον καὶ αὐστηρὸν ἐμφανέστατα ἔχων,” “a young man whose self-control and austerity were the most conspicuous traits in a character naturally inclined to every virtue"; cf. Tac. H. i 14, vultu habituque moris antiqui et aestimatione recta severus, deterius interpretantibus tristior habebatur: Dio lxiv 5, νεανίσκος εὐγενής, ἐπιεικής, φρόνιμος. testamento: Tacitus and Plutarch make no mention of Piso's having been named as heir in Galba's will. Dessau (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1, 313) regards Suetonius' statement here as quite unreliable.

: Bentley's insuper may be right; Cornelissen suggested nuper. If genuine, semper means that Galba never altered his will in the way, for example, that Julius Caesar did; cf. Iul. 83, where we learn that Caesar, from his first consulship to the beginning of the civil war, was wont to write down Cn. Pompeius as his heir and to read this to the assembled soldiers; in his last will, however, he named three other heirs, and at the end of the will adopted Gaius Octavius into his family and gave him his name (in familiam nomenque adoptavit). ..

: cf. Claud. 39, 2, (Claudius) adsciturus in nomen Neronem; Tac. H. i 15, Crassi subolem (i.e. Piso Licinianus) in penates meos adsciscere: A. iii 30, Crispum C. Sallustius in nomen adscivit. For the so-called adoption by will, which was really appointment of heir with direction to bear testator's name, see Roby, Roman Private Law, i 59 n. After his adoption as Galba's successor, Piso's name seems to have been Servius Sulpicius Galba Caesar; on Jan. 10, the day of his adoption, the Fratres Arvales sacrificed "[ob adoptione[m Ser. Sulpici Gal]bae C[aesaris]'' (Henzen, Acta Fratr. Arv. xci).

: this account differs from that in Tac. H. i 14 where we are told that Galba, having decided to adopt a successor, held a "council for the election of an emperor (comitia imperii)" at which were present Vinius, Laco, Marius Celsus (consul designate) and Ducenius Geminus (prefect of the city). Galba, after a few remarks on his advanced years, ordered Piso to be summoned "seu propria electione sive, ut quidam crediderunt, Lacone instigante." Galba knew that some of his friends would have preferred Otho or Dolabella (for whom see c. 12, 2) to Piso; Vinius was for Otho; Laco and Icelus were agreed, not in supporting any particular individual, but in opposing the nominee of Vinius (Tac., c. 13). Plutarch, Galb. 23, says that Galba without a word beforehand suddenly sent for Piso (ἄφνω μηδὲν προειπὼν μετεπέμψατο Πείσωνα) and went down with him to the camp to announce him as "Caesar" and as his successor.

: in presence of the assembled soldiers in the praetorian camp; Tac. H. i 18, apud frequentem militum contionem imperatoria brevitate adoptari a se Pisonem exemplo divi Augusti et more militari quo vir virum legeret, pronuntiat. Galba had previously discussed the advisability of making the announcement in this way or from the Rostra to the assembled people or in the Curia to the senate: Tас. с. 17, consultatum inde, pro Rostris an in senatu an in castris adoptio nuncuparetur. Iri in castra placuit: honorificum id militibus fore, quorum favorem ut largitione et ambitu male adquiri, ita per bonas artes haud spernendum. Augustus adopted Gaius and Lucius (Suet. Aug. 64, 65) and Claudius adopted Nero (Tac. A. xii 26) in the ordinary method prescribed by law, but Galba adopted Piso, not "lege curiata apud pontifices, ut moris est" (Tac. H. i 15), but by mere public declaration (nuncupatio pro contione); Nerva did the same in the case of Trajan (Dio lxviii 3), and this method was probably continued by later emperors (Mommsen, Staatsr. if³ 1137 sq.).

: Plutarch (Galb. 23) describes the "festering" discontent of the sullen soldiers when no largess was given: ἦν δὲ καὶ τὰ τῶν στρατιωτῶν ὕπουλα καὶ σκυθρωπὰ μηδὲ τότε δωρεᾶς αὐτοῖς δοθείσης. Tacitus too says that a little liberality on Galba's part would have gained for him the soldiers: constat potuisse conciliari animos quantulacumque parci senis liberalitate; nocuit antiquus rigor et nimia severitas, cui iam pares non sumus. It was usual to distribute a donativum when the emperor made an adoption, e.g. when Hadrian adopted Verus (Spart. Hadr. 23).

: see Plut. c. 24 for the ease with which the agents of Otho by bribes and promises won over the soldiers who were already rotten" with disaffection and only looking for a pretext (ἤδη σαθροὺς ὄντας καὶ δεομένους προφάσεως).

: Piso was adopted on Jan. 10 and Galba was slain on Jan. 15, which was the sixth day after, according to the Roman inclusive method of reckoning; so Plut. (l.c.) ἕκτῃ γὰρ ἀνῃρέθησαν (i.e. Galba and Piso were slain), ἣν ἄγουσι Ῥωμαῖοι πρὸ δεκαοκτὼ καλανδῶν Φεβρουαρίων (= ante diem octavum decimum kalendas Februarias). Tacitus says that Piso was 'quadriduo Caesar'" (H. i 48). Instead of a clause with quam after ante, post, intra, we find at times in post-Aug. authors a genitive depending on the accusative after these prepositions; e.g. Claud. 27, 1, ante quintum mensem divortii: Tac. A. i 62, sextum post cladis annum: id. H. ii 70, intra quadragesimum pugnae diem: Vell. Pat. i 10, 5, ante paucos triumphi dies. Already in class. Lat. we have post diem tertium eius diei, Cic. Att. iii 7, 1, Tusc. i 114 (see KühnerStegmann, i 405). Suetonius also uses quam, e.g. Iul. 35, 2, intra quintum quam adfuerat diem (so in Liv., etc.).

: an enumeration of the omens and prodigies foreboding the death of a Caesar is characteristic of the Lives; cf. Iul. 81, Aug. 97, Tib. 74, Calig. 57, Claud. 46, Ner. 46, Oth. 8, Vitell. 9, Vesp. 23, Tit. 10, Dom. 15. See Introd. c. ii.
: the whole length of his march from Spain to Rome to assume the empire.

: cf. Calig. 13 (Caligula's journey from Misenum to Rom, on his accession), inter altaria et victimas ardentesque taedas densissimo et laetissimo obviorum agmine incessit: Curt. v 1, 20 (Alexander's entry into Babylon), Plures obviam egressi sunt inter quos Bagophanes, arcis et regiae pecuniae custos, totum iter floribus coronisque constraverat, argenteis altaribus utroque latere dispositis, quae non ture modo, sed omnibus odoribus cumulaverat : Tac. H. ii 70 (Vitellius visits the battlefield of Betriacum), Nec minus inhumana pars viae quam Cremonenses lauru rosaque constraverant, extructis altaribus caesisque victimis regium in morem: Appian Bell. Civ. v 24 (the coming to Rome of Octavian and Antonius after peace had been made between them), παροδεύουσιν αὐτοῖς, οἷα σωτῆρσιν, ἐγίγνοντο θυσίαι. See also Hirt. Bell. Gall. viii 51. Such honours, as Casaubon says, were originally paid to the gods when their statues were moved from one place to another (cf. Cic. Verr. iv 35). =
: per oppida, κατὰ πόλεις. This adv., used also in Aug. 59, is not cited from any other author. For the remarkable number of adverbs in -im used by Suetonius see App. I. § 1. f.
: the larger victims were usually slain by an axe (securis, dolabra) or hammer (malleus); sheep, pigs, and birds had their throats cut with a knife (culter).

: a victim's breaking away from the altar was a sure portent of disaster; see on Tit. 10, 1. Cf. Amm. Marc. xxiv 6, 17 (describing a portent of Julian's approaching end), conplures hostias Marti parabat ultori, et ex tauris pulcherrimis decem ad hoc perductis, nondum aris admoti voluntate sua novem procubuere tristissimi, decimus vero, qui diffractis vinculis lapsus aegre reductus est, mactatus ominosa signa monstravit.

: these speculatores were picked soldiers (lancers) of the praetorian cohorts who formed a special bodyguard for the emperor at Rome, on journeys, and on military expeditions; cf. Claud. 35, 1, neque convivia inire ausus est (Claudius) nisi ut speculatores cum lanceis circumstarent: Tac. H. ii 11, ipsum Othonem comitabantur speculatorum lecta corpora cum ceteris praetoriis cohortibus, etc. They are distinct from the speculatores legionum of whom each legion had ten, acting as despatchbearers, etc. Marquardt (Staatsv. ii² 547) and Cauer (Eph. Epigr. iv 464) hold that they were, at least during the first cent., formed into a special corps, a mounted corps, under special officers, and distinct from the rest of the praetorians. On the other hand, von Domaszewski (Die Religion des röm. Heeres p. 94) thinks that the speculatores always formed an integral part of the praetorian cohorts; each cohort contained 24 of them (Tac. H. i 27, 31, 35), and as the cohorts were 12 in number, the total number of speculatores was 288, or roughly 300. See Daremberg-Saglio, iv 637; Smilda on Suet. Claud. 35.
: see on Vesp. 25.

: cf. Ner. 48, 2 (describing Nero's last flight from Rome), statim tremore terrae et fulgure adverso pavefactus. ‘“terrae tremor” for “terrae motus" (Vesp. 17) is a poetical expression used in post-Aug. prose.

: cf. Amm. Marc. xvii 7, 14, inter haec tria genera terrae motuum mycematiae (mycematias, μυκηματιάς, is a rumbling earthquake) sonitu audiuntur minaci, cum dissolutis elementa compagibus ultro absiliunt vel relabuntur concidentibus terris; tunc enim necesse est velut taurinis reboare mugitibus fragores fremitusque terrenos: Sen. N.Q. vi 13, 4, antequam terra moveatur, solet mugitus audiri ventis in abdito tumultuantibus; nec enim aliter posset, ut ait noster Vergilius (Aen. vì 256), “sub pedibus mugire solum et iuga celsa moveri,” nisi hoc esset ventorum opus.

div.p: § 2. monile margaritis gemmisque consertum: among the presents lavished by Caligula on the pampered horse Incitatus (which he once thought of making consul) were “monilia e gemmis” (Calig. 55, 3). For the adornment of the statues of goddesses with jewelry cf. Plin. N.H. ix 121, where we are told that the second of the two famous pearls from the earrings of Cleopatra (the companion to that which she dissolved in vinegar and drank) was cut in two to serve as pendants for the ears of Venus in the Pantheon at Rome. Julius Caesar dedicated to Venus Genetrix (in the temple which he built for her in the Forum Iulium) a breastplate (thorax) made of British pearls (Plin. N.H. ix 116, Solin. 54).

p.note: : for the story of this image of Fortune, which he treasured in his villa at Tusculum, see c. 4, 3.
: causal, see on Tit. 8, 1.

: Suetonius mentions a temple of the Capitoline Venus in Calig. 7, where he says that Livia dedicated there a statue of a son of Germanicus in the guise of Cupid (effigiem habitu Cupidinis in aede Capitolinae Veneris Livia dedicavit). There is no other reference to this temple, which some would identify with the shrine (or altar) of Venus Victrix on the Capitol (C.I.L. i² p. 245). Jordan (Topogr. Rom і 2, 42) says that there is nothing definite known of any other temple of Venus on the Capitol besides that of Venus Eryciną, vowed in 217 B.C. by Q. Fabius Maximus after the battle of Trasimenus and dedicated by him in 215. Platner and Ashby, Topogr. Dict. Rome p. 551, regard it as "altogether probable" that this is the aedes Capitolina Veneris.
: see on c. 4, 3.

: phantom" (= simulacrum, εἴδωλον) cf. Ner. 34, 4, saepe confessus exagitari se materna specie: Calig. 50, inter ceteras (imagines noctis) pelagi quondam speciem colloquentem secum videre visus: Claud. 1, 2; 37, 2: Aug. 96, 1. This poetical use of species is found in prose from Livy on.
: sc. imperium.

: cf. Petron. Satyr. 114, ut Lycas Tryphaenae somnium expiavit; Mart. xi 50, 8, expiet ut somnos garrula saga tuos. Sacrifice was one method adopted to avert the evil portended by bad dreams; the offering of salted cakes (salsae molae) and incense (tus) is often mentioned, e.g. Plaut. Amph. 740, sed, mulier, postquam experrecta es, te prodigiali Iovi | aut mola salsa hodie aut ture conprecatam oportuit; Tibull. i 5, 14, Ipse procuravi ne possent saeva nocere | somnia ter sancta deveneranda mola. Another method was lustration in running water, e.g. Pers. ii 16, noctem flumine purgas; Sil. Ital. viii 124, sub lucem ut visa secundent | oro caelicolas ac vivo purgor in amni.

: everything was the direct opposite of what it should have been for a successful sacrifice: the fire should have been blazing; the attendants on the sacrificing priest should have been young (like the camilli) and robed in white; the incense should have been carried in an ornate incense box (acerra); the wine should have been poured from a patera, which at this period was usually of silver or gold and richly wrought.

: from this glass dish or bowl the grains of incense would be thrown on to the fire-pan or brasier (cf. Rich 125, where a similar vessel of agate is illustrated). A catinus (or catinum) of black earthenware (like the black Etruscan pottery) was used at primitive sacrifices in the days of Numa; cf. Juv. vi 343, simpuvium (“libation-ladle'") ridere Numae nigrumque catinum: Apul. Mag. 18, eadem paupertas etiam populo Romano imperium a primordio fundavit, proque eo in hodiernum diis immortalibus simpulo et catino fictili sacrificat. For the various uses of the catinus see Pauly-Wissowa, iii 1790.
: the MSS. give thus, but in the other three passages where the word occurs they give the forms ture and tura, and Ihm restores tus here.

div.p: $ 3. coronam de capite excidisse: another portent of dire disaster; cf. Sil. Ital. xvi 268 (when Syphax was sacrificing), Vittaque, maiorum decoramen, fronte sine ullo | delapsa adtactu, nudavit tempora regis. | Talia caelicolae casuro tristia regno | signa dabant, saevique aderant gravia omina fati; Sen. Thyest. 701 (when Atreus, like a sacrificing priest, slays the children of Thyestes), regium capiti decus (i.e. his diadem) | bis terque lapsum est. When Vitellius set out from Germany on his march to Rome, the laurel wreath which he had donned fell into a stream (Vitell. 9); Alexander's death was foreshadowed by his diadem being blown from his head by the wind near Babylon (App. Syr. 56).

p.note: : omens were derived from the appetite of birds, generally chickens (pulli, hence auspicia pullaria used for such omens). The chickens were kept in a coop (cavea), and if a general or magistrate wished to get omens from them, they were let out and food was thrown to them, the pullarii drawing various conclusions from the degree of eagerness which they showed in eating, the most favourable sign (solistimum tripudium) being when they ate so greedily that some of the grain fell from their bills to the ground. Any attempt on the part of the birds to fly away was most inauspicious, and this was among the warning signs given to C. Hostilius Mancinus (cons. 137 B.C.) when starting on his disastrous campaign in the Numantine war in Spain: Val. Max. i 6, 7, cum Lavinii sacrificium facere vellet (Mancinus), pulli cavea emissi in proximam silvam fugerunt, summaque diligentia quaesiti reperiri nequiverunt. Claudius Pulcher began a sea-fight off Sicily (249 B.C.) though the sacred chickens would not eat, throwing them into the sea in defiance of the omen, and saying that they might drink since they would not eat (Suet. Tib. 2, 2).

: the adoption of Piso (c. 17) on Jan. 10, 69 A.D. Suetonius says nothing of the boding storm of rain and thunder accompanying the adoption, which is described in Tac. H. i 18 and Plut. Galb. 23. Tacitus adds 'observatum id antiquitus comitiis dirimendis non terruit Galbam, quo minus in castra pergeret, contemptorem talium, ut fortuitorum, seu, quae fato manent, quamvis significata, non vitantur.” Plutarch says it was manifest that heaven disapproved of the ill-omened adoption.

: the "campstool” placed for the commander-inchief on the tribunal from which he delivered his harangue to the troops; it resembled the ordinary sella curulis but was less elaborate; the sella curulis was a folding chair without back or arms and with legs curved like pincers, while the sella castrensis had straight legs; the seat was of straps covered with a cushion (see the illustrations in Daremberg-Saglio iv 1180; Smith Dict. Ant. ii³ 620). Like modern campstools, the sella curulis gave way at times and the occupant came ignominiously to the ground; this happened to Augustus at the games on the dedication of the theatre of Marcellus: evenit ut laxatis sellae curulis compagibus caderet supinus (Aug. 43, 5).

: when the emperor appeared in the senate he sat between the consuls and, like them, on a raised sella curulis; see Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 936. This seat was first assigned to Augustus in 19 B.с. (Dio liv 10). The adj. curulis is for * currulis from currus a chariot, this explanation being given in Gell. iii 18 on the authority of Gavius Bassus, “senatores enim dicit in veterum aetate, qui curulem magistratum gessissent, curru solitos honoris gratia in curiam vehi, in quo curru sella esset, super quam considerent, quae ob eam causam‘curulis' appellatur.”

: this perhaps means “back to the front," though there is no means of determining what difference there was between the back and the front of a sella curulis; another possible meaning is "askew” “sideways," and so La Harpe renders it "de travers.”

: this was the sacrifice at which Otho was present (see Oth. 6) and, as Plutarch says, was almost delivered up to Galba by the hand of the gods: Galb. 24, ἐκείνῃ (τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) γὰρ ἕωθεν εὐθὺς ὁ μὲν Γάλβας ἔθυεν ἐν Παλατίῳ τῶν φίλων παρόντων, ὁ δὲ θύτης Ὀμβρίκιος ἅμα τῷ λαβεῖν εἰς τὰς χεῖρας τοῦ ἱερείου τὰ σπλάγχνα καὶ προσιδεῖν οὐ δι' αἰνιγμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄντικρυς ἔφη σημεῖα μεγάλης ταραχῆς καὶ μετὰ δόλου κίνδυνον ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἐπικείμενον τῷ αὐτοκράτορι, μονονουχὶ τὸν Ὄθωνα τοῦ θεοῦ χειρὶ ληπτὸν παραδιδόντος. Cf. also Dio lxiv 5; Tac. H. i 27, Octavo decimo kalendas Februarias (i.e. Jan. 15) sacrificanti pro aede Apollinis Galbae haruspex Umbricius tristia exta et instantes insidias ac domesticum hostem praedicit, audiente Othone (nam proximus adstiterat) idque ut laetum e contrario et suis cogitationibus prosperum interpretante. The way in which Otho escaped from his dangerous predicament and was carried off to the camp to be proclaimed emperor is described in Oth. 6.

: 'soothsayer," lit. 'entrail-observer" (root ghar, cf. hirae, hillae, ilia, χόλιξ), one who foretold the future from the appearance of the entrails of the sacrifice. This was an Etruscan form of divination. Victims sacrificed for this purpose were called hostiae consultatoriae; ordinary sacrificial victims were called hostiae animales.

: Tacitus says that it was while Galba was still keeping on sacrificing and importuning the gods of an empire no longer his: ignarus interim Galba et sacris intentus fatigabat alieni iam imperii deos, cum affertur rumor rapi in castra incertum quem senatorem, mox Othonem esse qui raperetur; simul ex tota urbe, ut quisque obvius fuerat, alii formidine augentes, quidam minora vero, ne tum quidem obliti adulationis (H. i 29). So too Plutarch (Galb. 25) says that the soothsayer still held the entrails in his hands when the news arrived which dumbfounded even those who had been sceptical of the truth of such presages.
: this is one of the few instances of the historic present in Suetonius: see Appendix I. § 9. a.

: the castra praetoria (praetoriana Suet.) or permanent camp for the praetorian cohorts was an institution of Tiberius on the advice of Sejanus in 23 A.D.; cf. Tib. 37, 1, Romae castra constituit, quibus praetorianae cohortes, vagae ante id tempus et per hospitia dispersae, continerentur: Aug. 49, 1, numquam plures quam tres cohortes in urbe passus est (Augustus), easque sine castris. It lay to the N.E. of Rome, outside the Servian agger, between the Viminal and Colline gates, and so commanded the important roads (Salaria, Nomentana, Tiburtina) leading eastward. For a description of it see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Romi 3, 385 sqq. and the plan in Daremberg-Saglio iv 634. It figures largely in the history of the Empire from Claudius to Vespasian, and is mentioned in Tac. A. iv 2, xi 31, xii 69, xiii 14, xv 53, 59; H. i 31, ii 93, iii 84, etc. 1

: Tacitus (H. i 32 sq.) mentions the two courses of action suggested to Galba, one advocated by Vinius, the other by Laco and Icelus: Interim Galbam duae sententiae distinebant. Titus Vinius manendum intra domum, opponenda servitia, firmandos aditus, non eundum ad iratos censebat Festinandum ceteris videbatur, antequam cresceret invalida adhuc coniuratio paucorum Vel si cadere necesse sit, occurrendum discrimini; id Othoni invidiosius et ipsis honestum. ...
: see on ‘“nihil aliud quam,” Dom. 21.

: Suetonius here differs from Tacitus (H. i 34) who says that Galba decided to follow the advice of his more plausible supporters to go out and face the mutinous soldiery, and that he sent Piso (his adopted son) in advance to the praetorian camp, as being likely to gain the favour of the cohorts by his great name and popularity, and by his hostility to Vinius whom the soldiers hated. Plutarch (Galb. 25) agrees in the main with the account of Tacitus.

: Nero's legion “prima Adiutrix classicorum” (see on c. 12, 2) was at Rome; also chosen contingents from the armies of Germany, Britain, and Illyricum, which Nero had prepared to send against the Albani but had recalled on the revolt of Vindex (Tac. H. i 6). The legion which Galba had recruited in Spain (“septima Galbiana," see c. 10, 2), and which had accompanied him to Rome, had been despatched to Pannonia (Тас. Н. ii 11).
: see on "plurifariam,” Vitell. 9.

: "were quartered" (c. 12, 2, n.). The contingent of the Illyrian army was quartered at this time in the Porticus Vipsania (in the Campus Martius), and the contingent of the German army in the Atrium Libertatis (near the Circus Flaminius ?); see Tac. H. i 31.

: sumpto thorace, Tac. c. 35; τεθωρακισμένος, Plut. c. 27. A cuirass or corselet of linen is frequently mentioned in Greek writers. In Homer the epithet λινοθώρηξ is applied to the Locrian Ajax and the Mysian Amphios (Il. ii 529, 830), and a linen cuirass was worn by the Persians (Xen. Cyrop. vi 4, 2), Egyptians (Hdt. ii 182), Phoenicians (Paus. vi 19, 4), and Chalybes (Xen. Anab. iv 7, 15); cf. also Arr. Tact. 14. Nepos (Iphicr. 1) says of Iphicrates: genus loricarum mutavit, et pro sertis atque aeneis linteas dedit; quo facto expeditiores milites reddidit: nam, pondere detracto, quod aeque corpus tegeret et leve esset, curavit. Pausanias (i 21, 8) says that these cuirasses made of folds of linen were of little use in war, though a protection in hunting: οἱ δὲ θώρακες οἱ λινοῖ μαχομένοις μὲν οὐχ ὁμοίως εἰσὶ χρήσιμοι, διϊᾶσι γὰρ καὶ βιαζόμενοι τὸν σίδηρον, θηρεύοντας δὲ ὠφελοῦσιν, ἐναποκλῶνται γάρ σφισι καὶ λεόντων ὀδόντες καὶ παρδάλεων. Casaubon cites from the Byzantine historian Nicetas Acominatus (c. 1190 A.D.) a description of a linen cuirass worn by Conrad; it was made with eighteen folds and stiffened by steeping in vinegar and salt so as to be impenetrable by any weapon.
: see on Tit. 7, 2.

div.p: § 2. rumoribus falsis: there was a widespread rumour that Otho had been slain: Tac. H. i 34, vixdum egresso Pisone occisum in castris Othonem vagus primum et incertus rumor: mox, ut in magnis mendaciis, interfuisse se quidam et vidisse adfirmabant, credula fama inter gaudentes et incuriosos: Plut. Galb. 26, θροῦς διῆλθε πολύς, ὡς ἀνῃρημένου τοῦ Οθωνος.

p.note: : the use of conspirati as a subst. (= coniurati) is first found in Suetonius; cf. Iul. 82, 1: Dom. 17, 1.
: Tac. (l.c.), Multi arbitrabantur compositum auctumque rumorem mixtis iam Othonianis, qui ad evocandum Galbam laeta falso volgaverint. ..
: Tacitus says that everyone kept making positive assertions, though no one knew anything definite: nemo scire et omnes adfirmare.

: this rare adj. occurs first in Liv. vii 33; see on “osculabundus,” Vitell. 2, 5. Tacitus (c. 35) describes the crowd of all classes flocking to the Palace to congratulate Galba on the reported death of Otho: Tum vero non populus tantum et imperita plebs in plausus et inmodica studia, sed equitum plerique et senatorum, posito metu incauti, refractis Palatii foribus ruere intus ac se Galbae ostentare, praereptam sibi ultionem querentes, ignavissimus quisque et, ut res docuit, in periculo non ausurus, nimii verbis, linguae feroces.
: he was carried in a sella (φορεῖor) on account of the throng.

: this question was a proof of Galba's intrepidity in checking indiscipline; cf. Tac. (l. c.): Obvius in Palatio Iulius Atticus speculator (see note on c. 18, 1) cruentum gladium ostentans occisum a se Othonem exclamavit; et Galba “commilito,” inquit, “quis iussit?” insigni animo ad coercendam militarem licentiam, minitantibus intrepidus, adversus blandientes incorruptus. Dio (lxiv 6) supplies a version of the soldier's words as he showed the bloodstained sword: “Θάρσει, αὐτοκράτορ, Οθωνα γὰρ ἀπέκτεινα, καὶ ἔστι σοι δεινὸν ἔτι οὐδέν.” πιστεύσας οὖν ὁ Γάλβας πρὸς μὲν ἐκεῖνον εἶπε “Καὶ τίς σοι τοῦτο ποιῆσαι ἐκέλευσεν;” Plutarch (Galb. 26) adds that the soldier, a distinguished praetorian, replied to Galba that it was his oath of allegiance which bade him do the deed (τοῦ δὲ ἀνθρώπου τὴν πίστιν εἰπόντος καὶ τὸν ὅρκον, κ.τ.λ.).
: Bentley needlessly conjectured processerit.

: Tacitus (c. 40) gives a vivid account of the charge into the Forum which was ordered by Otho when he heard that Galba's supporters were arming the mob: Othoni tamen armari plebem nuntiabatur. Ire praecipites et occupare ("forestall'') pericula iubet. Igitur milites Romani, quasi Vologaesum aut Pacorum avito Arsacidarum solio depulsuri ac non imperatorem suum inermem et senem trucidare pergerent, disiecta plebe, proculcato senatu, truces armis, rapidi equis Forum irrumpunt. Nec illos Capitolii aspectus et imminentium templorum religio et priores et futuri principes terruere, quo minus facerent scelus, cuius ultor est quisquis successit.

: paganus (“rustic" or "peasant") is used at times in Silver Latin for a "civilian"; cf. Aug. 27, 3, concionante se, admissa turba paganorum, apud milites: Juv. xvi 32, citius falsum producere testem | contra paganum possis, quam vera loquentem | contra fortunam armati contraque pudorem: Tac. H. iii 24 (Antonius Primus rouses the praetorians with the taunt "vos, nisi vincitis, pagani"): i 53, inter paganos corruptior miles.

: this momentary halt on the part of Otho's attacking force is not mentioned by other writers. Plutarch (c. 26) says that the standard-bearer of the cohort accompanying Galba dashed to the ground the medallion of the emperor which was attached to the standard of the cohort, and at once the litter of Galba was attacked, first with javelins and then with swords; cf. Tac. (c. 41): Viso comminus armatorum agmine (i.e. Otho's troops) vexillarius comitatae Galbam cohortis dereptam Galbae imaginem solo adflixit. Eo signo manifesta in Othonem omnium militum studia, desertum fuga populi Forum, destricta adversus dubitantes tela.
: see on c. 20, 1, neque praesentium quemquam opem imperatori ferre conatum.

: there were various reports, friendly or otherwise, of the last words of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 41, Extremam eius vocem, ut cuique odium aut admiratio fuit, varie prodidere: alii suppliciter interrogasse quid mali meruisset, paucos dies exsolvendo donativo deprecatum; plures obtulisse ultro percussoribus iugulum: agerent ac ferirent, si ita e re publica videretur (Tacitus cynically adds "Non interfuit occidentium quid diceret"): Dio lxiv 6, τοῦτο μόνον εἰπών, “ Καὶ τί κακὸν ἐποίησα;”: Plut. Galb. 27, ὁ δὲ τὴν σφαγὴν (iugulum) προτείνας ‘“ Δρᾶτε” εἶπεν “εἰ τοῦτο τῷ δήμῳ ῾Ῥωμαίων ἄμεινόν ἐστι."
: these words form a trochaic septenarius (CCC-II-IC-II-CCI-II-I( - -) and seem to be a poetical quotation.
: Tacitus (l.c.) mentions this reported offer, but Plutarch and Dio say nothing of it. Galba had persistently refused to grant a donativum; see c. 16, 1, and c. 17.

: “agere" in the ritual of Roman sacrifice meant to slay the victim; the slayer (popa) before striking the blow asked the priest "Agone?”, “Shall I do it?", and he replied "Age” or “Hoc age"; cf. Ov. F. i 321, qui calido strictos tincturus sanguine cultros | semper agatne rogat, nec nisi iussus agit. This reply of the priest to the popa was a warning to the assembled people to keep silence and give attention to the solemn act; hence "hoc age" came to be used colloquially meaning "give attention." Suetonius uses it again in the sacrificial sense in Calig. 58, 2 (describing the assassination of Caligula by Chaerea): tradunt Chaeream cervicem gladio caesim graviter perculisse praemissa voce "Hoc age!” ..

: both Plutarch and Dio mention with great praise a centurion Sempronius Densus, who singlehanded made a gallant effort to protect Galba: Plut. Galb. 26, ῎Ημυνε δὲ οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ ὑπέστη πλὴν ἑνὸς ἀνδρός, ὃν μόνον ἥλιος ἐπεῖδεν ἐν μυριάσι τοσαύταις ἄξιον τῆς Ῥωμαίων ἡγεμονίας· Σεμπρώνιος ἦν Δῆνσος ἑκατοντάρχης, οὐδὲν ἰδίᾳ χρηστὸν ὑπὸ Γάλβᾳ πεπονθώς, τῷ δὲ καλῷ καὶ τῷ νόμῳ βοηθῶν προέστη τοῦ φορείου (“litter"). Καὶ τὸ κλῆμα (i.e. the vitis, or vine-switch carried by centurions) πρῶτον . . ἐπαράμενος τοῖς ἐπιφερομένοις ἐβόα καὶ διεκελεύετο φείδεσθαι τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος. Ἔπειτα συμπλεκ ομένων αὐτῷ σπασάμενος τὸ ξίφος ἠμύνατο πολὺν χρόνον, ἕως τυφθεὶς τὰς ἰγνύας ("knee-joints") ἔπεσε: Dio lxiv 6, καὶ αὐτῷ Σεμπρώνιος Δῆνσος ἑκατόνταρχος ἐπαμύνας ἐς ὅσον ἠδυνήθη, τέλος, ὡς οὐδὲν ἤνυσεν, ἐπεσφάγη. καὶ διὰ τοῦτό γε καὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐνέγραψα, ὅτι ἀξιώτατός ἐστι μνημονεύεσθαι. Tacitus, however, says that Sempronius showed this gallantry in defending Piso (Galba's adopted son), to whom he had been attached as a guard by Galba: Insignem illa die virum Sempronium Densum aetas nostra vidit. Centurio is praetoriae cohortis, a Galba custodiae Pisonis additus, stricto pugione occurrens armatis et scelus exprobrans ac modo manu modo voce vertendo in se percussores quanquam vulnerato Pisoni effugium dedit. Piso sought sanctuary in the temple of Vesta, but Otho's soldiers dragged him out and slew him.

: Galba had sent Celsus Marius to try and bring to his support the contingent of the Illyrian army quartered in the Porticus Agrippa; two centurions of the first rank (primipilares) were ordered to bring up the German soldiers quartered in the Atrium Libertatis (see on c. 19, 1). No confidence could be placed in Nero's legion "prima Adiutrix classicorum” which was incensed by Galba's massacre of their comrades (see on c. 12, 2). Three military tribunes were sent to the camp of the praetorians in a vain effort to recall them from the side of Otho. The Illyrian detachments drove Celsus away with a shower of javelins, and the legio classica joined the seditious praetorians who rejected with defiance the overtures of the tribunes sent by Galba. See Тас. с. 31.
: a correction by Turnebus of Germaniciorum; for the form "Germanicianus" see on Vesp. 6, 2.

: the vexillum, as distinct from the aquila and the signum (c. 12, 2, n.), was a special ensign reserved for a corps of temporary formation and for detachments; the name of such a detachment was vexillatio (first found in Suetonius); vexillum denoted both the ensign and the detachment, and vexillarius both the ensign-bearer and the soldier who formed part of the detachment. Another meaning of vexillarius was a time-expired soldier serving in the reserve company attached to each legion, such a company having a special vexillum or ensign.

: Tacitus says that the detachments from the German army wavered for a long while between Otho and Galba, being slow to desert Galba on account of his recent kindness: Germanica vexilla diu nutavere, invalidis adhuc corporibus et placatis animis, quod eos a Nerone Alexandriam praemissos atque inde rursus longa navigatione aegros impensiore cura Galba refovebat. Mommsen (Prov. Rom. Emp. ii 61) thinks that the sending of troops to Alexandria was in connexion with an Ethiopian war which Nero had planned inter reliqua bella (Plin. N.H. vi 29, 184), wishing to extend the imperial frontier in Africa. These plans were upset by the revolt of Vindex, and any troops which had been despatched were recalled.
: though the MSS. here and in Vesp. 21 give magnopere, their evidence in other passages is decisively in favour of the uncontracted forms magno (quanto, tanto) opere; see Ihm, p. liv.
: Wölfflin suggested refovisset (re- being lost after opere), as Tacitus (l.c.) has refovebat.

div.p: § 2. iugulatus est: “iugulum haurire" is the Virgilian mode of expression which Tacitus (c. 41) uses of the murder: De percussore non satis constat. Quidam Terentium evocatum (“one of the reserve" or "one of the select bodyguard" of Galba, see c. 10, 3), alii Laecanium; crebrior fama tradidit Camurium quintae decimae legionis militem impresso gladio iugulum eius hausisse. Ceteri crura brachiaque (nam pectus tegebatur) foede laniavere; pleraque volnera feritate et saevitia trunco iam corpori adiecta.

p.note: : Tac. (l.c.), iuxta Curti lacum trepidatione ferentium Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est: Plut. Galb. 27, τὸν δὲ Γάλβαν . περὶ τὸν Κουρτίου καλούμενον λάκκον ἐκκυλισθέντα. . ἔτυπτον ἐπιδραμόντες. The “lacus Curtius" was originally a pool or swamp in the centre of the site of the Roman Forum. It disappeared through being drained by the cloacae of Tarquin. Varro (L.L. v 148-150) mentions three traditions of the origin of the name: (1) the Sabine leader Mettius Curtius, hard pressed by the soldiers of Romulus, galloped his horse safely across the marsh (cf. Liv. i 12, Dion. Hal. ii 43); (2) in 362 B.C. a gulf opened in the Forum and the haruspices declared that the gods demanded that one of the courageous citizens whom Rome held dear should cast himself in and it would be closed; Marcus Curtius fully armed mounted his horse and plunged into the abyss (cf. Liv. vii 6); (3) the lacus was simply a puteal erected by the consul C. Curtius (445 в.C.) round a spot in the Forum struck by a thunder-bolt. Whatever the origin of the name, the place was surrounded by some kind of an ornamental structure, and altars were raised in the centre; cf. Ov. F. vi 397, Curtius ille lacus, siccas qui sustinet aras, nunc solida est tellus, sed lacus ante fuit. Every year, on the anniversary of the birth of Augustus, people of all classes came and cast in a small votive coin for the safety of the emperor; cf. Suet. Aug. 57, 1, Omnes ordines in lacum Curtii quotannis ex voto pro salute eius stipem iaciebant. As the lacus was connected with the underworld, these coins were probably offerings to the gods below; see Wissowa, Religion und Kultus der Römer² 235.

: "quia, ut reperi in commentariis Graecorum, adstiterit illi canis, quo vivo caput Galbae amputari non potuerit. Historia id sit, an fabula, nihil pronuntio.” (Casaubon.) What commentarii Graecorum" Casaubon is referring to I have not been able to ascertain. •

: Plutarch (Galb. 27) mentions those who were variously reported to have slain Galba, viz. Camurius (of the 15th legion), Terentius, Laecanius, and Fabius Fabullus, the last named being said to have also cut off his head and carried it away: οἱ δὲ (λέγουσι) Φάβιον Φάβουλον, ὃν καί φασιν ἀποκόψαντα τὴν κεφαλὴν κομίζειν τῷ ἱματίῳ συλλαβόντα διὰ τὴν ψιλότητα (calvitiem) δυσπερίληπτον οὖσαν· ἔπειτα τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ κρύπτειν οὐκ ἐώντων, ἀλλ᾿ ἐμφανῆ πᾶσιν ποιεῖν τὴν ἀνδραγαθίαν, περιπείραντα περὶ λόγχην καὶ ἀναπήλαντα... δρόμῳ χωρεῖν, ὥσπερ αἱ βάκχαι, πολλάκις μεταστρεφόμενον καὶ κραδαίνοντα τὴν λόγχην αἵματι καταρρεομένην. Tacitus (H. i 41, quoted above on “iugulatus est'") mentions Terentius, Laecanius, and Camurius, but not Fabius Fabullus. Groag (in Pauly-Wissowa vi 1769) infers (1) that Plutarch does not reproduce his original quite accurately; (2) that Fabius Fabullus was the gregarius miles who cut off Galba's head; (3) that he was not one of those who actually slew Galba, and so is not included by Tacitus among the reputed percussores.

: these unpleasant details are given even more fully by Suetonius than by Plutarch (l.c.); Tacitus omits them; presumably they were given by the common authority (most probably Pliny the Elder, see Introd. c. iii) followed by the three writers.

: Otho, according to Plut. (l.c.), when Galba's head was brought, said "This is nothing, my fellow-soldiers; show me the head of Piso” (“ οὐδέν ἐστι τοῦτο, ὦ συστρατιῶται, τὴν Πείσωνός μοι κεφαλὴν δείξατε"). The head of Piso, who had been adopted as son and successor by Galba, was shortly afterwards brought to him. Otho's ghoulish joy at seeing the head of Piso is described in Tac. H. i 44.

: Tac., c. 49, caput per lixas calonesque suffixum. "lixae” are defined by Festus as "qui exercitum sequuntur quaestus gratia"; they formed no part of the army (extra ordinem sunt militiae), but supplied the soldiers with supplementary provisions, etc., and so corresponded to sutlers or vivandiers. "Calones" were servants of the soldiers, discharging various menial duties; they were slaves, while lixae’” were freeborn or, more rarely, freedmen. ..

: Dio lxiv 6, καὶ τά τε ἄλλα τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ ἐλυμήναντο, καὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀποκόψαντες περὶ κοντὸν ἀνέπειραν: Tac. c. 44, praefixa contis capita (of Galba and Piso) gestabantur inter signa cohortium iuxta aquilam legionis, certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere, qui falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus iactabant. Such outrageous treatment of fallen foes was common in antiquity; cf. Justin xxiv 5 (describing the fate of Ptolemaeus Ceraunus, king of Macedon, slain by the Gauls c. 280 в.с.), Ptolemaeus multis vulneribus saucius capitur; caput eius amputatum, et lancea fixum, tota acie ad terrorem hostium circumfertur.
: the variant cupide (GX) is much less forcible..

: cf. Sen. Phaedr. 446, aetate fruere: mobili cursu fugit; Liv. xxvi 50, 5, frui ludo aetatis; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, multa eius in stipendiis damna proferentur, quae ab isto aetatis fructu dissoluta et compensata sunt. The use of aetas in the sense of adulescentia, iuventus, ὥρα, is fairly frequent, e.g. Cic. Off. ii 13, 45, tua aetas incidit in id bellum; Hor. Ep. i 20, 10, carus eris Romae donec te deserat aetas. So too the diminutive aetatula, Suet. Claud. 16, 1, invenem corruptelis adulteriisque famosum nihil amplius quam monuit ut aut parcius aetatulae indulgeret aut certe cautius. ..

: for the subject-clause expressing the report that had got out cf. Nep. Dat. 6, si in turbam exisset, ab homine tam necessario se relictum. Suetonius has an object-clause with “exiit opinio” in Ner. 53, exiit opinio descensurum eum ad Olympia inter athletas. ἔτι . . ἐστιν : words used by Diomedes (Il. v 254) and by Odysseus (Od. xxi 426).

: Tac. H. i 49, caput ante Patrobii tumulum (libertus is Neronis punitus a Galba fuerat) postera demum die repertum.. Tacitus (ii 95) couples him with Polyclitus as among the most hated of Nero's freedmen: nondum quartus a victoria mensis, et libertus Vitelli Asiaticus Polyclitos Patrobios et vetera odiorum nomina aequabat. Dio (lxiv 3) describes how, when Galba became emperor, Patrobius was punished along with Narcissus, Locusta, and others by being led in chains through the city and then put to death. The cognomen ‘“Neronianus” denotes a freedman of Nero.

: the aureus (sc. denarius), as standardised by Augustus, was equivalent to 25 silver denarii or 100 sestertii. It was a little heavier than a sovereign and in relation to English gold would be worth about a guinea. For the subsequent fluctuations in its weight (and value) see Mattingly, Roman Coins 123 sqq.

: Plutarch (Galb. 28) says that the head of Galba was given to the slaves of Patrobius; the head of Vinius was sold to his daughter for 2500 drachmae (= 10,000 sestertii); that of Piso was given to his wife Verania at her entreaty. Cf. Tac. i 47, Pisonem Verania uxor ac frater Scribonianus, Titum Vinium Crispina filia composuere, quaesitis redemptisque capitibus, quae venalia interfectores servaverant. Tacitus says nothing of the sale of Galba's head.

: apparently near the building called "Sessorium"; cf. Plut. 1.c., λαβόντες δ' ἐκεῖνοι (i.e. the slaves of Patrobius) καὶ πάντα τρόπον αἰκισάμενοι καὶ καθυβρίσαντες ἔρριψαν ᾗ τοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν Καισάρων κολαζομένους θανατοῦσιν. ὁ δὲ τόπος Σεσσώριον (so Bekker, Σηστέρτιον MSS.) καλεῖται. The meaning and derivation of "Sessorium" are very obscure; see Jordan-Huelsen Topogr. Rom i 3, 250, Hardy on Plut. l.c. A place of execution outside the Esquiline gate is mentioned in Tac. A. ii 32, extra portam Esquilinam more prisco advertere: Suet. Claud. 25, civitatem Romanam usurpantes in campo Esquilino securi percussit: Comm. Cruq. on Hor. S. i 8, 11, in Esquiliis publicis sepulti sunt extra portam in qua est Sessorium: Epod. 5, 100, Esquilina porta Romae dicitur, ubi certus erat locus sepulcrorum ad corpora pauperum aut sceleratorum viliumque comburenda aut canibus proicienda. Platner and Ashby (Topogr. Dict. Rome p. 488) point out, with reference to these statements of Cruquius, that the "Sessorium" was at least 1400 metres from the Esquiline gate. .. on ubi animadversum acting in accordance with the ancient belief that the vengeance which brought most comfort to the slain was that his slayer should be slain either at the same spot or at the tomb of his victim; cf. Soph. El. 1494: Val. Max. ix 2, 2: Flor. iii 21, 26: Sen. Troad. 1152: Curt. vii 5, 43: Justin xi 2, 1.
: the freedman of Patrobius was

: Tac. H. i 49, Caibae corpus diu neglectum, et licentia tencbrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum, dispensator Argius (= ᾿Αργεῖος, Plut.), e prioribus servis, humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis contexit; caput postera demum die repertum et cremato iam corpori admixtum est. Plutarch (c. 28) says that Argeius was a freedman of Galba's; that he buried the body by night; and that the body, in the first instance, was lifted up and carried away by Helvidius Priscus, with Otho's permission. For Helvidius Priscus see on Dom. 10, 3.
: the use of the sing. ceterus, which is rare in class. Lat. (5 exx. in Cic.), occurs 8 times in Suetonius. •
: cf. Eutrop. vii 16, iugulatus (Galba) in foro Romae sepultusque in hortis suis, qui sunt Aurelia via non longe ab urbe Roma.

: this road, dating at least from the second cent. B.C., led northwards from Rome; it touched the sea at Alsium in Etruria, and then ran along the coast of Etruria up to Pisa; the name was extended to the continuation of this road from Pisa to Arelate (Arles) in Gaul.

: 'iusta statura aestimatione Romana senûm pedum circiter fuit" (Casaubon). The Roman pes = 11.65 inches. In Liv. vii 10 we find the expression "media militaris statura," which is to be explained in the light of Veget. Mil. i 5, proceritatem tironum scio semper exactam ita ut senos pedes, vel certe quinos et denas uncias habentes inter alares equites, vel in primis legionum cohortibus probarentur. The "statura” of the other Caesars is thus described by Suetonius: -Julius, “excelsa''; Augustus, "brevis”; Tiberius, "quae iustam excederet"; Caligula, “eminens”; Nero, “prope iusta"; Otho, "modica"; Vespasian, "quadrata"; Titus, "non procera"; Domitian, “procera." The abl. of quality is usual in these descriptions, but the gen. is found in Oth. 12, 1.

: cf. c. 20, 2; Plut. Galb. 13, ἐπισκώπτων τὴν φαλακρότητα ("baldness") καὶ ῥυσότητα (“wrinkledness'") τοῦ Γάλβα. The compound praecalvus (found only here) most probably means "very bald” (valde calvus), though some explain it as 'bald in front.” Other compounds with intensive prae- used by Suetonius are praeclarus, praecupidus, praedives, praedurus, praeferox, praegrandis, praelautus, praepinguis, praetrepidus, praevalidus. He also has praeacutus sharp-pointed,” praemortuus “prematurely dead." The epithet praecanus which Horace applies to himself (Ep. i 20, 24) may mean "very grey," "grey before his time," or "grey in front" (see Wilkins ad loc.).

: similar descriptions are given in Iul. 45, nigris vegetisque oculis fuit; Aug. 79, oculos habuit claros ac nitidos, quibus etiam existimari volebat inesse quiddam divini vigoris; Tib. 68, cum praegrandibus oculis et qui, quod mirum esset, noctu etiam et in tenebris viderent, sed ad breve et cum primum e somno patuissent: deinde rursus hebescebant; Calig. 50, oculis et temporibus (“temples") concavis fuit; Ner. 51, oculis caesiis ("bluish-grey'") et hebetioribus fuit; Dom. 18, grandibus oculis, verum acie hebetiore fuit.

: to judge from his coins and busts (e.g. that in the Capitoline Museum) Galba had a very pronounced aquiline or hooked nose, and that presumably is the meaning here, though aduncus nasus is always explained as a "turned-up nose" in Hor. S. i 6, 5, naso suspendis adunco (cf. Pers. i 40, nimis uncis Naribus indulges), and in Ter. Heaut. 1062, virginem sparso ore, adunco naso. Suetonius describes the aquiline nose of Augustus, Aug. 79, habuit nasum et a summo eminentiorem et ab imo deductiorem (“bent inwards" i.e. a “Roman" nose).

: arthritis, inflammation of the joints due to gout in the hands or feet (cheragra, podagra); cf. Scrib. Larg. 101, ad articularem morbum quem ἀρθρίτιν vocant: Hor. S. ii 7, 15, iusta cheragra Contudit articulos: Pers. v 58, cum lapidosa cheragra Fregerit articulos: Plin. N.H. xx 195, anesum lenit articulares morbos (in Ser. Samm. 695 sqq. a number of cures for articularis morbus are given). The emperor Septimius Severus was crippled by this disease: Spart. Sept. Sev. 16, 6, quod consistere in curru adfectus articulari morbo non posset.
: cf. Apul. Met. v 10, ego vero maritum articulari morbo complicatum curvatumque sustineo, plerumque detortos et duratos in lapidem digitos eius perfricans.

: ἀναπτύσσειν, ἀνελίττειν, to unroll, to open for reading; cf. Aug. 89, 2, in evolvendis (= legendis) utriusque linguae auctoribus: Cic. Tusc. i 12, 24, evolvo diligenter eius eum librum, qui est de animo: Hor. S. i 3, 112, fastos evolvere mundi. =
: valere c. inf. is a poetical construction; Livy is the first prose writer to use it, and he has it only once (xxxviii 23, 4); Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 647.
: for the comparative see on ‘‘sinisteriore,” Dom. 17, 1.
: there is a variant gibbus, for which see on Dom. 23, 2.
: cf. Dom. 17, 1; Ov. A.A. iii 274, inflatum circa fascia pectus eat; Capit. Anton. Pius c. 13, tiliaceis tabulis in pectore positis fasciabatur, ut rectus incederet.

: cf. Aug. 76, 1, cibi minimi erat: Cic. Fam. ix 26, 4, non multi cibi hospitem accipies, multi ioci: Hor. C. i 36, 13, multi Damalis meri: iii 9, 7, multi Lydia nominis: Cic. Rosc. Am. 6, plurimarum palmarum gladiator: Cic. Att. xiii 28, Cornificia multarum nuptiarum. The descriptive genitive was preferred by Latin writers to express Greek compounds like πολυφάγος, πολυπότης, πολυώνυμος, πολυστεφής, πολύγαμος; in popular Latin we find compounds, e.g. multibibus (Plaut.), multiscius (Apul.).
: sc. fuisse; cf. Caes. B.G. v 6, quod eum magni animi, magnae inter Gallos auctoritatis cognoverat.
: vero is used intensively, with a special emphasis on the preceding word.
: sc. cibi. This is Graevius' correction for abundanti or abundans. In the Milan ed. of 1475 the reading is abundantem; Gruter suggested abundanter; Guyetus abutens (with subter for super). =

: a most obscure passage, which may mean that Galba ordered the leavings of the huge portions served to him to be carried round in handfuls and distributed (spargi dividi) among the servi a pedibus. It was customary to give the attendants what was left when dinner was over; cf. Sen. Ep. 77, 8, Marcellinum admonuit non esse inhumanum, quemadmodum cena peracta reliquiae circumstantibus dividuntur, sic peracta vita aliquid porrigi his qui totius vitae ministri fuissent: Plut. Quaest. Rom. 64. Hofstee and Rolfe follow Baumg.-Cr. in explaining super manus as = ante se (in mensa). Baumg.. Cr. is peculiar in taking stantibus as dat. of the agent, his interpretation being as follows:-‘“Inter cenam usque eo abundantis cibi fuit, ut congestas super manus, h.e. ante se, ante locum ubi sumserat cibum, reliquias circumferri iuberet, scil. circum mensam et convivas, ostentandi causa, quantum fauces et venter valerent, spargique (quod dicitur de rebus solidis, ut fundi de fluidis), sive in unum locum colligi, ad admirationem convivarum, et ut ipse acto labore delectaretur, ad pedes stantibus, h.e. a servis, ad lectum sive pedes ministrantibus, dativo, ut saepius, posito pro ablativo cum praepositione “a”, adeoque hoc loco, ne auris offenderetur excipientibus se verbis ab ad pedes stantibus.” D. C. Grimm (Dissert. on Galb. c. 22, Leipzig 1798) took super manus as = per manus and altered circumferri to circum se ferri, thinking that Galba was so gluttonous that he had the remains left by each diner passed along from hand to hand and set before him, and then having satisfied his appetite he gave anything that was over to the attendants. Stahr also takes super manus as = per manus, but interprets the passage differently:- "Bei Tafel nun gar häufte er eine solche Masse Speisen vor sich auf, dass er die Reste derselben von Hand zu Hand umherreichen und (zuletzt) unter die aufwartende Dienerschaft verteilen liess." The difficulty in extracting any satisfactory meaning makes it highly probable that the text is unsound.

: slaves who stood behind the diners as they reclined on couches at table; cf. Sen. Ben. iii 27, servus qui cenanti ad pedes steterat: Petron. Satyr. 58, Giton, qui ad pedes stabat. Caligula loved to humiliate senators by making them act in this capacity: Calig. 26, 2, quosdam summis honoribus functos . sibi cenanti modo ad pluteum modo ad pedes stare succinctos linteo passus est. For these servi a pedibus see Marquardt, Privatl.2 148, 322. Such slaves might be provided by the host (Daremberg-Saglio, iv 1276 n.), but at ordinary private dinner-parties they usually came with their masters, took charge of their shoes (soleae), stood behind them during dinner, and carried home any presents (apophoreta) made by the host to their masters. ..

: a very rare constr.; cf. Luc. i 461, ruendi mens prona viris: Claud. Ruf. ii 400, pronior audendi. Suetonius also uses pronus with the dat., with ad, and with in. R. Stephanus conjectured libidinis pronioris; Torrentius libidini . pronior; Boxhorn libidinibus pronior. In the Augustan poets and in later prose (isolated instances in old Lat. but not in class. Lat.) the genitive is used with a great number of adjectives of the most varied signification in order to define the sphere or respect in which the adj. is applicable; see the list in Kühner-Stegmann, i 443 sq. Suetonius has the gen. with certus, parcus, tenax, etc.; see Appendix I. § 3. B. g.
: contrast Claud. 33, 2, libidinis in feminas profusissimae, marum omnino expers.

: "well hardened", poetical and in late prose; cf. Verg. Aen. x 748, homo praedurus viribus: id. G. ii 531, corporaque agresti nudant praedura palaestrae: Columell. vi 2, 1, praedura aetas (opp. to tenera aetas). See on praecalvus, c. 21. exoletus: Festus defines exoletus as "qui adolescere, id est crescere, desiit.'' The word was used in the special sense of “adolescens alienae libidini inserviens”; cf. Tit. 7, 1: Calig. 24, 3: Tib. 43, 1: Iul. 49, 2: 76, 3: Tac. A. xv 37: Cic. Mil. 21, ille qui semper secum scorta, semper exoletos, semper lupas duceret. Suetonius also uses exoletus simply in the sense of obsoletus; see Galb. 4, 4 (n.): Aug. 86, 2: Claud. 22.
: see on c. 14, 2.
: for concubinus (= delicatus, a favourite slave) see R. Ellis on Catull. lxi 121-123, Nec nuces pueris neget Desertum domini audiens Concubinus amorem.

: Plutarch (Galb. 7) describes the arrival of Icelus in Spain bearing to Galba the news of Nero's death: Ἦν δὲ θέρος ἤδη, καὶ βραχὺ πρὸ δείλης ἧκεν ἀπὸ ῾Ρώμης Ικελος ἀνὴρ ἀπελεύθερος ἑβδομαῖος (i.e. in 6 days). Πυθόμενος δὲ τὸν Γάλβαν ἀναπαύεσθαι καθ' ἑαυτὸν ἐβάδιζε συντόνως ἐπὶ τὸ δωμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ βίᾳ τῶν θαλαμηπόλων (cubiculariorum) ἀνοίξας καὶ παρελθὼν ἀπήγγειλεν, κ.τ.λ.
: cf. Apul. Met. ii 13, eum amplexus exosculatur .. artissime. ..

: this use of sed for sed etiam occurs also in Tit. 7, 2, Aug. 88, Claud. 16, 2; the second clause in every case being stronger than the first. In Cicero when non modo is followed by sed, the second clause may be either stronger or weaker. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii '60.

: cf. Iul. 45, circa corporis curam morosior, ut non solum tonderetur diligenter ac raderetur, sed velleretur etiam, ut quidam exprobraverunt: Quintil. ii 5, 12, vulsi levatique et inustas comas acu comentes. Mayor (on Juv. viii 16 and 114, xi 157) has collected a number of passages on this practice and the contempt in which in it was held by Romans of the old type.

: cf. [Aurel. Vict.] Epit. 6, cum septuagesimum tertium aetatis annum ageret caesus est: Tac. H. i 49, hunc exitum habuit Servius Galba, tribus et septuaginta annis quinque principes (i.e. Aug., Tib., Calig., Claud., Ner.) prospera fortuna emensus et alieno imperio felicior quam suo: Dio (Xiphilinus) Ixiv 6, ἔζησε δὲ Γάλβας ἔτη δύο καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα (Zonaras adds καὶ ἡμέρας τρεῖς καὶ εἴκοσιν). Thus, according to Dio (Zonaras), Galba must have been born on Dec. 24, 5 B.C., for he died on Jan. 15, 69 A.D. It is impossible to reconcile Suetonius' statement here that Galba was in his 73rd year at the time of his death with the statement in c. 4 supr. that he was born on Dec. 24, 3 B.C., in which case he would only have been in his 71st year when he died. We must assume therefore that Suetonius has made a slip with regard to the year of Galba's birth which was 5 B.C. and not 3 B.C. further complication, however, arises from the fact that both Plutarch (Galb. 8) and Eutropius (vii 16) say that Galba was in his 73rd year when he became emperor in June 68 A.D. (and so must have been born in 6 B.C.); their statement is supported by what Suetonius tells us in Ner. 40 about the warning of the Delphic oracle to Nero to beware of the 73rd year; Nero understood this to mean that he would live to be 73, and never took into account Galba's age. For other chronological inconsistencies in Suetonius see on Oth. 11, 2; Vitell. 18; Tit. 11. A
: he reigned from June 9, '68 A.D. (the date of Nero's death) to Jan. 15, 69; cf. Eutrop. vii 16, insidiis Othonis occisus

: [Aurel. Vict.] Epit. 6, imperavit menses septem diesque totidem: Joseph. Bell. Iud. iv 9, 2, φθάνει Γάλβας ἀναιρεθεὶς μετὰ μῆνας ἑπτὰ καὶ ἴσας ἡμέρας: Tac. H. i 37 (Otho addressing the soldiers just before the murder of Galba), septem a Neronis fine menses sunt, etc. Dio (Xiph. Zon.), lxiv 6, says he reigned nine months and thirteen days (ἦρξε μῆνας ἐννέα καὶ ἡμέρας δεκατρεῖς), counting from the 2nd of April, 68 A.D., when he was proclaimed emperor by the soldiers in Spain (cf. c. 10, 1).

: this may have been, as Hofstee suggests, after the defeat of Otho by the Flavianists. When Antonius Primus, Vespasian's general, advanced from Pannonia into upper Italy, he ordered the images of Galba to be set up again in all the towns; Tac. H. iii 7, Desiderata. diu res interpretatione gloriaque in maius accipitur, postquam Galbae imagines discordia temporum subversas in omnibus municipiis recoli iussit Antonius, decorum pro causa (Flaviana) ratus, si placere Galbae principatus et partes revirescere crederentur. The decree which Suetonius mentions may have been passed between the occupation of Rome by the Flavian forces (about Dec. 20, 69 A.D.) and the arrival of Vespasian in person at Rome in the summer of 70.

: in 158 B.C. the censors ordered the removal of all statues from the Forum and Capitol unless they had been decreed by the people or by the senate. The right of granting them came to be confined to the senate, but the restriction was often evaded, and Claudius had to issue an edict that no statue was to be erected at Rome without the order of the senate unless by an individual who had built or restored some public building (Dio lx 25). We read of the emperor's sanction being obtained for the erection of a statue, e.g. Plin. Ep. i 17, Titinius Capito ab imperatore nostro (i.e. Trajan) impetravit ut sibi liceret statuam L. Silani in foro ponere; but the emperors did not directly authorize the erection, they asked the senate to decree the honour; cf. Capitol. Marc. c. 2, cui (Frontoni) et statuam in senatu petiit: c. 3, cui (Iunio Rustico) post obitum a senatu statuas postulavit. See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 1184 sqq. The most famous of the monuments decreed by the senate to Roman emperors was the Column of Trajan.

: columns adorned with the beaks (rostra) of ships were erected at Rome originally to celebrate naval victories, the best known being that in honour of C. Duilius for his defeat of the Carthaginians in 260 в.с. A columna rostrata formed the support of a triumphal statue decreed by the senate to Octavius in celebration of his naval victory over Sextus Pompeius at Naulochus in 36 в.с.; cf. Appian Bell. Civ. v 130, καὶ ἐπινίκιος ἐν ἀγορᾷ (Foro) χρύσεος ἑστάναι μετὰ σχήματος οὗπερ ἔχων ἐσῆλθε, περικειμένων τῷ κίονι νεῶν ἐμβολῶν (rostrorum): Servius on Verg. G. iii 29, navali surgentes aere columnas. Statues on a columna rostrata are depicted not only on coins of Augustus but also on those of Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian (Eckhel vii p. 85; Cohen i pp. 82, 396).

p.mentioned: in parte Fori qua trucidatus est
p.note: : i.e. beside the lacus Curtius, see c. 20. The people paid honours to the same spot in their exultation at Otho's death; cf. Tac. H. ii 55, populus cum laura ac floribus Galbae imagines circum templa tulit, congestis in modum tumuli coronis, iuxta lacum Curtii, quem locum Galba moriens sanguine infecerat.

: cf. Claud. 6, 2, quod decretum abolitum est: Tac. A. iii 28, quae triumviratu iusserat abolevit (Augustus): Spart. Sev. 17, 5, Salvii Iuliani decreta iussit aboleri. The verb used of the senate cancelling a decree already passed is inducere (διαγράφειν); e.g. Suet. Iul. 16, inducto priore decreto: Cic. de domo 4, 10, coeptum est referri de inducendo senatus consulto. When the senate of itself or at the direction of the emperor wished to cancel a decree already completed and registered (ad aerarium delatum), some one moved a resolution “ut senatusconsultum antea factum induceretur, tabulaque in qua perscriptum erat deleretur.” See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 1014.

: if the allegation is true (no other author mentions it), Galba was trying to remove a dangerous rival who was in command of a large army in Judaea (see Vesp. 4, 5), and he was using the same means as Nero had adopted to try to remove Galba himself when governor of Hispania Tarraconensis (see Galb. 9, 2).
